## What is being built

The smallest robust Controller that can safely supervise Workflow-driven
work in a managed repository, and that is strong enough to become the outer
orchestrator for subsequent Controller generations.

```
Workflow  ->  Workflow Manager / Bootstrapper  ->  Workflow Controller  ->  managed development repositories
```

The Controller **automates operation of** the Workflow. It never replaces
Workflow lifecycle semantics (which stay owned by the Workflow's own
commands and `WORKFLOW_STATE.json`) and never replaces Workflow Manager
responsibilities (install/update/verify/drift). The four layers stay
separate: Workflow owns legal lifecycle states and transitions, Workflow
Manager owns distribution/install/update/verify, the Controller owns
orchestration and job execution, and Claude workers own bounded reasoning
and execution.

Two structural consequences run through every checkpoint below:

1. **The Controller is a reader of Workflow state and a launcher of
   workers. It is never a writer of Workflow state.** Every durable
   Workflow lifecycle change in this design is made by a *worker* running a
   real Workflow command in the target repository — never by the Controller
   editing `WORKFLOW_STATE.json`. This is enforced mechanically (CP1's
   `runtime.write_json` refuses any destination outside the Controller's own
   runtime root; CP3's reader module exposes no write function at all), not
   only by convention.
2. **The Controller never crosses a human gate.** Under the revision-64
   baseline (frozen Workflow **2.5.1**, see "Supported Workflow baseline"
   below) **four** command files are user-only: `/approve-review`,
   `/accept-milestone` and `/request-plan-amendment` carry
   `disable-model-invocation: true`, and `/approve-review`,
   `/accept-milestone` and `/recover-implementation-provenance` carry a
   qualified `workflow_state.validate_…confirmation` guard — two
   overlapping but no longer nested populations, whose **union** is the
   denylist (CP4's *Deriving `USER_ONLY_COMMANDS`* section states the rule
   and the run). Only the user may invoke any of them. The Controller
   treats the four as a hard denylist enforced at two independent layers
   (CP4's decision engine never selects them; CP5's worker refuses to
   execute a task naming one), and never writes or requests a
   `USER_OVERRIDE`.

## Scope reassessment (revision 10) — what Generation 1 automates, and why

Revisions 1–9 went through nine fresh local plan-review rounds and never
reached `APPROVE`. Every round confirmed the four-layer architecture and
both structural invariants; every round also found new Blocking defects,
and all of them lived in one place: the *automatic* execution of
implementation- and functional-stage Workflow commands, and the
`ExpectedOutcome` machinery built to verify those executions. Rounds 7, 8
and 9 each found that the **previous revision's structural fix was itself
unsound** — a property that could not be written, then data the properties
could not check, then a property that would have passed the defect that
prompted it.

Round 9 named the reason, and it is not a defect in any one row:

> Every property compares one of the plan's own tables against another of
> its own tables, or against a command file *the table itself chose to
> cite*. **Nothing enumerates what frozen v2.3.1 actually ships.**

That is why `/recover-implementation-provenance` — the fifteenth command
file of the v2.3.1 surface as it stood at revision 10, which carries a
literal user-confirmation gate and whose sole legal source phase sits
inside CP4's own disambiguation — stayed invisible across nine rounds and
six properties. (Seventeen command files ship under the revision-64
baseline; the figure in this sentence is revision 10's own measurement and
is time-labelled rather than restated, per the historical-provenance
policy below.)

**Revision 10 is the architectural reassessment that finding requires**, and
it takes the honest option: *narrow what Generation 1 automates to the
surface that can be specified correctly, and report gates everywhere else.*

### The rule

**Generation 1 executes automatic actions at the plan-stage phases only.
At every other phase it observes, decides, and reports — it never launches
a worker.**

| Phase group | Generation 1 behaviour |
|---|---|
| `PLANNING`, `REVISING_PLAN` | **automatic, unconditionally** — decide, launch a fresh worker, verify the transition |
| `AWAITING_LOCAL_PLAN_REVIEW` | **automatic in the ordinary case**, with two non-automatic sub-cases: a current-round `Status: BLOCK` verdict (a human resolves it first) and a withdrawn bundle (`REJECTED` marker present) |
| `AWAITING_MANUAL_EXTERNAL_PLAN_REVIEW`, `AWAITING_EXTERNAL_PLAN_REVIEW` (`"1"`) | **automatic only once the human's artifact has arrived** — until an external reviewer's verdict is on file these are gates, and the Controller reports them as such |
| `AWAITING_PLAN_APPROVAL` | report the user-only gate (unchanged) |
| `IMPLEMENTING`, `SELF_REVIEWING_IMPLEMENTATION`, `AWAITING_EXTERNAL_IMPLEMENTATION_REVIEW`, `APPLYING_REVIEW_FEEDBACK`, `AWAITING_FUNCTIONAL_REVIEW` | **report only** — name the next action and who must run it; launch nothing |
| `LEGACY_READY`, `MILESTONE_COMPLETE`, the four vocabulary phases | unchanged |

### Why this converges where revisions 1–9 did not

The defects rounds 4–9 found were not distributed evenly. Every one of them
was a property of the *implementation- and functional-stage* commands:

- `MANIFEST.md` is written **unconditionally** at the plan stage
  (`prepare-ai-review.sh:581-584`) and only on an optional argument at the
  implementation/post-fix stages. Round 7's B1, round 8's B2 and round 9's
  I2 are all consequences of that one asymmetry, and none of them exists at
  the plan stage.
- `/apply-functional-review`'s broad branch creates durable remediation
  children with no idempotency (round 7's B2) — the only finding in nine
  rounds that damaged a target repository rather than a report. No
  plan-stage command creates a work item.
- `/apply-implementation-review`'s preamble writes `APPLYING_REVIEW_FEEDBACK`
  before any work (round 5's B2, round 8's B1), and no command can run from
  that phase. No plan-stage command has an entry-write preamble;
  `apply-plan-review.md` was verified across the whole file to have none.
- `/milestone-implement` is a partial-progress command whose ordinary
  outcome is its own pre-phase (round 6's I2). No plan-stage command is.

Removing five automatic rows leaves **six**. The eleven-row table had six
predicate-bearing rows (3, 5, 7, 8, 9 and 11); the narrowing removed
**four** of them — and with them the entire class of "is this predicate a
completion signal" reasoning that rounds 5–9 could not settle. **Two
predicate-bearing rows survived the narrowing, so four of the six needed
no predicate at all** — revision 10's own figures, over the six-row table
that narrowing produced. The live table has carried **seven** rows and
**three** predicates since revision 63 added row 7; CP6B's own
`ExpectedOutcome` section states the current figures and is the authority
for them.

### What this does not give up

The milestone brief names **ten** required capabilities
(`docs/ACTIVE_MILESTONE.md`, "Required capabilities"). Revision 10's audit
covered seven of them and renamed one; revision 11 reproduces all ten with
the brief's own numbering and wording (round 10's I3), because a
completeness check that covers seven of ten is not one.

| # | Brief's capability | Still proven under the narrowing? |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Managed repository inspection | **yes** — phase-independent, unchanged (CP2) |
| 2 | Workflow state reader | **yes** — all twenty phases, unchanged in mechanism (CP3; seventeen at revision 10, twenty under the revision-64 2.5.1 baseline) |
| 3 | Next-action decision engine | **yes, at all twenty phases.** Reporting an action a human or a later generation must run *is* a decision, and it is what capability 6 depends on |
| 4 | Fresh worker orchestration | **yes** — four distinct commands, of which `/review-plan` and `/apply-plan-review` form the unbounded plan-revision loop itself, with no human in it |
| 5 | **Real Workflow-action execution** (disposable-repository proof) | **yes** — `/milestone-plan` was already the chosen genuine operation and is a plan-stage action, so `REQ-T18` is untouched |
| 6 | Human-gate detection | **yes**, and better for the three phases whose classification kept coming out wrong — with the `DECLINED` outcome added so the two automation-safe phases are not miscalled gates |
| 7 | Durable resume | **yes** — unchanged (CP7) |
| 8 | Failure handling | **yes** — phase-independent; every refusal, worker-outcome and transition-verification path is unchanged (CP2/CP3/CP5/CP6B/CP7) |
| 9 | Generation handoff primitive | **yes** — phase-independent, unchanged (CP8) |
| 10 | Minimal CLI | **yes** — unchanged (CP9), plus the two new exit codes |

Revision 10's table listed "durable job records" as capability 5. That is
not the brief's capability 5, which is the disposable-repository proof —
and it is the single capability most worth re-checking under a narrowing,
since it demands a *genuine* Workflow operation through a worker. It
survives, for the reason in the table.

### What the Controller actually runs autonomously

Stated precisely, because revision 10 overclaimed it and revision 11's
correction was itself imprecise (rounds 10 I2, 11 O1). The **plan-revision
loop** is a **two**-command cycle, repeating without bound and with no human
in it:

```
AWAITING_LOCAL_PLAN_REVIEW --/review-plan--> REVISING_PLAN
        ^                                          |
        +-------------/apply-plan-review-----------+
```

`/milestone-plan` runs once to enter it and `/record-manual-plan-review`
once to leave it, so worker orchestration is exercised across **four
distinct commands**, two of them unboundedly. That is the cycle this work
item has itself executed seventy times.

The Controller **cannot** drive a milestone all the way from `PLANNING` to
`AWAITING_PLAN_APPROVAL`: a `"2.1"` item must stop at
`AWAITING_MANUAL_EXTERNAL_PLAN_REVIEW` for a human to fetch an external
review, and a `"1"` item at `AWAITING_EXTERNAL_PLAN_REVIEW`. Revision 10
claimed otherwise and the claim did not survive reading the next table
down. The loop claim is both true and stronger — and `/review-plan` is
itself a command whose own contract asks for a fresh independent session,
which is exactly what a `claude -p` worker is.

### The property that closes the class

Round 9's rule, stated once here and enforced in CP4:

> **A table derived from an external artifact needs one property that
> enumerates the external artifact, not the table.**

The plan already contains one working instance — CP3's two-directional
`KNOWN_PHASES` set-equality against a hand-copied literal, *"the test is
what keeps the copy honest"*, which is what caught `LEGACY_READY` in round
1. Revision 10 adds the same shape over `.claude/commands/`: enumerate
**every** command file — seventeen under the revision-64 baseline — and
assert the partition into **selected**, **deliberately-not-selected** and
**user-only** is *total*. A Workflow release that adds an eighteenth
command fails the suite rather than shipping an unmodelled command to a
user. That property is what would have caught round 9's B1 mechanically,
nine rounds earlier — **and it is what the 2.3.1 → 2.5.1 Manager update
actually exercised**: the two command files and three phases 2.5.x adds
are exactly the drift both two-directional properties exist to surface
loudly, which is how round 63's `B6` was found rather than shipped.

Workflow Manager updated this repository from 2.3.1 to 2.5.1 mid-flight
and round 63's `B6` found the table describing a release that is no longer
installed. A row that records a *past* measurement against a release that
is no longer installed is time-labelled rather than deleted, per the
historical-disposition provenance policy below; a row that states a fact
the Controller's own gates read is re-measured and restated:

| Fact | How it was verified | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| `workflow-manager` is a real installed CLI with `status`/`verify`/`bootstrap`/`update`/`uninstall`/`releases` subcommands | `workflow-manager --help`, re-run at revision 64 | CP2 integrates with it rather than reimplementing drift semantics |
| The Manager's `distribution/` currently carries **four** releases — `2.3.1`, `2.4.0`, `2.5.0` and `2.5.1` — and `bootstrap`/`update` without `--release-version` mean the newest | `workflow-manager releases`, run at revision 64 and **re-run at revision 69** (same four) | a target the Controller is pointed at is, **by default**, on the newest release the Manager holds — which since revision 68 is not the same thing as a release the Controller admits, because admission is exact membership of `VALIDATED_WORKFLOW_RELEASES` rather than of a line. ## Supported Workflow baseline (policy, revision 64; admission narrowed at revision 68)

**Stated once, as a policy with a named authority, rather than as N
counted literals that the next Manager update stales again** — which is
what round 63's `B6` asked for, and what revisions 1–63 did not have.

Between revision 62's approval and revision 63's amendment, the Workflow
Manager updated *this* repository from **2.3.1** to **2.5.1**
(`.workflow-manager/installation.json`, `updated_at:
2026-09-19T12:06:34Z`). `.claude/commands/`, `scripts/` and
`.workflow-manager/` are this work item's declared `excluded_prefixes`, so
that update could never stale an approval — but exclusion is a
*fingerprinting* guarantee and says nothing about whether this document's
normative claims about that content are still true. They were not: the
plan pinned a closed `{("2.3.1", …)}` admission set, a **seventeen**-phase
`KNOWN_PHASES` copy and a **fifteen**-file command partition, against a
live tree carrying twenty phases and seventeen command files. Reproduced
before this section was written: `python3 -m unittest tests.test_target_state
tests.test_decision` over the completed CP1–CP9 build answers **2 failures
and 6 errors**, every one of them this.

**The policy.** Generation 1's supported baseline is a **release line** for
*classification*, but admission itself is gated on a **closed, named set of
individually validated releases** (revision 68 narrows this from the bare
line revision 64 shipped; see "Why the line predicate alone was not
fail-closed" below):

- **`SUPPORTED_WORKFLOW_LINE = "2.5"`** — a manifest's `workflow_version`
  must parse as a dotted release whose **major and minor components are
  exactly `2` and `5`**, or it is refused outright (`2.3.1`, `2.4.0`,
  `2.6.0`, `3.0.0`, and anything that does not parse as a dotted release at
  all). This is a **necessary pre-filter and a diagnostic classifier**,
  never by itself sufficient for admission: it tells a refusal whether the
  observed release is even in the known line before the stronger check
  below ever runs, and it is what lets a refusal say "wrong line" instead
  of "not yet validated".
- **`VALIDATED_WORKFLOW_RELEASES = {"2.5.1"}`** — the actual admission
  gate (revision 68, manual external plan review round 67's `I1`).
  `workflow_version` must be an **exact member** of this closed set, not
  merely a member of the line above. `2.5.1` is its only element because
  it is the only release this document's three inventories and its
  seven-suite baseline-verification table were ever actually measured
  against. A manifest declaring a version that parses into the `2.5` line
  but is not `2.5.1` — including `2.5.0`, a real, currently-distributed
  release, and any later `2.5.x` patch the Manager has not shipped yet —
  is refused with `UnsupportedWorkflowVersionError`, with evidence stating
  explicitly that the release is in the known line but has not been
  individually validated, distinguishing it from a wrong-line refusal.
  Growing this set is a **deliberate act**, never automatic: re-read the
  three inventories and re-run the seven baseline-verification suites
  against the newly-installed release, and add its version string to the
  set by name, in a plan revision that states what was measured — never
  merely because the Workflow Manager reports a version string that parses
  into a supported line.
- **`SUPPORTED_PROFILES = {"runtime", "full"}`** — unchanged in membership
  and unchanged in its justification (both install the identical command
  and tooling surface; the Environment-facts row above is re-measured
  against the installed Manager).
- **`REFERENCE_WORKFLOW_RELEASE = "2.5.1"`** — the one concrete release
  every *inventory* in this document is derived from and re-derivable
  against. Since revision 68 it is also the sole member of
  `VALIDATED_WORKFLOW_RELEASES`, so the derivation pin and the admission
  gate currently name the same release; they remain two different
  mechanisms; a future validated release would extend the latter without
  necessarily moving the former.

**The authority for every inventory is the installed tree, never a count
in this prose.** Three derivations, each with its own named source and its
own two-directional property, all re-run at revision 64:

| Inventory | Authority (read at revision 64) | Value | Property that keeps it honest |
|---|---|---|---|
| the known-phase set | `scripts/workflow_state.py:331-371`, `KNOWN_PHASES` | **twenty** entries | CP3's two-directional set equality against the hand-copied literal |
| the command-file set | every `*.md` under `.claude/commands/` | **seventeen** files | CP4's total-and-disjoint partition over the shipped files |
| the user-only set | the same seventeen files, under the union rule CP4 states | **four** files | CP4's two-directional denylist assertion against a set derived fresh at test time |

**Why the line predicate alone was not fail-closed, and what changed at
revision 68.** Revision 64 argued that admitting the whole `2.5.x` line was
safe because an unmodelled *phase* or *command* — the only two things a
future patch could plausibly add — is already refused or unselectable by
construction, and the two two-directional properties below turn an
inventory mismatch into a loud test failure rather than a field surprise:

- **An unmodelled phase** is refused at CP3's reader with
  `UnknownPhaseError` before CP4 ever sees it — the fail-closed direction,
  and the behaviour that sentence has always promised.
- **An unmodelled command file** can never be *selected*: `decide()`
  returns one of four literal commands, and CP5's independent token scan
  refuses any task naming a user-only one. A file the partition does not
  know is therefore never run, only unclassified.
- **Both** turn into a **loud test failure** at the next release rather
  than a field surprise, because the two properties above are
  two-directional over the shipped artifact. That is precisely what
  happened here: the 2.3.1 → 2.5.1 update made them red, and that redness
  is what round 63's `B6` reports.

That argument is still correct as far as it goes, and revision 68 leaves
it in place. Manual external plan review round 67's `I1` finding is not
that an unmodelled phase or command could slip through — the properties
above still catch that, unchanged. It is that a **modelled** one could
change **underneath its own name**. `KNOWN_PHASES` and the command-file
partition are set-membership checks over *names*; neither property reads
what a same-named phase or command *does* — its preconditions, its
postconditions, the persisted-state writes CP6B and CP7 verify against. A
future `2.5.x` patch that renamed nothing and added nothing, but changed
one already-known command's persisted-state contract, would report the
identical twenty-phase, seventeen-command, four-user-only inventory this
section measures, pass both two-directional properties, and — under the
bare line predicate revision 64 shipped — be admitted silently, because
inventory equality is not semantic equality and the line predicate never
claimed to check the latter. A fourth case belongs alongside the three
above, and it is the one the first three cannot cover by construction:

- **A modelled command or phase whose semantics drift while its name and
  inventory position stay fixed** is refused by `VALIDATED_WORKFLOW_RELEASES`
  membership alone, never by an inventory check — this is the gap the
  two-directional properties structurally cannot see, since they compare
  *names*, and it is what revision 68 closes.

So `VALIDATED_WORKFLOW_RELEASES` is the *admission* rule; `SUPPORTED_WORKFLOW_LINE`
is a *pre-filter and diagnostic classifier*, not a second gate a validated
release must independently clear (every member of `VALIDATED_WORKFLOW_RELEASES`
is, by construction, a member of the `2.5` line); the reference release is
the *derivation* pin; and the two two-directional properties remain what
force a deliberate re-derivation of the inventories at whichever release is
being validated — now the actual mechanism by which a candidate release
earns membership in `VALIDATED_WORKFLOW_RELEASES`, rather than a safety net
under an admission rule that trusted the whole line by default. A closed
`{(version, profile)}` set was the same bargain revision 63 struck, without
the line's diagnostic value and without a stated procedure for growing it;
`VALIDATED_WORKFLOW_RELEASES` keeps that set's fail-closed discipline and
adds both. The operational cost `SUPPORTED_WORKFLOW_LINE` was widened to
avoid — a pinned single release refuses the Manager's own default install
the next time the Manager updates it, which is what round 63's `B6`
reproduced against this very repository — is not undone by this narrowing:
it is now an accepted, intentional cost, paid as a deliberate, recorded
revalidation (a new plan revision that re-measures the three inventories
and the seven baseline-verification suites, per the growth procedure
above) rather than absorbed by trusting an entire line of patches this
document has never measured.

**Governing-version vocabulary under this baseline.** Frozen 2.5.x adds
`governing_workflow_version: "2.2"` and declares
`TWO_STAGE_PLAN_REVIEW_VERSIONS = {"2.1", "2.2"}`
(`scripts/workflow_state.py`). `/apply-plan-review` step 0,
`/milestone-plan` step 0 and `publish_plan_revision`
(`scripts/workflow_state.py:7788-7792`) all take the **identical** branch
for both, and `"2.2"`'s own bump is to the *implementation*-review
protocol, which Generation 1 does not drive at all. **Wherever a
plan-stage row, predicate or `ExpectedOutcome` key in this document is
qualified `"2.1"`, it denotes membership of
`TWO_STAGE_PLAN_REVIEW_VERSIONS`** — `"2.1"` and `"2.2"` alike — and
contributes **one** triple to the coverage bijection, for exactly the
reason the wildcard rule already gives for not materialising a version
that makes no behavioural difference. The `"1"`-qualified rows are
unchanged. No row is added, removed or split by this re-reading; CP4's
mapping and CP6B's `ExpectedOutcome` table both keep the six automatic
triples they had.

## Architecture

### Package layout

| Path | Role |
|---|---|
| `pyproject.toml` | packaging, `requires-python = ">=3.12"`, no runtime dependencies, `workflow-controller` console script |
| `controller/__init__.py` | package marker; exports the public API surface |
| `controller/__main__.py` | `python -m controller` entry point delegating to `cli.main` |
| `controller/errors.py` | the refusal taxonomy — every fail-closed condition is a named exception |
| `controller/runtime.py` | `.controller/` layout, atomic JSON read/write, runtime-root containment guard |
| `controller/identity.py` | the pinned, immutable Controller source identity |
| `controller/managed_repo.py` | capability 1 — Workflow Manager integration and refusals |
| `controller/target_state.py` | capability 2 — read-only reader of the **target** repository's Workflow state |
| `controller/decision.py` | capability 3 — the phase → action mapping, the user-only denylist, the `Decision` shape |
| `controller/evidence.py` | capabilities 3 and 6 — the evidence-reading disambiguations and human-gate classification |
| `controller/worker.py` | capability 4 — fresh Claude worker process |
| `controller/job.py` | capabilities 5, 7, 8 — job records, execution, post-state validation, resume |
| `controller/handoff.py` | capability 9 — generation handoff primitive |
| `controller/cli.py` | capability 10 — the CLI |
| `tests/` | the automated suite (`unittest`), plus `tests/fixtures.py` |
| `.controller/` | Controller-owned runtime state — gitignored, never tracked |

The reader module is named `controller/target_state.py`, **not**
`controller/workflow_state.py`. Revision 1 chose the colliding name and
mitigated it with a module docstring; local plan review round 1 pointed out
that the mitigation is thin and the rename costs nothing before CP3 lands,
so the rename is taken. The two modules would have been unrelated in any
case — `scripts/workflow_state.py` is the Workflow's own state *writer* for
*this* repository, while `controller/target_state.py` is the Controller's
read-only *reader* of a **target** repository's state — but a name that
cannot be confused is better than a docstring explaining a name that can.
They never import one another, and the Controller never adds `scripts/` to
`sys.path`. CP3's module docstring still states the distinction.

### Dependency direction

```
cli -> job -> {managed_repo, target_state, evidence, worker, handoff} -> decision -> {identity, runtime, errors}
```

No module imports one to its left. `errors` imports nothing from the
package. A test asserts this graph (CP1), so a later checkpoint cannot
quietly introduce a cycle.

### Refusal taxonomy (`controller/errors.py`)

All refusals derive from `ControllerError`, which carries a machine-readable
`code`, a human sentence, and an `evidence` mapping. Named subclasses, each
introduced by the checkpoint that needs it:

`NotARepositoryError`, `UnmanagedRepositoryError`,
`MalformedInstallationManifestError`, `WorkflowManagerUnavailableError`,
`DriftedInstallationError`, `UnsupportedWorkflowVersionError` (CP2);
`MissingWorkflowStateError`, `MalformedWorkflowStateError`,
`AmbiguousWorkItemError`, `UnknownPhaseError`,
`MalformedTargetRegistryError` (CP3);
`UnsupportedInstallProfileError` (CP2);
`NoSupportedActionError`, `HumanGateError` (CP4);
`WorkerLaunchError`, `WorkerFailedError`, `WorkerInterruptedError`,
`WorkerAmbiguousResultError`, `UserOnlyCommandError` (CP5);
`TransitionNotObservedError`, `RuntimeContainmentError`,
`RuntimeRootUnwritableError` (CP1/CP6);
`StaleJobRecordError`, `UnreconcilableJobError` (CP7);
`GenerationHandoffPendingError`, `DirtyControllerSourceError`,
`SourceSnapshotError` (CP1/CP8).

Every one of these is a *stop*, never a retry-with-a-guess. `ControllerError`
is the only exception type the CLI catches; anything else propagates as a
crash, because an unexpected exception is not a state the Controller may
reason about.

### Exit codes

The CLI is designed to be driven by an outer supervisor, so its exit codes
are part of its contract and are tested:

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | requested work completed; nothing is pending |
| 2 | CLI usage error (argparse default) |
| 10 | stopped cleanly at a human gate — the normal, expected outcome for a supervised run |
| 15 | **this generation declines an action it can see is automatable** — the phase is automation-safe and a later generation may drive it, but Generation 1 does not |
| 16 | `run` hit `--max-steps` with work still outstanding |
| 20 | fail-closed refusal (`ControllerError`) — unmanaged/drifted repo, malformed state, unsupported phase |
| 30 | a worker ran and failed |
| 35 | a worker ran and stopped without completing its action — it refused for a stated reason, or was cut short — leaving no durable Workflow change to verify |
| 40 | the Controller itself was interrupted, or `resume` reconciled a record to `INTERRUPTED` |
| 50 | a generation handoff is pending; the running generation stopped intentionally |

Ordered numerically (round 12's O1, **applied in revision 14** — revision
13's disposition recorded it as done while the table was byte-identical,
which is round 13's B2a). This is the table the ADR carries normatively and
an outer supervisor's author reads it to write a `case` statement.

Exit 10 and exit 50 are *successes of the design*, not errors. Conflating
them with 0 would let an outer supervisor mistake "waiting for a human" for
"finished"; conflating them with 20 would make normal operation look like
failure. This split is why they are enumerated rather than left implicit.

**15 is the revision-11 addition, and it exists because neither 0 nor 10
is honest for `IMPLEMENTING` and `SELF_REVIEWING_IMPLEMENTATION`** (round
10's B1). Those two phases moved to report-only in revision 10, and neither
is a gate: `/milestone-implement` is model-invocable, on neither denylist,
and the brief's own hard-gate list names six gates and includes neither.
Reporting exit **10** there would tell an outer supervisor a human is
required for work the Workflow considers automation-safe — inverting
capability 6's first sentence, and misleading precisely the consumer exit
10 exists for, since that supervisor is what Generation 2 is meant to be.
Reporting exit **0** would be worse: "nothing is pending" is false while a
milestone is mid-implementation. 15 says the true thing — *this generation
declines; a later one need not* — and it is the same reasoning the plan
already applies to `LEGACY_READY`, which is neither an action nor a gate.

The three other report-only phases —
`AWAITING_EXTERNAL_IMPLEMENTATION_REVIEW`, `AWAITING_FUNCTIONAL_REVIEW` and
`APPLYING_REVIEW_FEEDBACK` — **are** genuine gates or their equivalent, so
they keep `GATE_BLOCKED` and exit 10 exactly as before. The split is not
cosmetic: it is the difference between "a human must act" and "a human need
not act, but this generation will not".

**16 is `--max-steps`** (round 10's O1), which was declared a stop reason
with no exit code. Exit 0 is wrong for the same reason as above and exit 10
names a gate that does not exist. The bound matters: the plan-revision loop
is the Controller's only unbounded autonomous cycle, this very work item ran
it seventy rounds without converging, at a real worker launch and real
spend per round, and `--max-steps`
is deliberately the only bound (review-convergence automation is out of
scope in the brief). Hitting it is therefore the operator's signal that the
loop did not converge, and it needs its own code to be one.

**40 no longer means "a worker was interrupted"** (revision 9, round 8's
O1). Since revision 8, an `INTERRUPTED` worker either verifies — status
`FINISHED`, the run continues — or fails step 8 and is recorded `FAILED`,
exit 30. Neither branch produces 40, so leaving the old wording in the one
table the ADR carries normatively would mislead an outer supervisor about
which of 30 and 40 to expect. The `worker_outcome` field still records that
the worker was interrupted; the exit code no longer duplicates it.

**35 is revision 7's addition** and it is the `INCOMPLETE` job status'
exit code (round 6's B2). It is deliberately not 30: the worker did not
*fail* — it typically exited 0 after refusing for a reason it printed, such
as `/apply-implementation-review` stopping at its own stale-feedback or
`REJECTED`-bundle check. Nor is it 40: the worker was not interrupted. An
outer supervisor needs to tell "the action could not proceed, and the
worker said why" from both, because the response differs — read the
worker's output, do not retry blindly.

### Controller-owned runtime state (the runtime root)

```
<runtime_root>/
├── identity.json            # the pinned source identity of the last run, plus the
│                            #   interpreter and exec-depth facts that make it
│                            #   checkable from outside (advisory record)
├── handoff.json             # pending-handoff record, when one exists
├── source/
│   └── <tree_digest>/       # an immutable, content-addressed snapshot of the
│       ├── controller/      #   Controller source a pinned run executes from
│       ├── pyproject.toml
│       └── SOURCE_PIN.json  #   commit/kind/generation/digest, written last
└── jobs/
    ├── <job_id>.json        # the durable job record
    └── <job_id>/
        ├── worker.stdout
        └── worker.stderr
```

The runtime root resolves by a **stated precedence**, and the ladder is
exhaustive (revision 36, local round 35's `OPUS-R35-B2` and `OPUS-R35-O2`):

| # | Source | Applies |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `--runtime-dir` | whenever given; it is a global option, so it is accepted only *before* the subcommand |
| 2 | `WORKFLOW_CONTROLLER_HOME` | when no `--runtime-dir` is given |
| 3 | `<origin_source_root>/.controller` | when neither is given **and** `origin_source_root` is a Git repository — the Controller's own checkout |
| 4 | `$XDG_STATE_HOME/workflow-controller/`, else `~/.local/state/workflow-controller/` | when neither is given and `origin_source_root` is **not** a Git repository — the ordinary installed copy |

**`.controller/` is row 3's name for this root, not the root's name, and
this is where that is stated** (revision 37, local round 36's
`OPUS-R36-O2`). The tree above is drawn at `<runtime_root>/` for that
reason. Where this document writes `.controller/<name>` — and it does,
because row 3 is the development configuration nearly everything here is
written against — it means *the record `<name>` in the run's resolved
runtime root*, whichever row resolved it. Where a passage runs under a
fixture that resolves some other row, the paths are written out instead:
CP8's steps 3, 6 and 7 read `<tmp>/`, because step 2 passes `--runtime-dir
<tmp>`. Revision 36 stated this convention once, inside **CP8 step 3** — a
test procedure — which is not where a reader meets the runtime tree, and
every site that still read as though `<origin>/.controller` were
unconditional stood above it.

**The flag beats the variable, and that order is load-bearing rather than
conventional**: CP1's re-exec passes the resolved root explicitly as
`--runtime-dir` precisely so the child cannot re-derive it (see the re-exec
below). If the variable won, that binding would not hold — parent and child
share an environment, so a child that preferred `WORKFLOW_CONTROLLER_HOME`
would silently ignore the value its parent resolved and passed.

Rows 3 and 4 are one rule — *durable state never lands inside a tree the
Controller does not own* — applied to the two things `origin_source_root`
can be. **Row 3** derives the root from the **origin** source repository,
never from the executing tree: a pinned run's own `source_root` is the
immutable snapshot, and a default derived from it would put durable state
inside a tree the Controller must never write to. CP1's re-exec therefore
passes the resolved runtime root explicitly across the exec boundary. That
root is gitignored (CP1 adds the entry), so Controller *development* never
overwrites the Controller's own *execution* record, which is the property
`docs/ACTIVE_MILESTONE.md` asks for — and that justification is precisely
why row 3 is **conditional** on the origin being the checkout. A
`site-packages` origin is not gitignored, is not developed in, and is not
the Controller's to write to, so the sentence that justifies row 3 is false
of it.

**Row 4 exists because rows 1–3 alone put `.controller/` inside
`site-packages`** on exactly the install revision 35 newly declared
supported for the three read-only commands. Three consequences made that
untenable, and row 4 closes each:

- **`status` could never do its job there.** It takes **no repository
  argument**, so its root can come from nowhere but this ladder. Under row
  3 on a non-checkout install that root is `<site-packages>/.controller` —
  never where any pinned run wrote, since a pinned run's parent origin is
  the checkout — so the one command whose entire subject is the
  Controller-owned runtime root would report on a permanently empty one.
- **On an unwritable install prefix it died outside the taxonomy.** With
  `pip install` as root, distro packaging or `pipx`, the record write
  raised a bare `PermissionError` — not a `ControllerError`, no code, no
  name — in a design whose whole premise is that every refusal is named and
  mapped to a code an outer supervisor can branch on.
- **Writing into `site-packages` at all is a side effect this design
  forbids itself elsewhere.** `runtime.write_json`'s containment guard
  would *pass*, because the runtime root **was** the install directory — so
  containment held while the Controller mutated the Python installation it
  was installed into, sharing one record across every target repository
  inspected from that install, and leaving state that a `pip uninstall`, a
  venv rebuild or an OS package upgrade destroys without the operator ever
  having been told that is where it was.

**A runtime root that cannot be created or written is a named refusal** —
`RuntimeRootUnwritableError`, exit **20**, carrying the resolved path and
the ladder row that produced it — never a bare `PermissionError`. Row 4
makes this rare rather than routine, but it is reachable at every row (a
read-only `--runtime-dir`, a `WORKFLOW_CONTROLLER_HOME` on a full disk), so
it is named once here rather than per row.

**`status` against a runtime root that has never been written** reports
exactly that — `no Controller runtime state at <path>` on stdout, exit
**0** — naming the resolved root and the ladder row that chose it, so an
operator who expected records elsewhere is told where the Controller
actually looked. It is not a refusal: an unwritten root is the correct
state of a fresh install, and exit 0 with a stated path is what
distinguishes it from a root being read wrongly.

**What that report measures is stated here, because `status` writes into
the very root it reports on** (revision 38, local round 37's
`OPUS-R37-I2`). `identity.json` is written by every command that reaches
its body, read-only ones included, immediately before that body runs — so
by the time `status` inspects the root, this process has already written
one, and *"a root that has never been written"* is a state `status` could
never observe under a literal reading. The report is therefore about the
**durable Controller records present when the process started**: `jobs/`,
`handoff.json`, and a **pre-existing** `identity.json`. The identity record
*this* run wrote is excluded by construction — it is written by the run
doing the reporting, and it describes that run rather than any work the run
could report on. Two consequences follow, and CP1 test 6(a) asserts both:
the first `status` against a fresh root prints `no Controller runtime state
at <path>`, exits **0**, and leaves an `identity.json` in that root; a
second `status` against the same root reports that identity record instead
of the empty-root line, which is what this command's surface row means by
*"pinned identity"*.

`runtime.write_json(path, obj)` resolves `path` and raises
`RuntimeContainmentError` unless it is inside the runtime root. That single
guard is what makes "the Controller never writes Workflow state" a checked
invariant rather than a promise: there is no other write path in the
package. Snapshot materialisation writes under `<runtime root>/source/` and
is covered by the same guard, so the one mechanism that writes *code* is
confined by the same rule as the one that writes records.

Writes are atomic — write to `<name>.tmp` in the same directory, `fsync`,
then `os.replace` — so an interruption never leaves a half-written record
that resume would then have to interpret.

The job record answers every question `docs/ACTIVE_MILESTONE.md` requires
it to:

```json
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "job_id": "<utc-timestamp>-<short-random>",
  "controller_generation": 1,
  "controller_source_commit": "<40-hex or null>",
  "controller_source_tree_digest": "<64-hex>",
  "target_repo": "/abs/path/to/target",
  "target_workflow_version": "2.5.1",
  "work_item_id": "<id or null>",
  "observed_phase_before": "PLANNING",
  "pre_state": {
    "phase": "PLANNING",
    "governing_workflow_version": "2.1",
    "target_head": "<40-hex>",
    "state_revision": 4,
    "plan_revision": 1,
    "implementation_revision": null,
    "last_completed_checkpoint_id": null,
    "checkpoints": {},
    "bundle_id": "<64-hex or null>",
    "bundle_manifest_readable": true,
    "bundle_manifest_generation_head": "<40-hex or null>",
    "bundle_generated_digest": "<64-hex or null>",
    "rejected_marker_present": false,
    "child_work_item_ids": [],
    "functional_review_consumed_blob": null,
    "functional_checklist_evidence": null,
    "pre_work_item_keys": []
  },
  "selected_action": {
    "kind": "slash_command",
    "command": "/milestone-plan <id>",
    "automatic": true,
    "declined": false,
    "reason": "...",
    "evidence": ["..."]
  },
  "expected_transition": {"from": "PLANNING", "to_any_of": ["AWAITING_LOCAL_PLAN_REVIEW"]},
  "worker": {
    "session_id": "...", "exit_code": 0, "is_error": false, "subtype": "success",
    "num_turns": 7, "duration_ms": 12345, "total_cost_usd": 0.12,
    "permission_denials": [], "terminal_reason": null, "stop_reason": null,
    "result_excerpt": "...", "stdout_path": "...", "stderr_path": "..."
  },
  "worker_outcome": "SUCCESS",
  "observed_phase_after": "AWAITING_LOCAL_PLAN_REVIEW",
  "transition_verified": true,
  "status": "FINISHED",
  "human_gate_pending": null,
  "handoff_pending": false,
  "created_at": "...", "updated_at": "..."
}
```

**`pre_work_item_keys` is revision 64's addition to this block** (round
63's `I1`). Revision 63 declared it a `PRE_STATE_FIELDS` member in CP6
step 1 — it is row 7's own `predicate_input` — and left this schema
rendering the other sixteen, so the document declared seventeen in one
place and rendered sixteen in the other while property 4 asserts
`set(record["pre_state"]) == set(PRE_STATE_FIELDS)`, a set **equality**.
That is round 8's `B3` one field over, and it is the exact shape CP6 step
1's own *"when a revision makes a rule depend on a value, the same pass
must name every place that value is captured and persisted"* forbids. It
is rendered as a JSON **array** of the pre-snapshot's `work_items` keys;
the in-memory declaration is a `frozenset`, and the capture serialises it
in sorted order so two runs over the same pre-state produce byte-identical
records.

**`NO_PHASE`'s durable form, and the single value used for "no phase"**
(revision 64, round 63's `B2`). Four fields in this record and in CP6B's
table can carry "there was no phase": `Decision.observed_phase`,
`observed_phase_before`, `expected_transition.from` and
`pre_state.phase`. Revision 63 introduced `NO_PHASE` as an
`is`-comparable sentinel for the third of them, said nothing about how it
is written to disk or read back, and had `decide_no_work_item` return
`observed_phase=None` for the first — two representations for one
concept, one of which does not survive a JSON round-trip at all. Both are
corrected here, as one declaration:

- **One value, everywhere.** `NO_PHASE` is the **only** in-memory value
  any of the four fields carries for "no phase". `decide_no_work_item`
  returns `Decision(observed_phase=NO_PHASE, …)`, not `None`;
  `pre_state.phase` for a `NoWorkItemYet` target is `NO_PHASE`;
  `observed_phase_before` is written from the decision, so it carries the
  same value; and row 7's `expected_transition.from` is that same
  sentinel. Python's `None` keeps the one meaning the schema already gives
  it (an absent optional, e.g. `work_item_id`) and the one the
  `ExpectedOutcome` schema already gives it (`governing_version=None`, the
  version wildcard), and is never overloaded a third way.
- **One durable form.** `NO_PHASE` serialises to the JSON **string
  `"__NO_PHASE__"`** — a reserved literal chosen so that it can never
  collide with a Workflow phase name, since `KNOWN_PHASES` is a closed
  set of `A-Z_` identifiers none of which begins or ends with a double
  underscore. It is declared once, as
  `NO_PHASE_WIRE = "__NO_PHASE__"`, beside the sentinel itself.
- **One round-trip rule, stated as an equality.** The writer maps
  `NO_PHASE → NO_PHASE_WIRE` and every real phase to its own name; the
  reader maps `NO_PHASE_WIRE → NO_PHASE`, any member of the known-phase
  set to itself, and **anything else — including a literal `null`, a bare
  `"None"`, or an unrecognised string — to a refusal**, never to a guess.
  A record read back off disk must compare `is NO_PHASE` exactly where the
  record that wrote it held `NO_PHASE`, and CP6's test list carries the
  round-trip case that asserts it from disk rather than from process
  memory. Reading is total over the domain and fail-closed outside it,
  which is the same posture CP3's `UnknownPhaseError` already takes for
  the phase field it reads out of the *target's* state.
- **Why a reserved string rather than `null`.** `null` is what an *absent*
  key deserialises to, and CP7's validation pass keys several of its cases
  on presence-versus-absence; a "no phase" written as `null` is
  indistinguishable from a field a buggy writer omitted, which is the
  discrimination CP6 step 4's own must-be-present/must-be-absent lists
  exist to make. A reserved non-null literal keeps "no phase" a **stated
  value** and leaves absence meaning absence.

`status` moves through `PLANNED → LAUNCHED → COMPLETED → FINISHED`, or
terminates at `FAILED`, `INTERRUPTED`, `INCOMPLETE`, `GATE_BLOCKED`,
`DECLINED` or `HANDOFF_PENDING`. **`VERIFIED` was removed in revision 15**
(round 14's I3): it sat in this progression from revision 1 and no step ever
wrote it — CP6B step 9 writes `FINISHED` directly once step 8 passes — so it
was a member with neither a producer nor a CP7 rule, which is exactly the
state a closed enumeration exists to make impossible. **`DECLINED` is revision
11's addition** (round 10's B1): the record a report-only, non-gate phase
produces. It carries the observed phase, the action the Controller can see
is next, and the reason this generation does not run it — and no worker was
launched, so it has no `worker` block. This enumeration is the **only** one in
the plan, and every status the design produces must appear in it: revision 6
created `INCOMPLETE` in CP6B without adding it here, which made CP7's closed
known-status table refuse the Controller's own output (round 6's B2).

**`pre_state` is revision 7's addition, and it is the record's most
consequential block** (round 6's B1). Every input any `ExpectedOutcome`
predicate reads is a field of it — not a top-level key, not something the
executing process merely holds in memory. The distinction is not editorial:
inside `execute_step` the pre-state is still in memory and an implementer
gets the right answer by accident, but at **`resume` the process that
captured it is gone and this record is the entire input**. Revisions 5 and 6
each added a predicate input (`state_revision`, then `bundle_id`) without
adding it here, which left CP7's predicate clause with nothing to evaluate
and its `INTERRUPTED`/`UnreconcilableJobError` rows with no `target_head` to
discriminate on — restoring, by omission, exactly the defect round 5 raised.

The general rule, the mirror of round 5's: **when a revision makes a rule
depend on a value, the same pass must name every place that value is
captured and persisted.** CP6B's record-completeness property (below)
enforces it mechanically, so a future row cannot declare a predicate the
record cannot answer. Each transition is persisted **before** the side effect
it authorises, never after — `LAUNCHED` (carrying the pre-state, whose
`PRE_STATE_FIELDS` already include the target's Git HEAD) is written and flushed *before* the worker process is
spawned. That ordering is the whole basis of CP7's resume logic: a crash
can leave a record claiming `LAUNCHED` for work that never started, but it
can never leave work that started with no record of it.

### CP1 — Package skeleton, packaging, runtime layout, refusal taxonomy, pinned source identity

**Owns**: REQ-9 (partly), REQ-10 (partly), REQ-11 (partly), REQ-12, REQ-13,
REQ-14 (partly), REQ-T14 (partly).

**Files**: `pyproject.toml`, `controller/__init__.py`,
`controller/__main__.py`, `controller/errors.py`, `controller/runtime.py`,
`controller/identity.py`, `controller/cli.py` (skeleton),
`controller/GENERATION.json`, `.gitignore`, `tests/__init__.py`,
`tests/fixtures.py`, `tests/test_runtime.py`, `tests/test_identity.py`,
`tests/test_package_structure.py`.

**Ordering requirement, load-bearing**: `.gitignore` gains `.controller/`
**in this checkpoint, before any Controller code is ever executed.**
`scripts/prepare-ai-review.sh` marks every untracked, non-ignored file
intent-to-add so it appears in the bundle diff; a `.controller/` tree that
is not yet ignored when the Controller first runs would enter the
plan-stage projection as an unclassified path and fail the bundle closed
mid-implementation. The artifacts declaration additionally excludes
`.controller/` at both stages as belt-and-braces, but the `.gitignore`
entry is the primary mechanism and must land first.

**`pyproject.toml`**: `[project] name = "workflow-controller"`,
`version = "1.0.0"`, `requires-python = ">=3.12"`,
`dependencies = []`, `[project.scripts] workflow-controller =
"controller.cli:main"`, and a `setuptools` build backend with explicit
`[tool.setuptools] packages = ["controller"]` so `tests/` is never packaged.
No runtime dependencies and no test-framework dependency: the suite is
`unittest`, matching the repository's existing stdlib-only Python and CI
(`python-version: "3.12"`, suites invoked as plain `python3 <file>.py`).

**`controller/identity.py`** — the immutable generation identity, and the
immutable execution root that makes it true:

**Why this is a mechanism and not a property of `pin()` alone** (revision
32, manual external round 31's `EXT-PLAN-R31-I1`). Revisions 1–31 recorded
`git rev-parse HEAD` as the run's identity while the interpreter imported
`controller/` from the ordinary mutable source worktree. Three consequences
followed, and none of them was closed by the no-reload rules below:
`--allow-dirty-source` let a run record a clean commit that did not
identify the bytes that executed; CP8's subprocess test proved that one
*already-loaded* behaviour did not change, not that a module or resource
first read *after* the worktree moved would still be Generation A's; and
the handoff invariant therefore rested on Python import timing rather than
on the identity REQ-9 claims. Revision 32 fixes the class rather than the
three symptoms: **every run that may write a job record or launch a worker
executes from an immutable, content-verified snapshot of the source tree**,
so a later import or resource read cannot reach the origin worktree at all.
The eager-load and no-late-read rules below are kept as an independent
second argument, not as the primary one.

- `ControllerIdentity` is a frozen dataclass: `generation: int`,
  `source_root: Path`, `origin_source_root: Path | None`,
  `source_kind: str`, `source_commit: str | None`,
  `tree_digest: str | None`, `generation_source: str`, `pinned_at: str`.
- **`source_kind` is a closed three-member enumeration**, and it is the
  field every rule below is keyed on:

  | `source_kind` | What executed | `source_commit` | `tree_digest` |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | `"commit"` | a snapshot materialised from a clean `HEAD` | the 40-hex commit | the 64-hex digest of the snapshot |
  | `"worktree"` | a snapshot materialised from a dirty working tree under `--allow-dirty-source` | **`None`** — the run is identified by content, never by a commit it does not match | the 64-hex digest of the snapshot |
  | `"unpinned"` | the ordinary mutable source worktree, in place | `HEAD` if the tree is a Git repository, else `None` — **advisory only** | `None` |

- **The guard is positive and total** (the same shape as CP6 step 2's):
  `inspect`, `explain` and `status` are the enumerated read-only commands
  and may run at any `source_kind`, including `"unpinned"`, since they
  mutate nothing and launch nothing. **Every other command — `step`, `run`
  and `resume` today, and any command added later by default — requires
  `source_kind != "unpinned"`.** A future command is covered by
  construction rather than by remembering to add it to a denylist.

  **Two mechanisms, and the plan says which does the work**, because a
  guard that can never fire in normal operation is worth being explicit
  about. The *acting* mechanism is `cli.main`: for a non-read-only command
  at an `"unpinned"` root it materialises the snapshot and re-executes (or
  refuses — `DirtyControllerSourceError` for a dirty tree without
  `--allow-dirty-source`, `SourceSnapshotError` when no snapshot can be
  established at all), so by the time the command function is dispatched
  the process is already pinned. The *asserting* mechanism is
  `require_pinned_execution()`, called by every non-read-only command
  function on entry; in normal operation it never fires, and it exists so
  that a future code path reaching dispatch without the materialise step
  stops instead of running unpinned. Test 6 below fires it deliberately by
  calling the command functions directly with an `"unpinned"` identity,
  which is the only way it is reachable.
- **Where `origin_source_root` comes from, and what it costs an install
  that is not the checkout** (revision 35, local round 34's `OPUS-R34-B3`).
  Every default in this design hangs off it — the runtime root
  (`<origin>/.controller`, **but only at ladder row 3**, which is precisely
  what revision 35 got wrong here and revision 36 repaired), the `git
  archive`, the dirty-scope `git status`, the generation read at `HEAD`, and
  CP8's approved-generation resolution —
  and revision 34 named it in `materialise()`'s signature, in
  `ControllerIdentity`, in `SOURCE_PIN.json` and in CP8's
  `identity.current().origin_source_root` without once saying how an
  **unpinned** run resolves it. It is `pin()`'s own `source_root`:
  `Path(__file__).parent.parent` for the module that is executing, by the
  same rule and for the same reason — the identity is a property of the code
  that is running, never of the process CWD. An unpinned process's origin is
  therefore where the Controller is **installed**, which is the checkout only
  for an editable install.

  **That is a real boundary and the document draws it rather than letting it
  arrive as a `git … 128`.** A Controller installed anywhere but its own
  checkout has an `origin_source_root` that is not a Git repository, so
  `materialise()` cannot establish a snapshot at all and every non-read-only
  command refuses with `SourceSnapshotError`. Measured on Python 3.14.7:
  `pip install ./checkout` resolves `Path(__file__).parent.parent` to
  `…/lib/python3.14/site-packages`, and `git -C <site-packages> archive HEAD
  -- controller pyproject.toml` exits **128**. Such an install serves exactly
  the three read-only commands — which is the boundary the positive guard
  above already draws, and whose failure mode CP1 test 6(c) already pins.
  CP9's CLI surface and `README.md`'s installation section both state it,
  because until revision 35 both read as though an ordinary install were
  usable for `step`, `run` and `resume`.

  **The runtime root is the first entry in this bullet's own opening list,
  and revision 35 did not follow it here** (revision 36, local round 35's
  `OPUS-R35-B2`). Resolving `origin_source_root` to the install location
  makes `<origin>/.controller` a `site-packages` path on every non-editable
  install — so the default whose entire purpose is to keep Controller state
  out of trees the Controller does not own would have put it *inside the
  Python installation*, on precisely the configuration the paragraph above
  newly declares supported. **The runtime-root ladder above is the
  resolution**: its row 3 is now conditional on `origin_source_root` being
  a Git repository, and row 4 sends every other install to a user-state
  root, so all three read-only commands work there and `status` reports a
  root a run could actually have written.

  The other four defaults in the opening list needed no second branch, and
  the reason is worth stating so the asymmetry does not read as an
  oversight: the `git archive`, the dirty-scope `git status`, the
  generation read at `HEAD` and CP8's approved-generation resolution are
  all **reads of the origin as a repository**, so a non-repository origin
  correctly makes them refuse — that refusal *is* the boundary drawn above.
  The runtime root was the one entry that is a **write**, and a write has
  nowhere to refuse to; it either lands somewhere defensible or somewhere
  it should not be. That is why it alone needed a branch.
- **`materialise(origin_source_root, runtime_root, *, allow_dirty) -> Path`**
  builds the snapshot, and it is content-addressed rather than
  commit-addressed so that both kinds share one scheme and can never
  collide:
  1. Extract into a temporary directory under
     `<runtime_root>/source/`, **over one fixed pathspec on both branches
     so the two kinds are byte-comparable and the snapshot holds only what
     is importable** — `controller/` and `pyproject.toml`, never the whole
     repository: `git -C <origin> archive HEAD -- controller pyproject.toml`
     for a clean tree, or a copy of the same two paths, including untracked
     files that are not ignored, for a dirty tree under
     `--allow-dirty-source`. A dirty tree without that flag is
     `DirtyControllerSourceError`, exactly as before.

     **"Dirty" is scoped to the snapshot's own pathspec, and the plan names
     the command** (revision 33, local round 32's `OPUS-R32-O1`, which
     observed that revision 32 left the scope to the implementer and that
     the two readings refuse differently from the same repository state):
     the tree is dirty **iff `git -C <origin> status --porcelain --
     controller pyproject.toml` produces any output**, which includes
     untracked non-ignored files under those two paths and excludes
     everything else. Pathspec scoping rather than whole-worktree scoping is
     deliberate and is the stronger of the two readings: the snapshot holds
     exactly those paths, so an edit anywhere else — `docs/`, `tests/`, this
     plan document — leaves the extracted bytes byte-identical to `HEAD`,
     and recording `source_kind: "commit"` with that commit is then
     *accurate* rather than generous. Under whole-worktree scoping every
     development-time run would carry a `null` commit while executing bytes
     a commit identifies exactly, which discards the provenance the field
     exists for. Test 9 pins the choice.
  2. Compute `tree_digest` — **over a mapping, not over a concatenation**
     (revision 34, local round 33's `OPUS-R33-O3`). Build
     `{<POSIX repository-relative path>: {"mode": "100755" | "100644",
     "sha256": <hex digest of the file's bytes>}}` over every extracted
     file, and hash the canonical JSON serialisation of that mapping with
     sorted keys. Revision 33 wrote this as *"SHA-256 over each file's
     repository-relative path and bytes, in sorted path order"*, which
     leaves the encoding ambiguous — a tree holding `ab`/`c` hashes
     identically to one holding `a`/`bc` — and covers no file mode, so two
     snapshots differing only in an executable bit would share a directory
     and one would silently execute as the other. Neither is adversarially
     interesting here, since the inputs are the origin repository's own
     bytes; the reason to name it is that this is the field the whole
     immutable-execution model is identified by, and the answer already
     exists in this repository rather than needing invention:
     `workflow_fingerprint.compute_bundle_id` keys entries by POSIX
     relative path in a mapping, each carrying **mode and content hash
     separately**, for exactly these two reasons. `SOURCE_PIN.json` is
     excluded from the mapping, since it is written after — and records —
     the digest.

     **The mapping is otherwise total over the directory, and that totality
     is a property the exec below *constructs* rather than assumes**
     (revision 35, local round 34's `OPUS-R34-B1`). `SOURCE_PIN.json` is the
     only exclusion at all three places that recompute this digest — here,
     step 3's reuse verification, and `pin()`'s two-way binding — because
     everything else in that directory is content the interpreter can
     execute, and a digest that does not cover it does not identify the
     bytes that ran. Revision 34 asserted that totality and broke it in the
     same document: the pinned child's first act is to import `controller`
     **out of the snapshot**, and CPython writes
     `controller/__pycache__/*.pyc` **into the snapshot** before `cli.main`
     is reached and therefore before `pin()` recomputes — so a **correct**
     build refused on its first pinned run, and on every run after it the
     origin's bytes were unchanged, the digest and therefore the directory
     name were unchanged, step 3's verification failed against the bytecode
     the previous correct run had written, and step 4's second state refused
     permanently. Revision 34's own new refusal branch, working exactly as
     specified, on a mismatch the design itself created. Measured on Python
     3.14.7: `PYTHONPATH=<snap> python3 -P -m controller` over a
     three-module package leaves `__pycache__/__init__.cpython-314.pyc`,
     `identity.cpython-314.pyc` and `__main__.cpython-314.pyc` inside
     `<snap>/controller/`; the same command with **`-B`** leaves the
     directory byte-identical.

     **The remedy is in the exec, not in an exclusion list, and the choice
     is stated rather than left to the implementer.** Naming `__pycache__/`
     and `*.py[co]` alongside `SOURCE_PIN.json` here would also stop the
     refusal, and it is the weaker of the two answers: a `.pyc` whose header
     matches is loaded *in preference to* the source, so everything such an
     exclusion admits is executable content outside the verified set. This
     document claims the stronger property — **the digest covers everything
     in the snapshot that can execute** — and `-B` in the re-exec argv is
     what makes it true.

     **The origin side of the same effect is already closed, and saying so
     is cheaper than having it rediscovered.** The *parent* is unpinned and
     imports `controller/` from the origin checkout, so it writes bytecode
     into the **origin**, never into the snapshot. That reaches neither the
     extracted bytes nor the dirty scope: the clean branch is `git archive`,
     which carries tracked files only; the dirty branch copies untracked
     files *that are not ignored*; and `git status --porcelain -- controller
     pyproject.toml` ignores the same set. This repository's `.gitignore`
     carries `__pycache__/` and `*.py[cod]` at `base_commit`, and CP1's
     `.gitignore` work must not remove them — without those entries a
     parent's own import would make every fixture checkout read as dirty and
     refuse `step` with `DirtyControllerSourceError`.
  3. If `<runtime_root>/source/<tree_digest>/` already exists **and
     verifies**, discard the temporary tree and reuse it; identical bytes
     are the same snapshot by definition. **Verifies** means the step-2
     digest, recomputed over the directory's own files with
     `SOURCE_PIN.json` excluded, equals **both** the directory's own name
     **and** the `tree_digest` that directory's `SOURCE_PIN.json` records —
     the same two-way binding `pin()` checks below, stated here because
     step 4 now branches on its outcome. **`SOURCE_PIN.json` is rewritten
     on reuse** — atomically, `fsync` then `os.replace`, with *this*
     materialisation's `source_kind`, `source_commit` and `generation`. The
     digest and the directory name are unaffected, since `SOURCE_PIN.json`
     is excluded from its own digest, and the effect is that the recorded
     identity always describes the run about to happen rather than
     whichever run created the directory first. A concurrent reader sees
     the old or the new file whole, never a torn one, and both describe the
     same bytes.

     **The temporary is written *outside* the snapshot directory**, as
     `<runtime_root>/source/.SOURCE_PIN.<token>.tmp`, and `os.replace`d in.
     This is the one place this design departs from the `<name>.tmp` **in
     the same directory** rule stated above, and the departure is the whole
     point (revision 36, local round 35's `OPUS-R35-I1`). Under that rule
     the rewrite would put `SOURCE_PIN.json.tmp` **inside** the verified
     directory, where the digest covers it: totality's stated justification
     — *everything else in that directory is content the interpreter can
     execute* — is not true of it, and the exclusion does not name it, so
     an interrupted rewrite (`SIGKILL`, a full disk, a crash between
     `fsync` and `os.replace`) leaves a stray file that changes the
     recomputed digest **permanently**. That is `OPUS-R34-B1`'s exact
     failure mode — a correct build refusing forever against a file its own
     previous run wrote, recoverable only by a manual `rm` — reappearing
     through a second write site, reachable by an interruption rather than
     by design. This document reasons carefully about crash-safety for step
     4's publish and did not for step 3's rewrite.

     Writing outside is chosen over excluding the temporary, and the choice
     is stated rather than left open: it keeps the snapshot's file set
     **literally constant** under reuse, so no second exclusion is needed
     and **`SOURCE_PIN.json` remains the only exclusion at all three
     recompute sites — a closed set of one**. A future `.bak` or `.lock`
     cannot arrive the same way, because with this rule nothing but
     `SOURCE_PIN.json` is ever written *into* a materialised snapshot at
     all. `<runtime_root>/source/` is the snapshot directory's own parent,
     so the rename is same-filesystem and atomic by construction; the
     leading dot keeps a stray temporary from being read as a snapshot
     directory by step 3, whose directory names are digests.

     **CP1 test 4 gains the instrument, and it has to exercise the
     *writer*** (revision 37, local round 36's `OPUS-R36-B2`). Revision 36
     specified that instrument as a third run with a stray
     `.SOURCE_PIN.<token>.tmp` **planted** in `<runtime_root>/source/`, and
     called the case red against the in-directory rule. It is not, and the
     claim was stated as measured fact in three places while being false in
     all three. That path lies outside the snapshot directory under **both**
     rules, so it is outside the recomputed digest under both and invisible
     to this step's existence-and-verification check under both; and it is
     not a file the in-directory rule ever produces, since that rule leaves
     `SOURCE_PIN.json.tmp` *inside* the snapshot. A case that cannot fail
     pins nothing: revert this clause and the planted-file run stays green
     while the permanent poisoning returns. **Moving the planted file inside
     the snapshot does not discriminate either**, in the opposite direction:
     this rule does not *exclude* that name from the digest, it merely never
     writes it there, so a planted copy is red under both rules. The
     guarantee this clause makes is about **where the writer puts its
     temporary**, so the instrument has to interrupt the writer — a real
     reuse whose `SOURCE_PIN.json` rewrite is killed between `fsync` and
     `os.replace`, which is the crash the clause exists for. Test 4 states
     it in that form.

     **Two runs can legitimately share a digest and disagree about the
     provenance** — a clean run and an `--allow-dirty-source` run whose dirt
     falls outside the pathspec extract identical bytes — so on reuse this
     file is shared mutable state that an overlapping run can rewrite under
     another's feet (local round 32's `OPUS-R32-O2`). **Concurrent
     Controller runs against one runtime root are out of scope for
     Generation 1**, and rather than defend against them the crossing is
     made loud: the child verifies the `source_kind`/`source_commit` it
     reads against the pair its own parent recorded in
     `WORKFLOW_CONTROLLER_EXEC_HANDOFF` (see the re-exec below) and refuses
     with `SourceSnapshotError` on disagreement. `tree_digest` still
     identifies the executed bytes exactly under either outcome, which is
     the property the immutable-execution root actually rests on; what the
     check adds is that a job record can never quietly attribute one run's
     bytes to another run's commit.
  4. **"Otherwise" is two states, and only one of them may be published**
     (revision 34, local round 33's `OPUS-R33-I2`, which measured what
     revision 33's single clause actually does to the second):
     - **The directory does not exist.** Write `SOURCE_PIN.json` into the
       temporary tree and `os.replace` it to
       `<runtime_root>/source/<tree_digest>/`. The publish is a single
       rename, so a crash mid-extraction can leave a temporary tree but
       never a half-populated snapshot under its digest.
     - **The directory exists and fails step 3's verification.** Discard
       the temporary tree and refuse with `SourceSnapshotError`, naming the
       directory and which of the two bindings failed. **Nothing is renamed
       onto it.** Revision 33's undivided *"otherwise"* covered both states
       while `os.replace` supports only the first: measured,
       `os.replace(<temporary tree>, <existing non-empty directory>)` raises
       `OSError: [Errno 39] Directory not empty`, so what the operator got
       was an unhandled exception and exit **1** — not a named refusal, not
       exit 20 — in a taxonomy whose entire premise is that every refusal is
       named and mapped to a code an outer supervisor can branch on. That
       was the one refusal path in the design that did not end in a
       `ControllerError`. Refusing is chosen over silently rebuilding the
       directory: a snapshot that does not match its own name is evidence of
       tampering or of a publish that was interrupted between rename and
       `SOURCE_PIN.json`, and rebuilding it destroys that evidence, while
       the recovery — delete the named directory — stays an explicit human
       act. CP1 test 5 is exactly this path, and reaches it through
       `materialise()` rather than through `pin()`.

  `SOURCE_PIN.json` records `schema_version`, `source_kind`,
  `source_commit`, `origin_source_root`, `generation`,
  `generation_source`, `tree_digest` and `materialised_at`. It is written
  after extraction and is **excluded from its own digest**.
- **`pin()` resolves the identity from where the code actually is**, using
  `Path(__file__).parent.parent` — the module's own location, not
  `controller.__file__` (which would make `identity` import the package
  that imports it) and not the process CWD. The running generation's
  identity is a property of the code that is executing.
  - If `<source_root>/SOURCE_PIN.json` exists, **this process is already
    inside a snapshot**: recompute the tree digest and refuse with
    `SourceSnapshotError` unless it equals **both** the recorded
    `tree_digest` **and** the snapshot directory's own name. Identity is
    then read from the file, with no `git` invocation at all — a snapshot
    stays valid even if the origin repository is moved or deleted. When
    `WORKFLOW_CONTROLLER_EXEC_HANDOFF` is present — it is in every process
    the Controller itself re-execed, and absent when a human runs a snapshot
    directly — the `source_kind`/`source_commit` read from the file must
    equal the pair it carries, or the run refuses.
  - Otherwise this is a mutable worktree and the pin is `"unpinned"`, with
    the commit read from `git -C <source_root> rev-parse HEAD` when the
    tree is a Git repository and `None` when it is not (a `pip`-installed
    copy in `site-packages`, say). `"unpinned"` is enough for the three
    read-only commands and, by the positive guard above, for nothing else.
- **The generation number is read from the origin repository's committed
  `HEAD`, not from its worktree** (`git -C <origin> show
  HEAD:controller/GENERATION.json`), resolved once at materialisation and
  recorded in `SOURCE_PIN.json`, which is the *same* source CP8 resolves
  the approved generation from. **This holds for a `"worktree"` snapshot
  too**, which is what keeps revision 1's composition defect unreachable:
  revision 1 read the pinned number from the worktree and the approved
  number from `HEAD`, and local plan review round 1 showed what that
  composition does — an uncommitted bump to generation 2 makes pinned (2)
  *greater* than approved (1), which is CP8's revert branch, so an ordinary
  editing state hard-stops the Controller with "the source repository
  declares an older generation than the one running". Reading both from
  `HEAD` makes that composition unreachable by construction rather than by
  a special case: pinned and approved can never disagree because they read
  the same bytes. An uncommitted `GENERATION.json` edit is then exactly
  what it is — a dirty source, refused outright or snapshotted as
  `"worktree"` under `--allow-dirty-source` — and never a phantom handoff
  or a phantom revert.
- `generation_source` records which read answered: `"head"` normally, or
  `"worktree"` in the one fallback case — `git show HEAD:controller/GENERATION.json`
  failing because the path does not exist at `HEAD` yet, which is the real
  state of this repository during CP1 itself, before the first Controller
  commit lands. In that case materialisation falls back to the worktree
  file and sets `generation_source: "worktree"`. A malformed or unreadable
  `GENERATION.json` at either source is a refusal (`SourceSnapshotError`),
  never a default of `1`.
- **The re-exec, the import root it constructs, and why it terminates.** A
  non-read-only command whose own `source_root` is `"unpinned"` materialises
  the snapshot and then re-executes itself:
  `os.execv(sys.executable, [sys.executable, "-P", "-B", "-m", "controller",
  "--runtime-dir", <resolved absolute runtime root>, *<the caller's
  `argv[1:]` with any `--runtime-dir` of its own removed, in both the
  `--runtime-dir X` and `--runtime-dir=X` spellings>])`, with
  `PYTHONPATH` **assigned** the snapshot directory — assigned, never
  appended to whatever the caller's environment carried — and
  `WORKFLOW_CONTROLLER_EXEC_HANDOFF` set as described below. Both variables
  are prepared in `os.environ` before the call, which `execv` inherits;
  `os.execve` with an explicit mapping is equivalent and the implementation
  may use either. The resolved
  runtime root is passed explicitly rather than re-derived, because after
  the exec `Path(__file__).parent.parent` is the *snapshot*, and a default
  derived from it would put the Controller's durable state inside the
  immutable tree.

  **It is passed *before* the subcommand, and that position is not a style
  choice** (revision 34, local round 33's `OPUS-R33-O2`). `--runtime-dir` is
  a **global** option in CP9's CLI surface, declared on the top-level parser,
  and argparse does not accept a top-level option that follows the
  subcommand. Measured: `["step", "/repo", "--runtime-dir", "/rt"]` →
  `error: unrecognized arguments: --runtime-dir /rt`, `SystemExit(2)`;
  `["--runtime-dir", "/rt", "step", "/repo"]` parses. Revision 33 appended
  it after `argv[1:]`, so **every** re-exec — that is, every non-read-only
  command an operator runs from an unpinned tree, which is the ordinary case
  — would have died in the child at exit **2**, which this document's own
  exit table calls *"CLI usage error (argparse default)"*: the Controller's
  own construction reported as the operator's typo, and read that way by an
  outer supervisor too. Dropping any caller-supplied `--runtime-dir` is part
  of the same clause rather than a nicety: the resolved absolute value
  supersedes it, and leaving both in argv makes the child's value depend on
  argparse's last-wins ordering rather than on what the parent resolved.

  **`-P` is one token and it is the whole of the mechanism** (revision 33,
  local round 32's `OPUS-R32-B1`). For `python -m <module>`, CPython
  prepends the process's **working directory** to `sys.path` ahead of every
  `PYTHONPATH` entry, and the Controller never `chdir`s — the only working
  directory it sets for a subprocess it launches is the *worker*'s
  `cwd=target_root` in CP5. So revision 32's exec, which relied on
  `PYTHONPATH` alone,
  imported the **origin** package whenever the invoking directory contained
  a `controller/` package, which is the ordinary case for a developer
  running the Controller from its own checkout. The child then found no
  `SOURCE_PIN.json`, resolved `"unpinned"` again, and re-executed without
  bound: not a refusal, not an unpinned run that proceeds, but an exec loop.
  `-P` — equivalently `PYTHONSAFEPATH=1`, both available since 3.11 and this
  project requires 3.12 — suppresses that entry, so the child's `sys.path` is
  the assigned `PYTHONPATH` plus the interpreter's own standard-library and
  site paths, with **nothing** derived from the invoking directory. It is
  passed in `argv` rather than in the environment so that it applies to this
  exec alone and is not inherited by anything the child later starts.

  **`-B` is the second token, and it is what makes the snapshot's digest true
  of a directory that is being executed** (revision 35, local round 34's
  `OPUS-R34-B1`). Without it the child's very first act — importing
  `controller` out of the snapshot — writes `controller/__pycache__/*.pyc`
  into the snapshot before `cli.main` runs and therefore before `pin()`
  recomputes the digest, so a **correct** build refuses on its first pinned
  run and, on every run after it, meets `materialise()` step 4's second state
  and refuses permanently against bytecode its own previous run wrote. `-B`
  — equivalently `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1`, and **`-P` does not imply it** —
  suppresses the write, so executing a snapshot cannot change it and step 2's
  digest stays literally total. It belongs in `argv` for exactly the reason
  `-P` does: it must apply to this exec alone and not be inherited by
  anything the child later launches, which would pay the cost of suppressed
  caching for no benefit. The cost here is one recompilation of the package
  per pinned run, and it is the price of the property the whole model rests
  on.

  **A snapshot run directly is a supported diagnostic act and it takes the
  same flag.** `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 python -P …` against
  `<runtime_root>/source/<tree_digest>/` is how a human reproduces a pinned
  run by hand, and it is the invocation this document means wherever it says
  *a human running a snapshot directly*. Omitting it is not silently
  tolerated and must not be: the directory acquires a bytecode cache, stops
  matching its own name, and is refused by name from then on — with the
  recovery being the same explicit human act step 4 already names, delete the
  directory and let the next run re-materialise it. That is this design's
  intended answer to *a snapshot that does not match its digest*, and stating
