  it here is what keeps it from arriving as a surprise.

  **The termination bound, restated to match the mechanism that delivers
  it.** It rests on two facts, both constructed by the Controller in the
  exec it builds and neither inherited from the caller: **(a)** the child's
  import root is exactly the snapshot, by `-P` together with an assigned
  `PYTHONPATH`, so `Path(__file__).parent.parent` in the child is the
  snapshot; and **(b)** the snapshot contains `SOURCE_PIN.json`, so the
  child takes the branch of `pin()` that contains no re-exec. **At most one
  exec can occur.** Revision 32 asserted (b) alone and called the bound a
  property of which branch runs rather than of an environment variable a
  caller could forge; that was a plausible argument standing in for a
  mechanism — the class of defect this document has found in itself most
  often — and it was false, because (a) did not hold.

  **A fail-safe that can only refuse.** `WORKFLOW_CONTROLLER_EXEC_HANDOFF`
  carries the parent's `exec_depth` and the `source_kind`/`source_commit` it
  materialised. A process that reaches the `"unpinned"` branch with
  `exec_depth >= 1` raises `SourceSnapshotError` instead of performing a
  second exec, so any future recurrence of this defect is a named refusal
  rather than a loop — and "hangs" is not a specified behaviour of this
  design at any point. **This raise sets `evidence['raised_by']` to
  `"cli.main"`**, naming the dispatch code that performs the check rather
  than either `materialise()`'s or `pin()`'s own verification path, since it
  runs after `pin()` has already returned `"unpinned"` and before `cli.main`
  would otherwise re-exec — the third and last member of the closed set the
  raised_by invariant states below (revision 52, required acceptance
  criterion 6, `OPUS-R51-B1`'s missing-tests obligation). The asymmetry is what makes this safe to add without
  reintroducing the trusted marker revision 32 was right to avoid: the
  variable can only ever cause a **refusal**, never admit a run. Forging it
  high refuses; forging it low, or deleting it, lands on the ordinary path,
  which fact (a) already bounds. The bound is (a) and (b); this is the guard
  against them being wrong again, and the same variable carries the
  provenance cross-check `materialise()` step 3 names. **The child deletes
  the variable from its own environment as soon as it has read it**, so
  nothing it launches inherits it — a worker that itself invoked a
  Controller would otherwise inherit an `exec_depth` of 1 and refuse for a
  reason that has nothing to do with its own run, which is the one way a
  refusal-only guard could still do harm. **The value it read is retained in
  memory**, and the `.controller/identity.json` record the next bullet
  describes reports it as `exec_depth` from that retained value, at the write
  point that bullet names — which is *after* the deletion, and deliberately
  so: the deletion must happen at entry, before anything can be launched,
  while the record must not be written by a process that refuses before
  dispatch. Revision 34 wrote *"written … before the variable is deleted"*,
  which placed the record earlier than any assertion reading it can tolerate
  (revision 35, local round 34's `OPUS-R34-I1`). That record, not the
  variable, is what the tests read.

  **The tests read the running child, not a reconstruction of it.** The
  exec depth, the child's actual `sys.path` and its `sys.flags.safe_path`
  are all measured from the child itself via the four process fields the
  record below declares — tests 1 and 8 here, and CP8's step 7 for the live
  end-to-end case.
- **The pinned run records the interpreter it actually got, and how many
  execs it took to get there**, because every claim above is about
  `sys.path` and about an exec bound, and a claim about either has to be
  measurable from outside the process or it is an argument again.
  `.controller/identity.json` — the advisory record of the last run —
  carries, besides the identity fields, `interpreter_executable`
  (`sys.executable`), `interpreter_safe_path` (`sys.flags.safe_path`),
  `interpreter_sys_path` (`list(sys.path)`, captured at `cli.main` entry
  before any Controller code touches it) and `exec_depth` (the integer read
  from `WORKFLOW_CONTROLLER_EXEC_HANDOFF` at entry, or `0` when that
  variable is absent). These four are the only fields in that record
  describing the *process* rather than the *pin*, and they exist so a test
  asserts what the child's import environment and exec history **were**
  rather than what they should have been.

  **When the record is written, stated once, because four separate
  assertions constrain that ordering and revision 34 left it to the
  implementer** (revision 35, local round 34's `OPUS-R34-I1`). An instrument
  whose moment of capture is undefined cannot settle the assertions that read
  it. `.controller/identity.json` is written **exactly once per process, at
  the point the pin has been resolved and the read-only/pinned guard has
  passed, immediately before the command body runs** — after `cli.main`'s
  materialise-and-re-exec step, and so before any orchestration boundary. Two
  consequences follow and each is asserted somewhere. A process that
  **refuses before dispatch** writes **no** record at all —
  `DirtyControllerSourceError`, `materialise()`'s `SourceSnapshotError` and
  the `exec_depth >= 1` fail-safe are all in that class — which is what makes
  CP1 test 2's *"no `identity.json` was written"* a property rather than an
  accident, and what tells CP1 test 5 to expect none after its refusal either.
  An **unpinned read-only** command *does* write one, recording `exec_depth:
  0`, because it reaches its command body; the rule is never "only pinned
  children write it". And CP8 step 3 depends on this ordering directly: it
  waits for `identity.json` to show commit A while the child is **paused in
  the run loop**, which holds only if the record precedes the first
  orchestration boundary rather than being written at process exit.

  **`exec_depth` is the exec counter, and revision 33 asserted on it three
  times without ever defining it** (revision 34, local round 33's
  `OPUS-R33-I1`). Tests 1, 2 and 8 read *"the exec counter"*; the phrase
  occurred nowhere else in the document, and this record carried no count —
  so the at-most-one bound, which is fact (a) plus fact (b) and therefore
  the whole termination argument, had no instantiation at all while three
  required tests claimed to assert it. A count is what is needed and the
  three interpreter fields cannot substitute for it: a build that execs
  three times and still ends pinned produces a byte-identical `source_root`,
  `interpreter_safe_path` and `interpreter_sys_path` to one that execs once,
  so only a depth distinguishes them. It costs no new plumbing — the value
  is already in the handoff variable the child reads for the fail-safe, and
  this record already exists so that a claim about `sys.path` is checkable
  from outside the process. A correct non-read-only command run from an
  unpinned tree records `exec_depth: 1`; a read-only command, or a human
  running a snapshot directly, records `0`; anything above `1` is the
  recurrence the fail-safe exists to refuse.

  **What containment actually guarantees, stated in a form that is true at
  the default runtime root** (revision 34, local round 33's `OPUS-R33-B1`).
  Under the rule above a pinned child shows `interpreter_safe_path` true and
  `interpreter_sys_path[0]` equal to its own `source_root`; and **no entry
  of `interpreter_sys_path` is the origin checkout root, and no entry lies
  inside the origin checkout other than the snapshot the Controller itself
  constructed under `<runtime_root>/source/`**. Revision 33 wrote that last
  clause as *"no entry anywhere in `interpreter_sys_path` inside the origin
  source tree"*, which is **false of this design's own default**: at this
  test's fixture the origin *is* the checkout, so the runtime root resolves
  by ladder **row 3** to `<origin>/.controller` and the snapshot is
  `<origin>/.controller/source/<tree_digest>/` — inside the checkout — and by
  construction it is `sys.path[0]`. The sentence therefore asserted of one
  and the same entry both that it equals `source_root` and that it is not
  inside the origin tree, which cannot both hold; an implementer writing it
  literally would have got a red test against a **correct** build, and the
  cheapest way to green it — relocating the fixture with `--runtime-dir` —
  would have moved the required test off the only layout an operator
  actually runs, which is this document's own recurring class again. The
  narrower form is also the stronger one: it forbids the checkout root
  outright — that is the entry which would reintroduce the mutable package —
  and admits exactly one exception, a directory whose name is the digest of
  the bytes inside it. CP1 tests 1 and 8 and CP8 step 7 all derive their
  assertion from this sentence.
- The result is cached in a module-level singleton. `current()` returns the
  cached pin and **never re-resolves**. Re-resolution is the exact thing a
  pinned generation must not do, so there is no public API that performs it
  twice; a private `_reset_for_tests()` exists and is named so it cannot be
  mistaken for production API.
- **Eager loading, as the independent second argument.**
  `controller/__init__.py` ends with a single literal
  `from . import errors, runtime, identity, decision, managed_repo,
  target_state, evidence, worker, handoff, job, cli` — in dependency order,
  so no cycle is created — and a test asserts that the names in that
  literal are exactly `{p.stem for p in controller/*.py} - {"__init__",
  "__main__"}` and that every one of them is in `sys.modules` after
  `import controller` returns. A module that a future checkpoint adds and
  forgets to list fails that test rather than becoming a late import.
- **No late resource read.** A source scan asserts that `controller/`
  contains no `importlib.resources`, no `pkgutil.get_data`, and no file
  read whose path is derived from the executing package's own directory
  (`Path(__file__).parent`), with **exactly two allowlisted exceptions,
  both named in the test, both in `identity.py`, and both performed before
  any orchestration**: `pin()`'s read of `<source_root>/SOURCE_PIN.json`,
  and the `generation_source: "worktree"` fallback read of the *origin*
  tree's `controller/GENERATION.json`. **The text model** (revision 47,
  local round 46's `OPUS-R46-B1`): `importlib.resources` and
  `pkgutil.get_data` are recognised by an AST walk over every
  `controller/*.py` module — any `Import`/`ImportFrom`/`Attribute` node
  whose resolved dotted name equals one of the two literals, matched
  regardless of import alias, is an occurrence, with no separate text-only
  scan needed since Python's own grammar is the parser. "A file read whose
  path is derived from `Path(__file__).parent`" is an AST **data-flow**
  rule, not a literal match: a call to `open(`, `Path.read_*`,
  `.read_text()`/`.read_bytes()`, or `Path(...)` used as such a call's
  argument is a violation when that argument expression's AST contains a
  `Name` or `Attribute` node that resolves, by straight-line
  reaching-definitions within the same function, to an expression rooted at
  `Path(__file__).parent` (or an import-aliased spelling of it) — a
  dynamically constructed path the scan cannot trace this way is a
  **failure naming the call site**, never a silent pass, which is what
  keeps the two allowlisted exceptions an exhaustive list rather than an
  escape hatch: both are named by their exact call site (`identity.py`'s
  `pin()` and its `generation_source: "worktree"` fallback), not by a
  pattern a third, unreviewed call could also match. The ordinary generation read is
  `git show HEAD:controller/GENERATION.json` against the origin repository,
  which is a `git` invocation rather than a package-relative file read and
  so is not in the scan's scope at all. Everything the allowlist admits
  either reads the snapshot — immutable by construction — or reads the
  origin tree once, at materialisation, before a worker can run.
- **No hot reload, and no override literal.** A source scan asserts that
  `controller/` contains no `importlib.reload`/`imp.reload` occurrence and
  that the literal `USER_OVERRIDE` appears nowhere in `controller/`, since
  the Controller has no reason to mention it at all (the milestone brief's
  "no hot reload... no `USER_OVERRIDE`" prohibitions, capability 9/
  `docs/ACTIVE_MILESTONE.md`). **The text model** (revision 50, local round
  49's `OPUS-R49-B2`, extending the AST model above from two literals to
  four rather than stating a second, separate one): `importlib.reload` and
  `imp.reload` are recognised by the identical AST walk the resource scan
  already runs — an `Import`/`ImportFrom`/`Attribute` node whose resolved
  dotted name equals one of the four literals now, matched regardless of
  import alias. `USER_OVERRIDE` is not a dotted name and gets its own
  rule, stated because none existed: a case-sensitive scan of each
  `controller/*.py` file's **raw source text**, comments and docstrings
  included, for the substring `USER_OVERRIDE`. The scan is deliberately a
  whole-file text search rather than an AST identifier match, so
  `USER_OVERRIDE_PATH` counts as an occurrence (the substring is present)
  and a docstring or comment mentioning the token also counts — a narrower
  rule that ignored either case would pass exactly the build the scan
  exists to catch, since the safety property is "the Controller never
  writes or reads this token anywhere", not "the Controller never binds it
  as an identifier".

`controller/GENERATION.json` is `{"schema_version": 1, "generation": 1}`.
It is the tracked, reviewable declaration of which generation a given
source tree *is* — CP8 compares the running pin's generation against the
one declared at the origin repository's current `HEAD`, and per the rule
above the running pin read its own number from that same `HEAD`.

**Every `SourceSnapshotError` raise sets `evidence['raised_by']`, from a
closed set covering every declared raise site** (revision 52, required
acceptance criterion 6, `OPUS-R51-B1`'s missing-tests obligation: the
channel test 5 and test 6(c) read was declared at those two call sites
only, not as a property of the class, which left every other declared raise
site free to omit it). `materialise()`'s own verification path sets it to
`"materialise"` — both of step 4's second-state refusals, the
malformed-`GENERATION.json` refusal, and the reused-snapshot handoff's
`source_kind`/`source_commit` disagreement. `pin()`'s own verification path
sets it to `"pin"` — the recomputed-digest mismatch against a snapshot's own
name and recorded `tree_digest`, and its own reading of
`WORKFLOW_CONTROLLER_EXEC_HANDOFF`'s carried pair. The `exec_depth >= 1`
fail-safe sets it to `"cli.main"`, named above, since that check runs in the
dispatch code rather than in either verification path. No fourth value
exists and no declared raise site is left unset: an implementation that
sets the key at only the two sites tests 5 and 6(c) read, and leaves it
absent everywhere else, is a `KeyError` waiting for the first operator who
reads a refusal from a third site.

**Tests**: runtime-root containment (a write outside the runtime root
raises `RuntimeContainmentError`); atomic write survives a simulated
interruption (the temp file is left, the target is untouched); `pin()`
records commit, kind and digest; `current()` returns the identical object on
repeated calls and performs no second `git` invocation (asserted by
patching the subprocess helper and counting calls) — this is **REQ-T14**'s
first half; the import-graph assertion; the reload/`USER_OVERRIDE` source
scan above, against the four-literal AST model and the whole-file text
rule, respectively, with the two discriminating fixtures the delimiting
rule requires (revision 50, local round 49's `OPUS-R49-B2` missing-tests
item): a module mentioning `USER_OVERRIDE` only inside a docstring or
comment (red under the stated rule — the substring is present regardless
of context) and a module defining `USER_OVERRIDE_PATH` (also red, for the
same reason) — a build that special-cased either context or word-boundary
would pass one of the two and fail the property the scan exists to prove;
and a `raised_by` invariant scan, over every `raise SourceSnapshotError(...)`
call site in `controller/*.py`, asserting each sets `evidence['raised_by']`
to a member of the closed set `{"materialise", "pin", "cli.main"}`
at the raise, under the model stated below (revision 55, required
acceptance criterion 4, `OPUS-R54-I4` — *"immediately before raising"* was
the superseded assign-then-raise-only rule's own delimiter, and stating it
here contradicted shape (1), which sets the value in the same expression
as the raise rather than in a preceding statement). **The text model, stated for the first time**
(revision 53, required acceptance criterion 4, `OPUS-R52-I2`: the two
siblings in this sentence are each cited against a declared model — the
four-literal AST model and the whole-file text rule, respectively — and
this clause, until now, against neither): the identical AST walk the
reload/resource scan already runs locates every `Raise` node whose raised
expression is a `Call` node resolving to the dotted name
`SourceSnapshotError`, by the same alias-independent resolution rule. A
located call site sets the invariant under either of two shapes, checked
in this order: **(1) inline** — the same `Call`'s own `evidence=` keyword
argument is itself a `Dict` literal carrying the string-literal key
`'raised_by'`, whose associated value is a string literal; or
**(2) assign-then-raise** — that `Raise` node's own preceding sibling
statement in the same block (a single adjacent statement, not a
reaching-definitions search across branches or into a helper) is an
`Assign` node whose target is a `Subscript` on a `Name` (matched by name,
not by tracing the value) equal to the name bound to the same call's
`evidence=` argument, subscripted by the string literal key `'raised_by'`,
with the assigned value itself a string literal. Both shapes are checked
because the invariant is about the value `evidence['raised_by']` holds at
the raise, not about which of the two ordinary ways a Python call site
can produce that value — a raise that is the first statement of its own
block (the `exec_depth >= 1` fail-safe has no preceding sibling at all)
can only ever satisfy shape (1), which is why the scan does not require
shape (2) universally. A call site matching neither shape, or whose
matched literal is not one of the three closed-set members, is a failure
naming the site and the file. **`SourceSnapshotError` is raised, everywhere
in `controller/*.py`, only as a direct `raise` of a `SourceSnapshotError(...)`
call carrying an `evidence=` argument in one of the two stated shapes — an
implementation contract for this checkpoint, not merely the syntax the scan
happens to locate** (revision 55, required acceptance criterion 6,
`OPUS-R54-I7`, replacing a third round of widening: enumerating admissible
syntax has no fixed point, since every widening leaves the next ordinary
construction outside it, so this closes the question by declaration
instead). Under that contract, the classification is stated as an
**ordered, first-match ladder** over a `Raise` node's expression — each
node matches exactly one limb, so the ladder is a function rather than a
set of independently-checked predicates, and no two limbs can disagree
about the same node the way the failure and exclusion clauses previously
could (revision 58, required acceptance criterion 3, `OPUS-R57-I1` — the
prior exclusion clause's third limb stated a head condition, "neither a
direct `Call` nor a bare `Name` resolvable under that rule," and an
appositive enumeration, "an `Attribute`, a `Subscript`, or a `Call` to
anything other than `SourceSnapshotError`," that disagreed about a
helper-call raise such as `raise _make_snapshot_error(path)`: read
literally, the head excludes any direct `Call` from the limb, since the
raise expression is itself a `Call` node, while the appositive names a
`Call` to another name as a member; the two readings produced different
totality verdicts, one of them reopening the exact gap `OPUS-R56-I3` was
raised to close). The **enclosing body** a bare `Name` raise resolves
against is the nearest enclosing function body, or, when the `Raise` node
has no enclosing function at all, the module body (for a raise directly at
module level) or the immediately enclosing class body (for a raise
directly in a class body, outside any method) — the same `Assign`-to-`Call`
binding rule applied within whichever body actually encloses the node,
rather than left undefined outside a function (revision 58, required
acceptance criterion 4, `OPUS-R57-I2`). The ladder, in order, first match
wins:

1. **A direct `Call`** — the raise expression is itself a `Call` node.
   Located and shape-checked as above: conforming under shape (1) or (2)
   satisfies the invariant; a `Call` resolving to `SourceSnapshotError`
   matching neither shape is a failure naming the site; a `Call` resolving
   to any other name (including a helper function, such as
   `_make_snapshot_error`, that is not itself an exception-class
   construction) is **silence** here — every direct `Call` is fully
   disposed of at this limb, positively (conforming), as a failure
   (non-conforming `SourceSnapshotError` construction), or as silence (a
   call to anything else, including a helper function that may itself
   construct and raise a `SourceSnapshotError` deeper in its own body —
   outside this scan's static, one-level domain by declaration, not by
   omission).
2. **A bare `Name` with exactly one qualifying binding** in its enclosing
   body — a single `Assign` node whose target is that name and whose value
   is a `Call`. Resolved single-valuedly: if that one `Call` resolves to
   `SourceSnapshotError`, the node is a failure naming the site
   (`err = SourceSnapshotError(...); raise err`); if it resolves to any
   other name, the node is **silence** — no claim, positive or negative
   (`err = StaleJobRecordError(...); raise err`).
3. **A bare `Name` with more than one qualifying binding** in its enclosing
   body — the one-hop rule does not resolve at all. Declared a failure of
   a third kind, "unresolvable under the one-hop rule, name rebound in the
   same body," naming the site and the file and reported to a human rather
   than silently classified either way (unchanged from revision 57,
   `OPUS-R56-I2`).
4. **A bare `Name` with zero qualifying bindings** in its enclosing body —
   no `Assign` node anywhere in that body targets the name with a `Call`
   value. **Also declared a failure of a third kind**, "unresolvable under
   the one-hop rule, name not bound by a single `Assign` to a `Call` in the
   enclosing body," naming the site and the file and reported to a human —
   the same disposition as limb 3 and for the same reason: an implementer
   who binds the name by annotated assignment
   (`err: SourceSnapshotError = SourceSnapshotError(...)`), by an
   `except … as` clause, by a function parameter, by tuple unpacking, or by
   a `for` target produces a zero-binding `Name` raise, and at least one of
   those constructions — the annotated assignment — is capable of carrying
   a real, unconforming `SourceSnapshotError` construction the scan would
   otherwise pass over in silence; reporting the zero case to a human,
   rather than declaring it out-of-domain, is the same choice made for the
   multiply-bound case and for the same reason (revision 58, required
   acceptance criterion 4, `OPUS-R57-I2`).
5. **A bare `raise` with no expression at all** (a re-raise inside an
   `except` block) — silence, no claim, positive or negative.
6. **Everything else** — an `Attribute` (`raise self._pending_error`) or a
   `Subscript` (`raise deferred_errors[0]`) raise expression, neither a
   direct `Call` nor a bare `Name` at all — declared outside this scan's
   domain and **recorded as unclassified** rather than silently dropped,
   with the contract sentence's own scope noted as broader than the scan
   over this limb: conformance in that region is an implementer obligation
   the scan does not check (unchanged from revision 57, `OPUS-R56-I3`,
   restated as the ladder's own final limb rather than as a separately
   checked fourth exclusion case).

Limbs 1, 3, 4 and 6 each also assert, as part of their own fixture
obligations, that **no second limb matches the same node** — the ladder's
own partition property, checked rather than assumed (missing-tests item
(16), below). Every `Raise` node in `controller/*.py` falls into exactly
one limb: limbs 1–4 are mutually exclusive by construction (a node is a
`Call`, or a bare `Name`, or neither, and among bare `Name`s the binding
count is exactly one number), limb 5 is disjoint from all four (an
expression-less `raise` is neither a `Call` nor a `Name`), and limb 6 is
exactly the residue — neither a `Call`, nor a `Name`, nor expression-less —
so the six limbs partition the full space of `Raise` node shapes rather
than leaving the head-versus-appositive ambiguity `OPUS-R57-I1` found. The
invariant's own scope (*"every `SourceSnapshotError` raise"*) and the
scan's scope (every `Raise` node disposed of by exactly one of the six
limbs above — located and shape-checked, declared non-conforming, declared
silent, declared unresolvable of the third kind by rebinding or by zero
binding, or declared unclassified) therefore coincide by declaration,
closing the gap `OPUS-R54-I7` found without reopening the one
`OPUS-R53-I4` closed and without leaving the classification partial or
contradictory the way `OPUS-R56-I2`, `OPUS-R56-I3` and now `OPUS-R57-I1`,
`OPUS-R57-I2` found it in turn: a future raise added anywhere in
`controller/*.py` that constructs a `SourceSnapshotError` — directly, by
binding it once (or by annotated assignment, by an `except … as` clause,
by a parameter, by tuple unpacking, or by a `for` target, all zero-binding
shapes under limb 4) to a name in the same enclosing body and then raising
that name, or by rebinding that name a second time — without `evidence=`
in one of the two stated shapes is caught here, as a contract violation, a
shape failure, or a declared unresolvable case under limb 3 or limb 4; a
raise of any other taxonomy member, a bare re-raise, or a raise the scan
cannot resolve to a `Call` or a `Name` at all, is declared outside the
scan's domain rather than silently passed over — rather than surfacing as
a `KeyError` at the first operator who reads the refusal, and rather than
passing silently unlocated the way a `Name`-valued raise of
`SourceSnapshotError` itself did under the enumeration this contract
replaces, the way a helper-call-valued raise of `SourceSnapshotError` did
under the classification revision 55 closed, and the way an
annotated-assignment-bound raise of `SourceSnapshotError` would have done
under the undomained zero case revision 57 left open
(revision 52, required acceptance criterion 6; extraction model added
revision 53, required acceptance criterion 4, `OPUS-R52-I2`; widened to
admit the inline-literal shape and the no-preceding-sibling case, revision
54, required acceptance criterion 4, `OPUS-R53-I4` — the assign-then-raise-only
rule was red against ordinary code that already satisfies the invariant,
including the fail-safe site's own first-statement-of-block raise; closed
by declared contract rather than a fourth widening, revision 55, required
acceptance criterion 6, `OPUS-R54-I7` — the widened rule's own completeness
claim was false of exactly the two constructions just named: a `Name`-valued
`Raise` expression is never located at all, and `evidence=dict(raised_by=
"materialise")` is a `Call` to `dict`, not a `Dict` literal, so it matches
neither shape; the failure predicate bounded to the name-binding-resolvable
domain rather than every unresolved raise, revision 56, required acceptance
criterion 2, `OPUS-R55-I2` — the undomained predicate condemned every
ordinary raise of the other refusal-taxonomy members and every bare
re-raise, the same defect measured from the opposite side of the one
`OPUS-R54-I7` closed; the resolution rule made single-valued and the
multiply-bound name given a declared third verdict, and the classification
made total over non-`Call`/non-`Name` raise expressions, revision 57,
required acceptance criterion 4, `OPUS-R56-I2` and `OPUS-R56-I3` — the
bounded rule from revision 56 assigned contradictory verdicts to a single
rebound name under its existential reading, since a name bound once to
`SourceSnapshotError` and once to another taxonomy member satisfied both
the failure clause and the exclusion clause at once with no stated
tiebreak, and either clause winning unconditionally broke one of the two
properties the bounding was adopted to hold simultaneously: the failure
clause winning reintroduced `OPUS-R55-I2`'s own defect through the
quantifier rather than the predicate, and the exclusion clause winning
lost the true-positive case `OPUS-R54-I7` exists to catch; choosing "the
name has more than one binding" as its own decidable, single-valued
condition — rather than a reaching-definitions search over which binding
reaches the raise, the analysis this design already refuses to require —
resolves the contradiction without reopening either finding, reporting the
case as evidence for a human instead of classifying it by fiat; separately,
the exclusion clause's first two limbs left the classification non-total,
since a raise resolving to neither an exception class the scan names nor
`SourceSnapshotError`, because it is not a `Call` or a `Name` at all,
fell into neither the failure clause nor either exclusion limb, leaving an
implementer with no instruction, and since a helper call resolving to
`SourceSnapshotError` is a real violation of the contract sentence, the
scan was silently wrong about it rather than declaring the residue, the
same "passing silently unlocated" outcome `OPUS-R54-I7` closed for the
`Name`-valued case, one construction over, which the third, catch-all limb
then closed by declaration; **restated as an ordered, first-match ladder
that partitions the `Raise` node space, with the zero-binding name and the
no-enclosing-function case each given their own declared, reported
verdict, revision 58, required acceptance criteria 3 and 4, `OPUS-R57-I1`
and `OPUS-R57-I2`** — the previous exclusion clause's third limb stated a
head condition and an appositive enumeration that disagreed about a
helper-call raise, one reading of which reopened `OPUS-R56-I3`'s own gap
and the other of which made two limbs overlap and prescribe different
outputs for an ordinary direct raise of another taxonomy member; and the
previous resolution rule never stated a verdict for a `Name` with zero
qualifying bindings — reachable by an annotated assignment, an
`except … as` clause, a function parameter, tuple unpacking or a `for`
target, of which the annotated-assignment case can carry a real,
unconforming construction the scan would otherwise silently pass — or for
a `Raise` node with no enclosing function body at all, at module level or
directly in a class body, for which "the enclosing function body" was
undefined rather than merely empty). Seven fixture pairs (and one
additional single-fixture pin) pin the model. Two discriminating fixtures
pin the widened rule (revision
54, missing-tests item 4, `OPUS-R53-I4`): a raise site whose `evidence=`
argument is an inline `Dict` literal carrying `'raised_by'` (classified
correctly only because shape (1) inspects the call itself, not a preceding
statement), and a raise that is the first statement of its enclosing
block, with no preceding sibling to inspect at all (reachable only through
shape (1), since shape (2) does not apply) — both must classify as
satisfying the invariant under the rule as stated, and neither was
reachable by the rule before revision 54. **A third fixture pair pins the
contract boundary, extending missing-tests item (5) below** (revision 55,
`OPUS-R54-I7`): a
raise site of the form `err = SourceSnapshotError(...); raise err`, and one
whose `evidence=` argument is `dict(raised_by="materialise")` rather than a
`Dict` literal — both must classify as contract violations naming the
site, neither as unlocated nor as silently satisfying the invariant. **A
fourth, negative fixture pins the same boundary from the other side, and
gains a third, rebinding case at revision 57** (revision 56, required
acceptance criterion 3, `OPUS-R55-I2`; case three added revision 57,
required acceptance criterion 4, `OPUS-R56-I2`): a
`raise StaleJobRecordError(...)` site, and a bare `raise` re-raise with no
expression inside an `except` block — neither is a `SourceSnapshotError`
construction under the name-binding rule stated above, and the scan must
not flag either as a contract violation or as a shape failure; the third
fixture pair's two cases are unchanged and remain contract violations
under the ladder. The third case is a function with two
refusal paths reusing one local name, one bound to a `SourceSnapshotError`
call and the other to a different taxonomy member's call — the
`SourceSnapshotError`-bound raise must be reported, the
other-taxonomy-member-bound raise must not, and if a name is bound to more
than one such call the multiply-bound raise is reported under the declared
third verdict rather than as either, and the fixture asserts that **no
second limb also matches** the multiply-bound node (revision 58, required
acceptance criterion 3, `OPUS-R57-I1`, missing-tests item (16)). **A fifth
fixture pair pins the totality boundary** (revision 57, required
acceptance criterion 4,
`OPUS-R56-I3`): raise sites of the `Attribute` shape
(`raise self._pending_error`), the `Subscript` shape
(`raise deferred_errors[0]`), and the helper-call shape
(`raise _make_snapshot_error(path)`) — each must be classified as
**out-of-domain and recorded as unclassified**, not merely as not flagged,
so a scan that silently drops them is distinguishable from one that
records them; the helper-call case also asserts it is disposed of by limb
1's own silent branch and matches no other limb, closing the exact
head-versus-appositive ambiguity `OPUS-R57-I1` found (revision 58,
required acceptance criterion 3). **A sixth fixture set pins the
zero-binding case** (revision 58, required acceptance criterion 4,
`OPUS-R57-I2`, missing-tests item (17)): a raise site whose name is bound
only by an annotated assignment
(`err: SourceSnapshotError = SourceSnapshotError("unpinned", evidence={"detail": root}); raise err`)
must be reported under the declared third verdict, since it is a genuine,
unconforming `SourceSnapshotError` construction the scan would otherwise
pass over in silence; and at least one ordinary zero-binding raise — a
name bound by an `except … as` handler, or by a function parameter — must
receive the same declared third verdict without being a true positive,
distinguishing the repair that catches the annotated-assignment case from
one that merely declares the residue. **A seventh fixture pins the
no-enclosing-function case** (revision 58, required acceptance criterion
4, `OPUS-R57-I2`, missing-tests item (18)): a bare `Name` raise with no
enclosing function body at all — directly inside a class body's own
method-less statement, or at module level — must receive the same
declared third verdict, under the enclosing-body definition stated above,
rather than raise inside the scan itself or leave the case undefined.

**Nine tests pin the immutable-execution model**, and they are listed
individually because revision 32 exists precisely because a plausible
argument stood in for them, revision 33 exists because two of the seven it
wrote were pointed at the case that passes, revision 34 exists because
four of the nine *those* produced asserted a property that is false at the
default layout, read an instrument that was never defined, or named an error
the specified path cannot raise, and revision 35 exists because the mechanism
all nine observe could not survive its own first execution — importing the
snapshot modified it — and because two of the fixture coordinates revision 34
named resolve to something the tests cannot run against. Revision 35 adds none
and changes three, tests 1, 4 and 8:

1. a clean source tree materialises `source_kind == "commit"` with
   `source_commit` equal to `HEAD` and `tree_digest` equal to a
   recomputation over the snapshot; and `step` is then run as a subprocess
   with **all four of its fixture coordinates named rather than inherited**
   — **working directory** that source checkout itself, **invocation route**
   the installed `workflow-controller` console script, **installation mode** a
   default editable install (`pip install -e`) of that same checkout, and
   **runtime root** the default, no `--runtime-dir` passed. Each is chosen,
   not defaulted.
   The working directory is the directory that contains `controller/` and
   therefore the exact case revision 32's exec looped in. The console script
   is the operator's real invocation and is the only route that leaves the
   *child* as the process under test: for a script Python prepends the
   **script's** directory rather than the working directory, whereas
   `python -m controller` from here would have the **parent** import the
   checkout's own package before any Controller code ran, and `python -P -m`
   would hand the parent the very flag under test (revision 34, local round
   33's `OPUS-R33-O1`). The default runtime root is chosen because
   `<origin>/.controller` is what an operator actually gets and is the layout
   in which containment is hardest to state correctly; CP8 step 7 covers the
   relocated layout, since its step 2 passes `--runtime-dir <tmp>` outside
   the clone, so the two together cover both (revision 34, local round 33's
   `OPUS-R33-B1`).

   **The installation mode is the fourth coordinate, and revision 34 left it
   unnamed — which made the route it had just named undecidable** (revision
   35, local round 34's `OPUS-R34-B3`). *"The installed console script"* is
   three different fixtures, and measured across all three on Python 3.14.7
   only one of them is this test. `pip install ./checkout` resolves the
   parent's `Path(__file__).parent.parent` to `site-packages`, which is not a
   Git repository, so `materialise()` cannot run and every assertion below is
   not merely unmet but unreachable — the boundary the `origin_source_root`
   bullet now states. `pip install -e ./checkout` — setuptools' default, a
   `.pth` that installs a `sys.meta_path` **finder**, *appended* after
   `PathFinder` so `sys.path` still decides — resolves it to the checkout and
   puts **nothing** of the checkout on the child's `sys.path`; measured, the
   child's `sys.path` holds the snapshot and the interpreter's own entries and
   no other path inside the checkout. That is the fixture this test requires.
   `pip install -e ./checkout --config-settings editable_mode=compat`, and
   legacy `setup.py develop`, write a `.pth` holding the bare project root,
   which puts **the checkout root itself** on the child's `sys.path`;
   measured, it appears as an entry while the import still resolves to the
   snapshot, so the mechanism is correct and only the containment assertion
   below is red — `OPUS-R33-B1` recurring under a coordinate revision 34
   introduced while fixing it. The fixture is therefore the default editable
   install, named, **and the property it must have is stated so that a future
   packaging change is caught rather than silently weakening the test**: the
   console script's `controller` package resolves to the checkout, and no
   installation artefact puts the checkout root on the child's `sys.path`.
   Naming the mode is chosen over restating the assertion to permit that
   entry, which would weaken the one property this test exists for. It then
   asserts: `.controller/identity.json`'s recorded
   **`exec_depth` is exactly `1`**; the child's `source_root` is inside
   `<runtime_root>/source/<tree_digest>/`; its recorded
   `interpreter_safe_path` is true; `interpreter_sys_path[0]` equals that
   `source_root`; and **no entry of `interpreter_sys_path` is the checkout
   root, and no entry lies inside the checkout other than that snapshot** —
   the identity bullet's form, not revision 33's *"no entry … lies inside the
   checkout"*, which at the default runtime root is unsatisfiable against a
   correct build because the snapshot is inside the checkout by design.
   Naming all three coordinates is load-bearing for one reason: a test that
   inherits any of them passes in whatever environment the harness happened
   to create and says nothing about the invocation an operator actually
   makes, which is how revision 32's specification could carry a defect that
   a *required* test was supposed to cover (local round 32's
   `OPUS-R32-B1`);
2. a dirty source tree refuses `step` with `DirtyControllerSourceError`,
   and **no snapshot directory is created and no exec occurs** — the
   refusal precedes the side effect. *"No exec occurs"* is observed rather
   than assumed, and needs no counter, because this case runs **in process**:
   `cli.main` is called directly, and the assertion is that the call raised
   `DirtyControllerSourceError` and **returned control at all**. `os.execv`
   never returns, so a call that comes back is itself the proof — a stronger
   instrument here than `exec_depth`, which by construction cannot be written
   by a process that was replaced, and which answers nothing when no child is
   ever created (revision 34, local round 33's `OPUS-R33-I1`). The test
   asserts alongside it that no snapshot directory and no `identity.json`
   were written;
3. the same dirty tree under `--allow-dirty-source` materialises
   `source_kind == "worktree"` with `source_commit is None` and a
   `tree_digest` that differs from the clean tree's, and the job record
   carries that pair;
4. the same bytes materialised twice reuse one snapshot directory, and a
   single byte changed in the source produces a different directory — **and
   the two materialisations are two real pinned runs, not two calls to
   `materialise()`** (revision 35, local round 34's `OPUS-R34-B1`). The test
   runs `step` twice through test 1's fixture, and asserts between and after
   them that the snapshot directory's recomputed digest still equals both its
   own name and its `SOURCE_PIN.json`'s recorded `tree_digest`, that the
   second run **reused** the directory rather than publishing a new one or
   refusing, and that `controller/__pycache__/` does not exist inside the
   snapshot. A reuse-verification exercised only *before* the snapshot has
   ever been imported cannot observe the one thing that actually modifies a
   snapshot in normal operation — executing it — which is exactly how
   revision 34 specified a design whose second correct run refused
   permanently. The `__pycache__` assertion is the direct instrument for the
   `-B` token in the re-exec argv, and it goes red if a later edit drops it.
   **A third run adds the instrument for the reuse rewrite's temporary,
   and it interrupts the rewrite rather than planting a file** (the clause
   is revision 36's, from local round 35's `OPUS-R35-I1`; the fixture is
   revision 37's, from local round 36's `OPUS-R36-B2`). The third run is a
   real reuse whose `SOURCE_PIN.json` rewrite is **interrupted between
   `fsync` and `os.replace`** — the crash the clause exists for, injected
   at that seam — and the test then asserts two things: that the snapshot
   directory afterwards contains **nothing but the extracted sources and
   `SOURCE_PIN.json`**, which is the clause stated as an assertion; and
   that a **fourth** run still **reuses** the snapshot and still passes the
   two-way binding. Both are red against the same-directory temporary rule,
   which leaves `SOURCE_PIN.json.tmp` inside the verified directory and so
   changes its recomputed digest permanently, and both are green against
   the rule step 3 now states. **Neither planted-file variant discriminates,
   which is why the fixture is an interruption**: a file planted at
   `<runtime_root>/source/.SOURCE_PIN.<token>.tmp` — revision 36's own
   specification for this case — is outside the digest and outside step 3's
   check under *both* rules, so it is green against both and pins nothing;
   and one planted inside the snapshot is red under both, since this rule
   never excludes that name, it only never writes it. It is the direct
   instrument for that clause exactly as the `__pycache__` assertion is for
   `-B`, and it is a fixture change rather than a new test: test 4 stays
   one of CP1's nine;
5. a snapshot whose content is altered after materialisation refuses with
   `SourceSnapshotError` on the next run rather than executing, and so does
   one whose `SOURCE_PIN.json` digest is edited to match the alteration —
   the directory-name binding is what catches the second. **Both refusals
   are raised by `materialise()`, not by `pin()`, and the test names the
   entry point** (revision 34, local round 33's `OPUS-R33-I2`), **asserted
   through a stated channel rather than by reading a traceback**: both
   raise the same `SourceSnapshotError` class, and the raising function
   sets `evidence['raised_by']` to the literal string `"materialise"` or
   `"pin"` naming itself at the raise (revision 55, `OPUS-R54-I4`, swept in
   the same pass as CP1's `**Tests**:` clause above), so the test asserts
   `exc.evidence["raised_by"] == "materialise"` for these two cases and
   `== "pin"` for the third case below (revision 51, local round 50's
   `OPUS-R50-B2`: the entry-point identification is category-(B) under the
   fifth source and had no declared channel before this revision). On that next
   run the operator is unpinned in the origin, so `cli.main` materialises
   before any child exists; the origin's bytes are unchanged, so the digest
   and therefore the directory name are unchanged; step 3 finds the
   directory and its verification fails; and step 4's second state refuses by
   name, at exit **20**. Under revision 33's undivided step 4 that path
   `os.replace`d onto a non-empty directory instead and raised `OSError:
   [Errno 39] Directory not empty`, so the error this test named was not the
   error the specified path produced — the test would have been red against a
   build that followed the specification exactly. The test also asserts the
   altered directory is left **untouched** by the refusal, since it is the
   evidence. A third case covers the other entry point, where it genuinely is
   `pin()`: the altered snapshot run **directly**, with no origin repository
   and no materialisation, refuses on the recomputed digest against both the
   recorded `tree_digest` and the directory's own name;
6. the guard's two mechanisms, tested apart because only one of them is
   reachable in ordinary use: **(a)** `inspect`, `explain` and `status`
   succeed at `source_kind == "unpinned"`, including from a directory that
   is not a Git repository at all, and materialise no snapshot. **Its
   installation mode and runtime root are named, for the same reason test
   1's four coordinates are** (revision 36, local round 35's
   `OPUS-R35-B2`): this is the test whose subject *is* the non-checkout
   install, revision 35 left it inheriting both, and measured, the mode
   decides the outcome. It runs in **three** installation modes — the
   default editable install (origin is the checkout, ladder row 3), a
   non-editable install into a writable venv, and that same non-editable
   install with its prefix made read-only (`chmod a-w`), which is the
   ordinary system-package case. The last two resolve the runtime root by
   ladder **row 4** — and **row 4's own coordinate is named as a fixture
   coordinate rather than inherited from the harness** (revision 37, local
   round 36's `OPUS-R36-I1`): each of those two modes sets `XDG_STATE_HOME`
   to its own fresh temporary directory, and the test asserts the resolved
   root **equals** `$XDG_STATE_HOME/workflow-controller/`. Revision 36 named
   the mode and left the root unnamed, which resolves it to the developer's
   or CI runner's real user-state directory — a directory this test then
   *writes* to, since the identity record is written by every command that
   reaches its body, read-only ones included, at `exec_depth: 0`. That is
   the same inherited-coordinate defect `OPUS-R35-B2` charged against this
   test, reappearing inside the fix for it, and the reason test 1 names four
   coordinates. With the root named, *"`.controller/` is **never** created
   anywhere inside `site-packages`"* is a check rather than an observation
   about one machine; it holds in all three modes, and all three read-only
   commands exit **0** in all three — including the read-only prefix, which
   under rows 1–3 raised a bare `PermissionError`. Two further cases pin
   what the ladder added: `--runtime-dir` pointed at an unwritable directory
   raises `RuntimeRootUnwritableError` at exit **20**, not `PermissionError`;
   and `status` against a never-written root exits **0**, naming that root —
   **that case gets a third, fresh `XDG_STATE_HOME` of its own**, because
   the only root its siblings establish is one modes 2 and 3 have just
   written `identity.json` into, which would make *"never-written"* true or
   false by execution order rather than by construction. **What that case
   asserts is the report itself, not only the exit code** (revision 38,
   local round 37's `OPUS-R37-I2`): stdout reads `no Controller runtime
   state at <path>` with the resolved root and the **ladder row** that chose
   it named, the exit is **0**, and — free from the same fixture, and the
   assertion that pins the identity-write ordering — `identity.json`
   **exists** in that fresh root afterwards. A **second** `status` against
   that same root then reports the identity record rather than the
   empty-root line. That pair is what discriminates the two readings of
   *"never written"*; asserting exit 0 and the path alone passes under
   either, which is what revision 37 shipped. **(b)** the
   three non-read-only command *functions*, called directly with an
   `"unpinned"` identity — bypassing `cli.main`'s materialise step, which
   is the only way the assertion is reachable at all — each raise
   `SourceSnapshotError`, asserted by iterating the CLI's own command table
   so a command added later is covered without editing the test; and
   **(c)** the acting mechanism's own failure, `step` invoked through
   `cli.main` in a **non-Git** unpinned directory, which raises
   `SourceSnapshotError` from materialisation rather than from the
   assertion, because no snapshot can be established there — asserted, as
   in test 5, via `exc.evidence["raised_by"] == "materialise"` (revision
   51, local round 50's `OPUS-R50-B2`), the same channel and the same
   discriminating pair test 5's own third case already supplies the other
   half of;
7. the eager-load and no-late-read assertions above, run as the two
   structural halves of the same property;
8. **the decoy case, which fails loudly instead of hanging**: the same clean
   tree, `step` run **through the installed `workflow-controller` console
   script** — the same default-editable-install fixture test 1 names, for the
   same measured reasons — with the working directory set to a scratch
   directory containing
   a `controller/` package that is **not** the Controller — a single
   `__init__.py` that raises on import. The route is named for the same
   reason as test 1's, and here it is not interchangeable at all: measured,
   `python -m controller` from that directory imports the decoy in the
   **parent** (`RuntimeError: DECOY IMPORTED`, exit 1, out of `runpy`), so
   the test fails without ever reaching the mechanism it exists to measure,
   while `python -P -m` works but hands the parent the flag under test
   (revision 34, local round 33's `OPUS-R33-O1`). It asserts that
   `identity.json`'s recorded **`exec_depth` is exactly `1`**, that the decoy
   is never imported, and that `interpreter_sys_path` holds neither the
   scratch directory nor the origin checkout root as an entry and no entry
   inside the checkout other than the snapshot. **Under revision 32's
   specification this case is an attributable first-exec failure, not a
   loop**: revision 33 wrote *"an unbounded exec loop"* here and contradicted
   its own next sentence two clauses later — a decoy that raises on import
   kills the child on the **first** exec, which is exactly why a decoy was
   chosen over a bare counter. The looping case is **test 1's**, where the
   working directory holds a real `controller/` package that resolves, runs
   unpinned and execs again; saying which case is which is what makes the
   pair's division of labour visible instead of overlapping (revision 34,
   local round 33's `OPUS-R33-O1`). The decoy is what turns *the wrong root
   was imported* into an immediate, attributable failure rather than a
   timeout,
   and a timeout is what matters here: the natural repair for a hanging test
   is to point it at a harmless working directory, which turns it green and
   leaves production broken. That is this document's own recurring class — a
   required test satisfied by the wrong fixture — and the decoy is chosen
   specifically so the wrong fixture cannot satisfy it;
9. **dirt outside the snapshot's pathspec is not dirt**: a source tree whose
   only modification is to a path the snapshot does not contain — a `docs/`
   file, say — runs `step` **without** `--allow-dirty-source`, materialises
   `source_kind == "commit"` with `source_commit` equal to `HEAD`, and
   produces a `tree_digest` equal to the same tree's when clean; and a
   modification to `pyproject.toml` or anything under `controller/` refuses
   without the flag. The pair pins the `git status --porcelain -- controller
   pyproject.toml` scoping from both sides rather than leaving it to the
   implementer.

Three further tests pin the generation-source rule specifically, because it
is a composition defect that only shows up across two checkpoints: a source
tree whose committed `GENERATION.json` says 1 while the **worktree** file
says 2 pins `generation == 1` and `generation_source == "head"` under
`--allow-dirty-source` — and CP8's `detect()` against it returns `None`,
not an error (this is the exact case round 1 found, asserted by name at
both ends); a source tree with no `controller/GENERATION.json` at `HEAD`
materialises from the worktree with `generation_source == "worktree"`, and
a worker-launching command against it refuses with
`DirtyControllerSourceError` unless `--allow-dirty-source` is passed; a
malformed `GENERATION.json` refuses rather than defaulting.

### CP2 — Managed-repository inspection

**Owns**: REQ-1, REQ-8 (partly), REQ-T1, REQ-T2, REQ-T3, REQ-41 (partly, revision 64), REQ-43 (revision 68), REQ-T18B (revision 68).

**Files**: `controller/managed_repo.py`, `tests/test_managed_repo.py`,
`tests/fixtures.py` (extended).

`inspect(path, *, manager_bin=None) -> ManagedRepository`, in this fixed
order, refusing at the first failure:

1. `git -C <path> rev-parse --show-toplevel` must succeed and the result is
   the canonical repository root → else `NotARepositoryError`.
2. `.workflow-manager/installation.json` must exist → else
   `UnmanagedRepositoryError`. It must parse and declare `schema_version`,
   `workflow_version` and `profile` → else
   `MalformedInstallationManifestError`. **`schema_version` is gated on its
   value, not only its presence** (revision 49, local round 48's
   `OPUS-R48-O1`): absent or not `1` → `MalformedInstallationManifestError`,
   the same shape CP3 already states in its own fail-closed list for
   `WORKFLOW_STATE.json`'s own `schema_version` absent or not `1` and the
   same defect this step's own
   `profile` paragraph below names and closes for `profile` — a parsed
   field with no consumer.
3. The `workflow-manager` executable is resolved from `--workflow-manager`,
   then `WORKFLOW_CONTROLLER_WORKFLOW_MANAGER`, then
   `shutil.which("workflow-manager")`. Unresolvable or not executable →
   `WorkflowManagerUnavailableError`. **Absence is never treated as
   "assume clean"** — that is precisely the unsafe-operation case the
   milestone brief asks to refuse.
4. **`workflow-manager verify <root>` is the admission gate; it must exit
   0.** `status <root>` is also run, and must exit 0 too, but as a
   *corroborating* signal — a non-zero exit from either is
   `DriftedInstallationError`, carrying both commands' verbatim
   stdout/stderr as evidence.

   **Which subcommand is authoritative is not symmetric, and revision 2
   recorded it as if it were.** Round 2 measured it and revision 3 records
   it in the Environment-facts table above: for an **unmanaged**
   repository `status` exits **0** while printing `not a managed
   repository`, and only `verify` exits non-zero (2). So "both must exit 0"
   is true of the *check* but false of the *reasoning*: `status`'s exit
   code carries no admission signal at all in the case that matters most.

   As written CP2 is saved by ordering rather than by this rule — step 2
   already refuses an unmanaged repository on the missing manifest, before
   step 4 runs, and `verify` would refuse anyway. It is recorded here
   because the *stated fact* is what a later generation reasons from, and a
   future reordering that dropped step 2 in favour of "just ask the
   Manager" would silently reopen the hole. `verify` is named the admission
   gate so that reordering cannot.
5. **The manifest's `(workflow_version, profile)` pair must satisfy the
   Controller's supported-baseline rule**, checked here — before any
   command file or Workflow state is read. **Revision 64 replaced the
   closed pair-set with a line predicate; revision 68 narrows admission
   again, to a closed set of individually validated releases inside that
   line** (manual external plan review round 67's `I1`), and the
   "Supported Workflow baseline" policy above, not this step, is the
   authority:

   - `workflow_version` must parse as a dotted release whose **major and
     minor components are exactly those of `SUPPORTED_WORKFLOW_LINE`
     (`"2.5"`)** — a value that does not parse as a dotted release at all
     is `UnsupportedWorkflowVersionError` naming the observed string, never
     a best-effort prefix match. This is checked first because it is the
     cheaper, coarser refusal, and because its evidence names a different
     defect class from the check below (a release outside the known line
     at all, versus one inside it that has never been individually
     validated);
   - `workflow_version` must **also** be an exact member of
     `VALIDATED_WORKFLOW_RELEASES` (`{"2.5.1"}`) — the admission gate
     itself. A version that parses into the `2.5` line but is not in this
     set (`2.5.0`, or any `2.5.x` patch newer than `2.5.1`) is refused with
     `UnsupportedWorkflowVersionError`, with evidence stating explicitly
     that the release is in the supported line but has not been
     individually validated — distinct wording from the line-predicate
     refusal above, so the two failure classes are never conflated in a
     report a human reads;
   - `profile` must be a member of `SUPPORTED_PROFILES =
     {"runtime", "full"}`;
   - `REFERENCE_WORKFLOW_RELEASE = "2.5.1"` is carried alongside both and
     is **not** a third admission gate: since revision 68 it is also the
     sole member of `VALIDATED_WORKFLOW_RELEASES`, so the same value names
     the release every phase, command and denylist inventory in this
     document was derived from *and* the one release currently admitted;
     it is what a refusal message quotes when it says which release the
     Controller's inventories were measured against.

   An unsupported *version* — wrong line, or right line but unvalidated —
   is `UnsupportedWorkflowVersionError`; a supported, validated version
   with an unsupported *profile* is `UnsupportedInstallProfileError`; every
   refusal names the observed value, and the version refusal additionally
   names which of the two checks it failed. Revisions 1–31 required the
   manifest to declare `profile` in step 2 and then gated on
   `workflow_version` alone, leaving a parsed field with no consumer —
   the same shape as the `VERIFIED` status revision 15 removed. Revision 32
   closed that with the pair-set `{("2.3.1", "runtime"), ("2.3.1",
   "full")}` (external round 31's `EXT-PLAN-R31-O1`); revisions 32–63 kept
   it, and its only distinguishing effect once the Manager shipped 2.4.0
   and 2.5.x was to refuse the Manager's own default install — including
   **this repository's**, which is the reproduction round 63's `B6`
   carries. Revision 64's line predicate over-corrected that: it admitted
   every `2.5.x` patch sight unseen, which manual external round 67's `I1`
   found was not fail-closed against a same-named command's semantics
   drifting between patches. Revision 68's `VALIDATED_WORKFLOW_RELEASES`
   keeps revision 32's fail-closed discipline — nothing is admitted until
   it has been measured — while keeping the line predicate's diagnostic
   value and its stated, repeatable growth procedure, rather than reverting
   to an unexplained closed pair-set. **Both profiles are supported rather
   than only the one this repository happens to use**, because the
   Environment-facts row above measures that they install the identical
   command and tooling surface; a profile the Manager may add later is
   refused until it has been measured, which is the fail-closed direction,
   and so is every release outside `VALIDATED_WORKFLOW_RELEASES` — whether
   or not it is inside the `2.5` line.

**Two design decisions worth challenging explicitly:**

- **Exit code is authoritative; text is evidence — but only `verify`'s
  exit code is an admission signal.** Neither subcommand has a
  machine-readable output mode (verified above). Parsing
  `workflow 2.3.1 (full profile) — clean` for semantics would couple the
  Controller to the Manager's prose and re-derive drift judgement from
  strings — exactly the "do not reimplement Workflow Manager
  install/update/drift semantics" prohibition. So the Controller takes the
  Manager's verdict from its exit status and stores the text unparsed, for
  a human to read in a refusal report. The refinement revision 3 adds is
  *which* exit status: `verify`'s, because `status` exits 0 on an
  unmanaged repository (measured). Reading the text to recover what
  `status`'s exit code failed to say would be exactly the prose-parsing
  this decision rejects, so the Controller does not do that either — it
  relies on `verify` and on the manifest.
- **The installed version and profile come from the manifest, not from the
  Manager's stdout.** `.workflow-manager/installation.json` is the record
  the Manager itself writes; reading its own `workflow_version` and
  `profile` fields is integration, not reimplementation, and it does not
  depend on output formatting that the Manager is free to change. The
  Manager's `status` prose does name the profile (`workflow 2.3.1 (full
  profile) — clean`), and the Controller still does not read it there, for
  the same reason it does not read the version there.

**Tests** (`REQ-T1`/`T2`/`T3`): a fixture-built managed repository verifies
clean; a bare `git init` directory raises `UnmanagedRepositoryError`; a
truncated/invalid manifest raises `MalformedInstallationManifestError`; a
manifest whose `schema_version` is absent, or present but not `1`, raises
`MalformedInstallationManifestError` (revision 49, local round 48's
`OPUS-R48-O1`) — two cases, since a build that checks only presence
passes the absent case and fails the wrong-value one; a
stub `workflow-manager` script that exits non-zero raises
`DriftedInstallationError` and the evidence contains the stub's output; a
missing executable raises `WorkflowManagerUnavailableError`.

**The baseline predicate gets its own seven cases** (revision 64, round
63's `B6`; widened from four to seven at revision 68, manual external round
67's `I1`, `REQ-T18B`), because a bare line predicate, a bare closed set
and the two-tier rule revision 68 adopts each agree on a different subset
of them, and a suite written against any one of the first two passes cases
it should not: a manifest declaring **`2.5.1`** is admitted (the reference
release, this repository's own, and `VALIDATED_WORKFLOW_RELEASES`'s only
member); one declaring **`2.4.0`** raises `UnsupportedWorkflowVersionError`
naming the observed version, the line and the reference release, with
evidence stating the release is outside the supported line entirely (as
does `2.3.1`, the superseded baseline, which is asserted explicitly so that
"the Controller no longer runs against the release it was designed on" is
a *stated, tested* fact rather than a side effect); one declaring
**`2.6.0`** raises the same wrong-line refusal, which is what keeps the
line predicate a line rather than a floor; and a manifest whose
`workflow_version` is not a dotted release at all (`"latest"`, `""`) raises
`UnsupportedWorkflowVersionError` too, never a prefix match — four cases,
unchanged in shape from revision 64's own four, all still wrong-line
refusals.

**Two further cases were revision 64's own discriminator and are now the
opposite of what revision 64 asserted, which is the change `I1` requires.**
A manifest declaring **`2.5.0`** — a real, currently-distributed release —
now raises `UnsupportedWorkflowVersionError` too, but with evidence naming
the *other* reason: the release is inside `SUPPORTED_WORKFLOW_LINE` but is
not a member of `VALIDATED_WORKFLOW_RELEASES`, so its refusal message and
its evidence dictionary are asserted to differ from `2.4.0`'s — this is
what discriminates the two-tier rule from a bare line predicate, the same
role revision 64 gave this case for discriminating a line from a closed
pair-set, inverted: revision 64 asserted `2.5.0` **admitted** (no closed
`2.5.1`-only set would have that), and revision 68 asserts it **refused**,
by name, as the direct consequence of `I1`'s acceptance criterion 1.

**The seventh case is the one `I1`'s own missing-test requirement asks
for, and it is the case the six above cannot exercise: same inventory,
different, unvalidated release.** A fixture repository is built whose
`.claude/commands/` tree and whose `scripts/workflow_state.py`
`KNOWN_PHASES` block are byte-identical copies of the reference `2.5.1`
tree — so the phase set, the command-file partition and the user-only set
CP3/CP4/CP5 read are, by construction, identical to the admitted case — and
whose `installation.json` alone declares `workflow_version: "2.5.2"`, a
release that does not exist in the Manager's own `distribution/` and was
never measured. This manifest is refused with `UnsupportedWorkflowVersionError`,
carrying the same "known line, unvalidated release" evidence as the
`2.5.0` case. The test asserts refusal **and** that CP2 never reaches
CP3/CP4's inventory reads for this fixture — the assertion that
discriminates this design from one that (wrongly) falls back to an
inventory-equality check when the exact version is unrecognised, which
would readmit exactly the case `I1` exists to close. `REQ-T18` (CP9's
disposable-managed-repository integration test) continues to exercise the
repository's actually-installed, actually-validated release and is
unaffected; this seventh case is `REQ-T18B`, a CP2 unit-level fixture, not
a live-Manager integration test, since the release it names is
deliberately one the Manager cannot produce.

**The profile pair gets its own three tests** (revision 32, re-pointed at
the reference release in revision 64): a manifest declaring
`profile: "runtime"` at `2.5.1` is **admitted**, and the same fixture
asserts the seventeen command files CP4 partitions are all present under
it, which is the fact that licenses admitting it; a manifest declaring an
unknown profile at `2.5.1` raises
`UnsupportedInstallProfileError` naming both the observed value and
`SUPPORTED_PROFILES`; and the refusal is asserted to happen **before**
any command file or `WORKFLOW_STATE.json` read, by pointing the fixture at
a repository whose Workflow state is deliberately unparseable — if CP3's
`MalformedWorkflowStateError` surfaces instead, the ordering regressed.
Where the real Manager is reachable the `runtime` fixture is additionally
built with `workflow-manager bootstrap --profile runtime`, and is skipped
when it is not, the same posture as the existing real-Manager test.

**The asymmetry gets its own test** (revision 3, round 2's I3): a stub
Manager whose `status` exits **0** while `verify` exits non-zero must still
produce `DriftedInstallationError`. Revision 2's tests only ever made the
stub fail both subcommands together, so nothing pinned the case the real
Manager actually exhibits, and a regression that started trusting `status`
would have gone unnoticed. The stub
Manager keeps this suite hermetic and offline; one test additionally runs
against the **real** installed `workflow-manager` and is skipped when it is
absent, so the integration is genuinely exercised where available without
making the suite depend on it.
