`record_local_plan_review`, a durable state write — and passes only under
the branch reading, because on `BLOCK` that step is *"a true no-op"*
(`scripts/workflow_state.py:12419-12420`). The branch is now declared, so
the property can express it. Row 5's branch is the governing-version one,
already a key field; its `"1"` exit is `apply-plan-review.md`'s step 7,
report-and-stop with no durable write, so step 5's generator call really is
that branch's last.
Rows 5 and 9 of the old table were the two the last three rounds kept
finding defects in; row 9 is gone with the implementation stage, and row 5
survives with the predicate round 8 established (the generator's own
completed output, `apply-plan-review.md` verified across the whole file to
have no entry-write preamble).

### `bundle_generated_digest` — what row 5 reads

A digest the **Controller** computes over `<bundle_dir>`, covering only the
files `prepare-ai-review.sh` itself writes on every supported invocation
form — `CHANGED_FILES.txt`, `COMMITS.txt`, `DIFF.patch` and `files/` — and
explicitly **excluding** the author-written files (`REVIEW_REQUEST.md`,
`IMPLEMENTATION_SUMMARY.md`, `TEST_RESULTS.md`, `CONTEXT_FILES.txt`),
`MANIFEST.md`, and **`PLAN.md`**, which the generator derives from a pinned
snapshot of the protected paths and which therefore moves whenever the plan
document moves rather than only when a regeneration runs (round 9's O1).

It answers exactly one question — *did the generator run?* —
and `CHANGED_FILES.txt` carries a `generated:` line, so it moves even for a
byte-identical `same_content` round.

Three rounds established why it has to be this and not the alternatives.
`MANIFEST.md`'s declared `bundle_id` is a record of a *past* generation
that no live Workflow consumer reads (`prepare-ai-review.sh:677-679`) and
that an omitted-id round never refreshes (round 7's B1). The
`Workflow-Bundle-Generation-Record` commit is required to land *before* the
generation it attests to (`WF8B-003`), so it is true of rounds that then
failed (round 6's B3). And digesting the *whole* directory is satisfied by
in-bundle file refreshes that precede the generator (round 8's B1).

This is Controller-owned **derivation**, not a reimplementation of Workflow
identity semantics — the boundary CP3 draws for
`StalePlanApprovalRegistryReadError`, and the same category as
`registry_complete`. `bundle_id` is an identity the Workflow's gates bind
approvals to; `bundle_generated_digest` is a private answer no Workflow
gate consumes, never presented as, compared against, or named like a
`bundle_id`.

**Row 3's predicate is a genuine post-condition**, and the contrast is
worth keeping: `AWAITING_LOCAL_PLAN_REVIEW` is entered by
`publish_plan_revision`/`transition_to_awaiting_local_plan_review` with the
bundle regenerated in the same step, so the prior round's feedback cannot
match the new `bundle_id` — false before the worker ran, true after.

**The plan stage is where `MANIFEST.md` is written unconditionally**
(`prepare-ai-review.sh:581-584`), so rows 3's staleness input is always
available. Every defect rounds 7–9 found in the manifest-based inputs was a
property of the implementation/post-fix stages, whose `[work_item_id]`
argument is optional; none of it reaches this table.

**The predicate-validity rule, in three halves.** Round 4 gave the first:
*a predicate is evidence only if it reads an artifact the **worker**
produces, not one the **selection** already required.* Round 5 gave the
second, which revision 5 lacked: *a predicate must read something the
action produces when it **completes**, not when it **begins***. Both are
about discriminating power; they name the two distinct ways a predicate can
be true while nothing was accomplished — the fact was already true before
launch (round 4), or it became true at the action's entry write (round 5).
Each row therefore names *which writer call* produces its evidence, which
is what makes the second half mechanically checkable rather than a
judgement.

Round 7 added the discipline that makes all of this stick: **when a
revision adds a property, the same pass must evaluate it against every
existing row, and the property is not finished until it can fail.** Revision
7 wrote the disjunction corollary and ran it over the one row that prompted
it, leaving rows 5, 7 and 11 unaudited. Revision 8 re-audited all eleven rows *of the then-current table* against every property as worded,
and round 8 found the audit itself trusted two wrong `kind` labels — which
is why revision 9 adds the **declaration-against-artifact** property —
numbered 6 then, **5** since revision 11's renumbering — the only one that
checks a declaration
against the artifact it describes. Revision 9's own re-audit: rows 5 and 7 survive it (each names
a single writer read two ways), row 11 did not.

Round 6 added the corollary that catches the remaining case: **a
disjunction is only as strong as its weakest disjunct.** Row 9's
generation-record commit was a legitimate signal *and* one the Workflow
requires to be written before the work it attests to, so offering it as an
alternative made the whole predicate satisfiable by a pre-work write. A
predicate whose row names more than one writer call must **conjoin** them
unless every one of them is itself a completion write.

The first half in detail (round 4's I1): Revision 4's
`/record-manual-plan-review` predicate — "this round's feedback with
`Status: BLOCK`" — was satisfied by the very file whose presence selected
the action, so it had zero discriminating power. That is a signal the *row*
is wrong, not the predicate: `/record-manual-plan-review` on `BLOCK`
produces nothing durable at all, so no read-only predicate can exist for
it. Revision 5 removes the case from CP4's selection instead, which is why
row 4 needs no predicate. Row 3's predicate passes the same test and shows
the contrast: `AWAITING_LOCAL_PLAN_REVIEW` is entered by
`publish_plan_revision`/`transition_to_awaiting_local_plan_review` with the
bundle regenerated in the same step, so the prior round's feedback cannot
match the new `bundle_id` — false before the worker ran, true after.

**Seven properties are asserted, six over this table and one over the
frozen release itself.** The seventh is the one round 9's diagnosis
requires and CP4 owns: the command-file partition
(**selected / deliberately-not-selected / user-only** must be total and
disjoint over every file in `.claude/commands/`). It is listed here because
it is the property that makes the other six trustworthy — they are all
closed over the plan's own vocabulary, and the partition is what enumerates
the artifact instead of the table.

**Six properties are asserted over this table, not per row.** Each of the
last three rounds found a defect that the previous round's properties, as
worded, could not see:

1. **Coverage.** Every automatic `(from-phase, governing_workflow_version,
   action)` triple in CP4's mapping has exactly one row here, and every row
   corresponds to a triple. This is what catches a missing row (round 4's
   B1) rather than trusting a prose count. **A row or mapping entry carrying no
   version qualifier contributes exactly one triple, whose version
   component is the wildcard `*`** — meaning "every governing version that
   can legally occupy this phase, with the same outcome". A qualified row on
   one side must be qualified on the other; a wildcard matches only a
   wildcard. That keeps the comparison a genuine set bijection whatever the
   qualifiers are, which the "materialise every version" reading would not:
   `AWAITING_EXTERNAL_IMPLEMENTATION_REVIEW` and `AWAITING_FUNCTIONAL_REVIEW`
   are reachable under both versions with identical outcomes, and
   materialising them would manufacture a second row each for no
   behavioural difference. Revision 6 left the rule unstated and the two
   sides disagreed by one row (round 6's I1). Where a phase is reachable
   under only one version, both sides carry the qualifier explicitly rather
   than relying on the wildcard: `AWAITING_LOCAL_PLAN_REVIEW`,
   `AWAITING_MANUAL_EXTERNAL_PLAN_REVIEW` and `REVISING_PLAN` are all
   `"2.1"`-only in practice (`publish_plan_revision` maps `"1"` →
   `AWAITING_EXTERNAL_PLAN_REVIEW`, `scripts/workflow_state.py:7791-7792`;
   `REVISING_PLAN`'s only writers are `record_local_plan_review` `:12418`
   and `record_manual_plan_review` `:12537`, both `"2.1"` paths).

   **Revision 63 (B2, `REQ-40`) states one explicit exception to this
   bijection, rather than silently widening what "every row corresponds to
   a triple" means.** Row 7's own `from_phase` is `NO_PHASE`, not a member
   of any Workflow phase vocabulary, so it corresponds to no
   `(from-phase, governing_workflow_version, action)` triple in CP4's
   mapping at all -- CP4's own table is keyed entirely over
   `WorkItemView.phase`, and `NoWorkItemYet` is not a `WorkItemView` (see
   CP4's own `decide_no_work_item` paragraph). Coverage is therefore
   checked in two parts from revision 63 on: the bijection above,
   unchanged, over every row *except* row 7; and, separately, exactly one
   row (row 7) with `from_phase == NO_PHASE`, corresponding to
   `decide_no_work_item`'s own single, unconditional call site rather than
   to any table entry. A test asserting the ordinary bijection over all
   seven rows unfiltered would itself be wrong from revision 63 on -- it is
   the property that must name its own exception, not the row that must
   pretend to a phase it does not have.
2. **Pair-keyed writer reachability.** Every phase in a row's `to_any_of`
   is one that action's own writers produce **when the command is invoked
   from that row's `from` phase**, for an item of that
   `governing_workflow_version`. Revision 4's version quantified over
   phases alone — both `IMPLEMENTING` and `SELF_REVIEWING_IMPLEMENTATION`
   are produced by real writers, so it passed against the defective row.
   The defect was never in a phase; it was in the
   *(action, from-phase) → to_any_of* relation, which is round 4's answer
   to revision 4's own challenge question 6: a fourth negative class.

   **Row 7's own reading (revision 63, B2):** "invoked from that row's
   `from` phase" means, for `NO_PHASE`, invoked against a target whose
   Workflow state resolves zero non-terminal work items and named none
   explicitly -- the precondition `decide_no_work_item`'s own single call
   site already enforces, never re-derived here. Under that precondition,
   `publish_plan_revision` unconditionally produces
   `AWAITING_LOCAL_PLAN_REVIEW` for a `"2.1"`-defaulted installation
   (`milestone-plan.md` step 0/1, unchanged, unmodified by this
   amendment), so row 7 passes this property by the same reasoning as
   rows 1/2, over a precondition stated in `NO_PHASE` terms rather than in
   phase terms.
3. **Predicate presence and validity**, asserted over `writer_calls` and
   `predicate_inputs` rather than over prose, **stated in one direction
   and, since revision 65, with its converse decided explicitly rather
   than left to the built validator alone** (round 64's `I1`). **Forward,
   unchanged since revision 5**: a row whose `to_any_of` contains its own
   `from` phase and carries no predicate fails at construction. **Converse,
   asserted, with row 7 exempted by name the way property 1's bijection
   exempts it above**: a row whose `to_any_of` does **not** contain its own
   `from` phase and carries a predicate anyway also fails at construction —
   a predicate is either required by `to_any_of`-reachability or it is an
   unintentional leftover, the same reasoning the forward direction states
   — **except row 7**, whose `to_any_of` (`{AWAITING_LOCAL_PLAN_REVIEW}`)
   can never contain its `from_phase` (`NO_PHASE`, which is never a member
   of any `to_any_of` at all — property 1's own reading, above) and which
   carries a predicate anyway for the independent defence-in-depth reason
   its own paragraph states, above ("row 7's predicate is the plan's own
   key-set-difference rule, restated as data"). The exemption is keyed to
   `from_phase is NO_PHASE`, not to "any row failing the ordinary
   `to_any_of`-containment test", so a second, unrelated row that carried a
   predicate its own `to_any_of` did not require would still fail — the
   negative instantiation below is exactly that case, kept distinct from
   the one the exemption admits. `controller/job.py:466-476`'s
   `property_table_violations` already enforces this converse over the six
   rows that exist today (*"predicate declared but to_any_of never contains
   from_phase"*); the exemption is new data this property gains once row 7
   is implemented, not a change to how the six existing rows are read.
   **Its own negative instantiation, alongside property 1's**: a synthetic
   row carrying a **real** `from_phase` (never `NO_PHASE`), a `to_any_of`
   that does not contain it, and a predicate anyway must still fail
   construction under the converse — proving the exemption is scoped to
   row 7's own identity and not to the shape "predicate present, containment
   absent" in general, which a build that read the exemption as the latter
   would pass wrongly. A predicate already implied by its row's CP4
   selection condition fails; **every** `WriterCall` on a predicate-bearing
   row must be `kind=COMPLETION` — an `ENTRY` kind fails (round 5's B2) and
   a `CONDITIONAL` kind fails (round 7's B1: a writer gated on an optional
   argument is not performed on every supported invocation); and a row
   naming more than one `WriterCall` must conjoin them, never disjoin
   (round 6's corollary, enforced over **every row of the table** rather than
   the one that prompted it — which is mechanically why round 7's B2
   survived the revision that wrote the corollary).

   **The row-level `branch`, made total and fail-closed** (revision 66,
   round 65's `I1`). `writer_calls` is a **tuple** and `branch` is a
   **per-call** field, so "the row's own `branch`" — which step 8's third
   clause now *dispatches on*, and which property 5 reads to locate a
   span — is not a primitive of the schema and had no defined value for a
   row naming more than one call. **The rule, stated once and here rather
   than inside step 8's prose**: *every `WriterCall` on a row must declare
   the identical `branch`; the row's `branch` is that shared value, and a
   row whose `writer_calls` disagree fails at construction, naming the row
   and both values.* It is **total** — every constructible row has exactly
   one row-level `branch`, `None` included — and **fail-closed**: the
   undecided shape is refused rather than resolved by an implementer's
   silent pick among "all-equal?", "any-named?" and `writer_calls[0]`.
   Round 6's conjunction corollary is **untouched and still needed**: a
   row may still name several writer calls and must still conjoin them;
   what it may not do is straddle two branches, because a single row
   declares a single observation and property 5 walks a single span.
   `ExpectedOutcome`'s declared shape does not move — no field is added,
   removed or renamed, and `writer_calls` stays a tuple (per required
   acceptance criterion 6 of round 65) — so this is a construction
   property over existing data, exactly as the `kind` constraints above
   are. **Its own negative instantiation**: a synthetic predicate-bearing
   row with two `WriterCall`s, one `branch=None` and one `branch="BLOCK"`,
   must fail construction; and a second, with two *different* named
   branches, must fail identically, so the rule is not read as "`None` is
   the odd one out". Rows 3, 5 and 7 each declare exactly one
   `WriterCall`, so no existing row's `branch`, and no existing row's
   verdict, changes — which is what makes the synthetic row the only
   instrument that can distinguish the readings.
4. **Record completeness**, asserted against a **captured** record, not
   against another declaration. Build a `pre_state` from a fixture and
   assert `set(record["pre_state"]) == set(PRE_STATE_FIELDS)` and
   `set().union(*[r.predicate_inputs for r in TABLE]) <= set(record["pre_state"])`.
   Round 7's I1 made the inputs data; round 8's B3 showed the same argument
   applies one level down — *a test cannot enumerate what a capture function
   writes either, unless the capture reads the same declaration.* The
   negative instantiation is the one that would have caught revision 8: a
   field in `PRE_STATE_FIELDS` omitted from the capture must fail. (Revision
   8 instantiated the opposite direction, which was never going to fire.)
5. **Declaration against artifact.** Each `WriterCall` declares a writer
   **function** and a **`branch`** (or `None`), and a test **reads that
   frozen command file** and asserts the named write is the last durable
   write *within that branch*. Both fields are declared data, not rendered
   prose — round 10's B2 was that revision 10 required the branch and never
   promoted it to the schema, so the property could not be evaluated
   against row 3, the very row that prompted it. A row whose predicate
   belongs to a branch and declares `branch=None` fails construction — not a preamble (`ENTRY`), not gated on an optional argument
   (`CONDITIONAL`), and not followed by a further durable write. This is the
   property round 8's diagnosis demands: *a property over declared data must
   have one instance where the declaration is checked against the artifact
   it describes, not against another declaration.* Properties 3 and 4 are
   both satisfiable by consistent, wrong data; rows 5 and 9 were exactly
   that. The command files are workflow-manager-managed and hash-verified,
   so reading them is stable, and a Workflow release that reorders a command
   fails this suite rather than the field.

   **The text model** (revision 47, local round 46's `OPUS-R46-B1`; the
   call search rescoped to the declared branch and its admissible forms
   widened, revision 48, local round 47's `OPUS-R47-B2`), reusing the
   *principle* of CP4's own call-vs-citation rule — a call is the file's
   own procedural instruction for what a step does, a citation names the
   same identifier while attributing the mechanism to a *different*
   command — without reusing CP4's rule verbatim: CP4's rule scans a whole
   file for one qualified literal, and this property must instead
   discriminate **which of several branches** invokes the same function, a
   shape CP4 never has to resolve. A **call** to the declared writer
   function is a line, read within the declared branch's own span (never
   the whole file — see below for why revision 47's "first line of the
   frozen command file, read top to bottom" was the wrong search scope),
   whose text names the function's identifier either **(i)** inside a
   `workflow_state.<fn>(...)` invocation, **(ii)** immediately following a
   verb such as "calls"/"via"/"performed by", or **(iii)** as a bare
   `` `<fn>(...)` `` occurrence inside the branch's own dispatch bullet,
   stating what running *this* branch of *this* command does — as opposed
   to a **citation**, which names the same identifier inside a
   parenthetical or prose aside that attributes the mechanism to a
   **different**, explicitly named command (`recover-implementation-provenance.md:97`'s
   bare `` `validate_user_confirmation` ``, inside "identical in spirit to
   `/approve-review`'s own … guard", is exactly this shape — it names
   `/approve-review`, not this file's own step, so it fails forms (ii) and
   (iii) alike). Form (iii) exists because a command's own dispatch table
   routinely states its own step's writer in bare form once per branch —
   row 3, below, is exactly that shape — and "this branch's own dispatch
   bullet, naming no other command" is what keeps form (iii) from ever
   admitting a citation, by its own wording rather than by the qualifying
   prefix alone. **This leaves CP4's own denylist derivation untouched**:
   it is a distinct rule over a distinct population (all **seventeen**
   command files, and since revision 64 a **union** of two recognisers,
   with no branch and no citation-of-self reasoning), is not restated
   here, and its guard-literal half re-run fresh over those seventeen
   files still answers **three** matching
   (`approve-review.md:36`, `accept-milestone.md:24,55`,
   `recover-implementation-provenance.md:104`) and fourteen not, with
   `recover-implementation-provenance.md:97` still excluded — form (iii) is
   property 5's own admissible-call form and is never folded into CP4's
   single-literal rule.

   A **branch** is a span of the file's text: either the whole file
   end-to-end (a row declaring `branch=None`), or — for a row naming a
   branch — the text from that named case's own opening marker (a
   `- **VERDICT**:` / `- VERDICT:` bullet in a step's enumerated dispatch,
   an `On <VERDICT>` heading, or a governing-version clause introduced by
   `**"<version>"**:`) to the next sibling marker at the same list depth or
   the end of the enclosing numbered step, whichever comes first. **The
   search for the row's declared call is performed within the located
   branch's own span, not over the whole file** (revision 48, local round
   47's `OPUS-R47-B2`): revision 47's wording searched the whole file for
   one global first admissible occurrence and only then asked whether it
   fell inside the declared branch — correct for a `branch=None` row, whose
   span *is* the whole file, but wrong for a row whose writer is invoked
   once per branch, since the file's first admissible occurrence then
   belongs to whichever branch happens to come first in file order, never
   to the branch the row actually names. A row whose located branch
   contains no line admissible under forms (i)–(iii) is a **construction
   failure naming the row and the branch** — never a silent pass — which
   generalises, to every row, the failure a `branch=None` row's call
   falling inside some other step's own branch span already named. The
   test then asks whether any further **durable write** — a further
   `workflow_state.<writer>(...)` call, or a raw `WORKFLOW_STATE.json`
   write, recognised by the same rule — occurs later in plain file order
   **within that same span**. Property 5 passes the row when none does.

   **Row 3** (`/review-plan`, `BLOCK` branch) is the worked case this
   resolves, re-derived against the frozen file rather than asserted: its
   `BLOCK` branch's span runs from its own `` - `BLOCK`: `` bullet
   (`.claude/commands/review-plan.md:124`) through step 8's own closing
   sentence at lines 127-128 — the next numbered step, 9, begins at line
   129. Within that span, lines 124-125 read `` `record_local_plan_review(...,
   verdict="BLOCK", ...)` `` — a bare identifier naming no other command,
   stating this file's own step 8 outcome for this branch — which
   qualifies under form (iii) and is the located call. No further durable
   write occurs later in that span: lines 125-126 state only that the call
   "is a true no-op" and that the work item "stays at
   `AWAITING_LOCAL_PLAN_REVIEW`," and lines 127-128 close with a sentence
   naming no writer at all — neither a `workflow_state.<writer>(...)` call
   nor a raw state write. Property 5 therefore **passes** row 3, by the same
   rule that resolves every other row, rather than by the row's own prose
   being taken as its evidence. (Revision 66, round 65's `I3`: three of this
   walk's four line numbers — `111`, `107` and `108-111` — were the
   pre-2.5.1 values revision 63 wrote, left standing when revisions 63 and
   64 moved only the *opening* citation to `:124`, so the span this
   paragraph described ran **backwards**, from 124 to 111. The conclusion
   survived re-derivation at the true lines and the apparatus did not,
   which is the one failure mode a property that checks a declaration
   against an artifact exists to prevent.)

   **Row 5** (`/apply-plan-review`, `governing_version="1"` branch) is
   walked the same way, because it is the only other row the schema
   populates a branch for and `OPUS-R47-B2`'s own acceptance criteria ask
   for it. Its branch marker is form three, matched (loosely, since the
   file's actual text reads `` **`governing_workflow_version: "1"`**: ``
   rather than the bare `**"1"**:` the declared form pictures) at
   `.claude/commands/apply-plan-review.md:39-40` — a two-line span reading
   only "steps 1-7 execute exactly as written, exiting to
   `AWAITING_PLAN_APPROVAL`." Row 5's declared call site,
   `apply-plan-review.md:137`, is `` `./scripts/prepare-ai-review.sh` ``,
   inside step 5 — the step whose own text, at lines 108-109, states that
   this call runs unconditionally "on both this step's governing-version
   branches alike," never nested inside either version bullet's own span
   (revision 49, local round 48's `OPUS-R48-I1`: the quotation is step 5's
   own words about itself, not step 0's — step 0, lines 27-58, carries the
   `"1"` bullet "steps 1-7 execute exactly as written" at lines 39-40 and
   the `"2.1"` bullet "steps 1-6 execute identically" at line 41, **plus
   two further bullets the 2.5.0 update added** — a `"2.2"` branch at lines
   51-55 and an "any other `governing_workflow_version`" refusal at lines
   56-58 — and never uses the "governing-version branches alike" phrase at
   all; the proposition the citation supports is unaffected, only its
   location was wrong). (Revision 66, round 65's `I3`: `:96-97` was the
   pre-2.5.1 location of the quoted phrase, which now sits at `:108-109`;
   and the 2.5.0 update grew step 0 from `:27-46` to `:27-58`, which made
   the previous sentence's "states **only**" false of the step it names —
   both corrected against the installed tree rather than against the
   previous revision's claim about it.) **This row does
   not resolve under the model above, and this revision does not resolve
   it**: the branch's own span contains no call at all, admissible or
   otherwise, because the actual invocation sits in a step the branch's
   text merely references by number rather than contains. This is a
   different failure shape from row 3's — row 3's branch genuinely
   contains its call in bare form; row 5's branch never could, because the
   file's dual-mode structure separates "which steps run" from "what each
   step does" into two different locations, and the branch-as-text-span
   model has no notion of one span pointing at another. Recorded as an
   open item for a future revision rather than patched here, on this
   document's own rule against folding an unresolved case into a closure
   claim: either the branch-span model gains a declared way to follow a
   "steps N-M execute" reference to the step it names, or row 5's branch is
   restated to point at step 5's own text directly, and whichever is
   chosen must be checked against every other `governing_version=` row
   this schema might later add, not only this one. **CP6B cannot pass its
   own verification gate while row 5 stays unresolved** (revision 49,
   local round 48's `OPUS-R48-I2`): the coverage rule stated immediately
   below specifies a row whose branch is locatable but whose span admits
   no call as a *failure naming the row and the branch*, never a silent
   pass, and row 5 is exactly that case by this section's own analysis. An
   implementation that builds property 5 exactly as declared, over the six
   declared `WriterCall` rows, therefore produces a suite with row 5
   specified to report a failure, and CP6B's checkpoint cannot be reported
   `COMPLETE` in that state. Before CP6B's verification gate can pass, one
   of the two remedies named above must be chosen: teach the branch-span
   model to follow a "steps N-M execute" cross-reference to the step it
   names, or restate row 5's own declared branch to point at step 5's text
   directly — either is acceptable, and whichever is chosen must hold for
   every other `governing_version=` row the schema may later add, not only
   this one.

   **Coverage and no-match.** The rule runs over every `WriterCall` row in
   this table; each resolves to *pass*, *fail*, or — for a row whose
   declared branch is locatable but whose own span contains no line
   admissible under forms (i)-(iii) — a **failure naming the row and the
   branch**, stated as such rather than treated as an automatic pass or a
   skip (`OPUS-R47-B2`'s own acceptance criterion 3; row 5, above, is
   exactly this case and is recorded as an open item rather than silently
   carried past). A row whose frozen file cannot be read, or whose declared
   branch cannot be located in it at all, is likewise a **failure naming
   the row and the file** — never a skip — the same non-skip discipline
   `KNOWN_PHASES` and CP4's command-file partition already state for their
   own enumerations.
6. **Completion.** Every phase in a row's `to_any_of` is one the action
   produces **when it completes** — not merely one its writers can produce
   from that pair. This is the fifth negative class, and round 5 found it
   in a row that passed all three of the properties above:
   `APPLYING_REVIEW_FEEDBACK` really is produced by
   `/apply-implementation-review`'s own writer, invoked from exactly that
   `from` phase, so reachability was satisfied and *correct* — and the
   phase still means the action did not finish. Reachability and completion
   are different questions, and revision 5 asserted only the first.

Every predicate above is a pure read of state CP3 or CP4B already gathers —
including row 3's own `REVIEW_FEEDBACK.md` evidence predicate (`Reviewed
bundle ID:`, `Reviewer role:`, `Status:`), whose text model is therefore
CP4B's labelled-line text model stated at its own admissibility clause
table above, by this same deflection, and not a second reader restated
here (revision 47, local round 46's `OPUS-R46-B1`: the deflection was true
before this revision and pointed at a reader with no stated model of its
own; it is true now and points at one).

**CP7 depends on this whole table — the sets, the predicates and the rule
that combines them.** Its reconciliation row 2 opens by citing CP6B step 8's
rule by name rather than paraphrasing it, so a correction to any of the
three propagates by reference. A future edit to one must still move the
other: the record's `pre_state` block is the third party to that
dependency, and the record-completeness property is what keeps all three in
step.

**Tests** (`REQ-T11`, second half): a fake worker that performs the
expected state edit → `transition_verified: true`, record `FINISHED`;
**the persisted `status` sequence for that same successful `execute_step`
is exactly `["PLANNED", "LAUNCHED", "COMPLETED", "FINISHED"]`** — CP6
asserts the first three as a prefix and **CP6B owns this extension to the
fourth**, because step 9 is what appends it through the same
`runtime.write_json` path (revision 24, round 23's I1: an equality
assertion over three values would be green at CP6 and red here for a
correct implementation, and the natural repair destroys the property CP6's
prefix exists to pin); a
fake worker that exits 0 and changes nothing → `FAILED` with
`TransitionNotObservedError`; a fake worker that moves the phase somewhere
*else* → `FAILED` naming both phases; a `BLOCK`-shaped no-transition
outcome **with its evidence predicate satisfied** reported as success
rather than failure; an `AMBIGUOUS` worker whose post-state nevertheless
matches → still not `transition_verified`.

**The six properties are stated once**, in the numbered list above, and
this section does not restate them (round 10's B3). Revision 10 carried a
second, ninety-lines-later copy that had drifted out of step for two
rounds — its completeness check was still the declaration-against-declaration
form round 8's B3 called Blocking, its predicate-validity entry stopped at
three of four halves, the declaration-against-artifact property (6 then,
**5** now) was missing from it entirely, and its count said four over six
bullets. An implementer building these tests from the stale copy wrote the
wrong completeness check and never wrote the declaration-against-artifact
property at all, and both suites went green. One authoritative statement,
referenced by name from everywhere else, is the fix; a second copy is a
defect generator.

CP6B's tests therefore assert **properties 1–6 as numbered above**, plus
the cases below.

Revision 10's narrowing removes most of what these cases were for. What
remains, over the (now seven, revision 63) rows: **row 5's mid-action
case** — a `"1"` worker killed after `publish_plan_revision` and before
the regeneration must not verify, since the predicate reads the
generator's completed output; **row 3's `BLOCK` case** — a worker that
writes a current-round `Status: BLOCK` feedback leaves the pre-phase and
*does* verify, while a worker that exits 0 writing nothing does not;
**row 3's `APPROVE` and `REVISE` cases (revision 65, round 64's `B1`,
required acceptance criterion 2)** — a worker that returns `APPROVE`
(reaching `AWAITING_MANUAL_EXTERNAL_PLAN_REVIEW`) and a worker that
returns `REVISE` (reaching `REVISING_PLAN`) each **verify**, with no
current-round `REVIEW_FEEDBACK.md` declaring `Status: BLOCK` needed at
all — row 3's predicate is never even consulted on these two
observations, since the observed post-phase does not equal the row's
`from_phase`. Both are **required to verify**, and both are **red**
against a build written verbatim from revision 64's rule: under that
rule the third clause fires on every `to_any_of` member, so it evaluates
`_predicate_row3_block_feedback_current` against a fixture whose
`REVIEW_FEEDBACK.md` (if any) declares `Status: APPROVE` or
`Status: REVISE`, the predicate returns `False`, and `transition_verified`
is wrongly `False` — the case the declared BLOCK-only suite never
exercised, which is what let revision 64's own defect ship green;
**row 7's cases (revision 63, B2)** — a worker that creates exactly one
new `work_items` key verifies; a worker that creates zero (e.g. frozen
Workflow itself refuses, or exits before step 1) does not; a worker that
somehow creates two or more (a malformed or concurrently-modified target,
never a supported frozen-Workflow outcome, but the predicate is never
trusted to that good behaviour any more than any other row's is) does
not, since `len(...) == 1` is the literal predicate, not "at least one";
**the case that discriminates a declared-but-never-evaluated predicate**
(revision 64, round 63's `B1` and its own missing-tests item) — none of
the three cases above can fail against a build that ships row 7's
predicate as data and never runs it, because under revisions 5–63's rule
*every* build is such a build for this row: the zero-key and two-key
fixtures are run against a build whose step-8 implementation is written
from the rule **verbatim**, and each must be **red** unless the third
clause triggers on row 7's own declared `branch` being `None` — which is
what makes row 7's predicate evaluated on every one of its `to_any_of`
members. **Stated as the property rather than as the fixture, since the
fixture is the same one** (restated at revision 66 in the direction
revision 65's rule actually holds — round 65's `B1`; revision 64's wording,
*"evaluated on **every** verification path"*, was true of revision 64's
rule and became false of revision 65's the moment the trigger was keyed on
`branch`, contradicting this same checkpoint's two new row-3 cases twenty-six
lines below):

> *Every declared predicate is evaluated on the observation it is declared
> over, and a build in which some declared predicate is never consulted on
> **any** path fails.*

This is the formulation step 8 itself already reaches — *"A predicate
declared on a row and never run is the defect; the rule now says a
declared predicate is always run on the observation it is declared over"* —
and it is a property of the **declaration**, not of the path count, which
is why it survives a rule that deliberately consults some predicates on one
observation and others on all of them. **The observation each
predicate-bearing row is declared over is named here rather than left to be
re-derived**, since "the observation it is declared over" is the whole
content of the property:

- **row 3** (`branch="BLOCK"`) is declared over the **`BLOCK`
  observation** — the one where the post-phase equals its own `from_phase`,
  because that branch's step is a true no-op. Its `APPROVE` and `REVISE`
  observations are *not* observations of that branch's write and the
  predicate is correctly unconsulted on them;
- **row 5** (`branch="governing_version=\"1\""`) is declared over its
  **single `to_any_of` member**, which is its own `from_phase` — the same
  observation by the same reasoning;
- **row 7** (`branch=None`) is declared over **every member of its
  `to_any_of`**, because its writer runs unconditionally, so every member
  is an equally legitimate observation of that one call.

**Its negative instantiation is restated with it, and strengthened**
(round 65's required acceptance criterion 2): the discriminating build is
one in which **row 3's predicate is never consulted on any path** — e.g. a
step-8 that drops the third clause for branch-bearing rows altogether, or
that evaluates predicates only for `branch is None` rows — which must fail
this suite on row 3's own `BLOCK` cases, positive and negative. The
superseded phase-equality mutation revision 64 named is **kept as a second
instantiation and reclassified**: it still fires, because it differs from a
correct revision-66 build exactly on `branch is None` rows and so still
passes row 7's zero-key and two-key cases wrongly — but it instruments
**row 7's** clause, not the clause this property is now about, and saying
so is the difference between a property that fails for the right reason and
one that merely fails. And **the negative
instantiation of every property**, since a property
that cannot fail is not a property: a `CONDITIONAL` writer kind, an
`ENTRY` writer kind, a disjunction of two writer calls, a
`predicate_input` absent from the captured record, a `PRE_STATE_FIELDS`
entry omitted from the capture, a missing row, a `to_any_of` member that
is not a completion, (revision 63) a row with `from_phase == NO_PHASE`
wrongly counted toward property 1's ordinary six-row bijection, and
(revision 65, round 64's `I1`) a synthetic row with a real `from_phase`,
a `to_any_of` that does not contain it, and a predicate anyway —
distinguishing property 3's row-7 exemption, keyed to `from_phase is
NO_PHASE`, from a wrongly-general reading that would admit any row
failing the containment test, and (revision 66, round 65's `I1`) a
synthetic **predicate-bearing row with two `WriterCall`s whose `branch`
values disagree** — one `branch=None` and one `branch="BLOCK"`, and
separately two different *named* branches, so the rule is not read as
"`None` is the odd one out" — each fail construction. The
two-`WriterCall` case is the discriminating instrument for property 3's
new row-level-`branch` rule precisely because rows 3, 5 and 7 all declare
a single writer call, so no existing row can tell the admissible readings
apart.

`INCOMPLETE` remains a defined status and CP7 still classifies it, but
after revision 10's narrowing no Generation 1 action can produce it: its
only producer was `/apply-implementation-review` reaching
`APPLYING_REVIEW_FEEDBACK`, and that action is no longer selected. It is
kept rather than deleted because a record written by a *future* generation
that does drive that phase must still be readable by this one — which is
what CP7's closed status table is for.

Five positive cases pin the three predicate-bearing rows that exist: row
3 — a `/review-plan` worker returning `BLOCK` writes a current-round
`REVIEW_FEEDBACK.md`, leaves the pre-phase and **verifies**; row 3 again —
a worker returning `APPROVE` and a worker returning `REVISE` each leave
row 3's own predicate unconsulted and **verify** (revision 65, round 64's
`B1`) — neither is an observation of row 3's `BLOCK` branch, which is the
observation that predicate is declared over, so the restated property
above is satisfied by exactly the build these two cases require rather
than contradicted by it (revision 66, round 65's `B1`); row 5 — a
`"1"`-governed `/apply-plan-review` worker completing step 5's regeneration
leaves the pre-phase and **verifies**, because `bundle_generated_digest`
moved; and row 7 — a bare `/milestone-plan` worker against a
zero-work-item target creates exactly one new `work_items` key, reaches
`AWAITING_LOCAL_PLAN_REVIEW` and **verifies** (revision 64: two positive
cases and two predicate-bearing rows were the figures revisions 10–62
carried, revision 63 widened the table without widening this sentence to
three, and revision 64 widened the trigger without adding the two cases
that would have caught its own defect — round 64's `B1`'s own missing-tests
item). Revisions 10–13 named
`/milestone-implement` and `/apply-implementation-review` here; neither has
a row after the narrowing and neither is ever selected (round 13's B1c).

### CP7 — Durable resume

**Owns**: REQ-7, REQ-8 (partly), REQ-11 (partly), REQ-T12, REQ-T13.
Depends on CP6B.

**Files**: `controller/job.py` (extended), `tests/test_resume.py`.

`resume(managed_repo, *, identity, runtime) -> list[JobRecord]` loads
**every** job record for this target repository — not only the non-terminal
ones — and classifies each from the closed status table below. Revision 7
said "non-terminal", which made its own `INCOMPLETE` row unreachable (the
loader had filtered it out, so the declared test passed vacuously) *and*
contradicted the unknown-status row, since a status this generation does not
know cannot be classified as terminal before it is read (round 7's I2).
Loading everything makes both rows reachable, and it is what makes "never
relaunch" rest on the table rather than on a loader filter mentioned in
passing.

**Before the terminal/non-terminal dispatch, `resume` runs one named
validation pass over every record: `validate_record(record) -> Validity`,
with four cases in a stated order.** Revisions 15–19 accumulated these one
at a time as separate paragraphs, and each addition had to remember to say
where it sat relative to the others; the fourth was declared in CP6B and
never given a mechanism here at all (round 19's B1). One pass with four
cases is the shape that makes omitting a case structurally hard, which is
what challenge question 5 asked for in revision 19 and what round 19's B1
demonstrates the need for.

Every case answers the same question — *can this record be believed?* —
and each returns either `VALID` or a refusal carrying the reason. **None
of them reads the target's post-state**, which is what the reconciliation
table is for; case 2 is the only one that touches the target at all, and
only to ask whether it and its work item still exist, which is strictly
less than comparing an observed phase against an expected set (round 19's
I2 — revision 19 said the checks *"require no observed reality"*, true of
the other three and not of that one). The order is load-bearing
and is stated because the inference went the other way once already:

1. **Uninterpretable record** — `schema_version` unknown, or
   `controller_generation` **greater** than the running one. It was written
   by something this generation cannot read, and every later case would be
   reading fields whose meaning it has just declared unknown.
2. **Unresolvable subject** — `target_repo` does not resolve, or
   `work_item_id` is **present and** absent from the target's state. The
   record describes work against something that is no longer there.

   **A `null` `work_item_id` is not an unresolvable subject, and revision
   64 states which it is** (round 63's `B2`). Row 7's action carries
   `work_item_id=None` by design — the Controller never supplies an id to
   a bootstrap `/milestone-plan`, because frozen Workflow alone derives
   it — so the record's `work_item_id` is `null` both while the job is in
   flight and forever after. Read as *"absent from the target's state"*,
   that `null` matches nothing in any target's `work_items` map, and this
   case would raise `StaleJobRecordError` and **abort the whole call**: a
   crash in the two-flush window of a bootstrap job — on a brand-new
   target, the exact population `REQ-T18` exercises — would leave a record
   that can never be reconciled, and even a *successful* bootstrap's
   terminal record would abort every later `resume` against that target.
   The rule is therefore stated over three cases rather than two, and the
   third is the one revision 63 left unstated:

   - `work_item_id` **absent** from the record entirely → refusal, as CP6
     step 4's must-be-present list already requires;
   - `work_item_id` **is a string** and is not a key of the target's
     `work_items` → refusal, unchanged;
   - `work_item_id` **is `null`** → **`VALID` for this case**, and the
     record is dispatched normally. `null` is the *declared* value for a
     bootstrap job, not a missing subject: the record's subject is the
     **target repository**, which `target_repo` already resolves, and the
     work item it created is identified by row 7's own key-set difference
     rather than by a name the Controller never chose. A row-7 record is
     distinguishable from a malformed one without guessing, because
     `expected_transition.from` reconstructs to `NO_PHASE` exactly for
     those records and to a real phase string for every other row — so
     *"`work_item_id` is `null`"* and *"`expected_transition.from` is
     `NO_PHASE`"* must **agree**, and a record in which one holds and the
     other does not is itself a refusal, naming both fields. That keeps
     the carve-out keyed on a stated pair rather than on a single
     permissive `null`.

   **What this costs, stated rather than hidden**: a reconciled row-7
   record names no work item, so `resume`'s report for it names the
   target, the job id and the single key the predicate found, not an id
   the record carries. That is the honest report for a job whose entire
   point is that the id did not exist when it started.
3. **`worker_outcome` disagrees with the step that owns the record's
   status.** Stated over the three named non-terminal statuses, one rule
   each, total over the premise below (revision 22, round 21's I1):
   - on **`PLANNED` or `LAUNCHED`**, `worker_outcome` must be **absent**.
     Present *at all* — recognised or not — is a refusal.
   - on **`COMPLETED`**, it must be **present and one of**
     `{SUCCESS, FAILURE, AMBIGUOUS, INTERRUPTED}`. Absent or unrecognised
     is a refusal.

   The premise is one sentence and each rule is exactly its consequence for
   one status: CP6 step 6 is the only writer of `COMPLETED` and records the
   outcome in the same act; CP6 step 4 is the only writer of **both**
   `PLANNED` and `LAUNCHED`, in that order and in two flushes, and writes
   each *before* the worker is spawned, so neither carries an outcome. A
   record contradicting either was written by something that did not follow
   the step that owns its status. **Every status this case rules on now
   names the step that writes it**, which is what *"one rule each, total
   over the premise"* has to mean — until revision 23 the premise named an
   owning step for two of its three statuses and disposed of `PLANNED` with
   a parenthetical, because no step wrote it (round 22's I1).

   **Two revisions narrowed this rule below its own premise before it was
   stated this way.** Revision 20 stated the inference generally and
   performed it for `COMPLETED` alone (round 19's B1 → round 20's I1), so a
   `LAUNCHED` record carrying `worker_outcome: "PARTIAL"`
   passed every case and then satisfied step 8's negatively-stated first
   clause, and was written `FINISHED, transition_verified: true` — the
   *"already succeeded"* durable write, on a record whose own content
   proves this design did not produce it. Revision 21 fixed that half by
   stating clause 1 positively and refusing *unrecognised* outcomes, and
   left the same hole at the two values clause 1 explicitly admits: a
   `LAUNCHED` record carrying `"SUCCESS"` or `"INTERRUPTED"` still reached
   row 2 and still earned the same write (round 21's I1). Keying on
   **presence** rather than on the value closes it, and it closes a second
   thing with it — a `LAUNCHED` record carrying `"FAILURE"` whose
   post-phase moved *into* `to_any_of` matched **no row** of the table this
   document asserts is total over `LAUNCHED`, because clause 1 rejected it
   and rows 3 and 4 both require the phase to be unchanged. No `LAUNCHED`
   record carrying an outcome reaches the table at all now, so the
   partition claim is true again.

   **The rules name the three statuses rather than the non-terminal
   *class*, deliberately** (round 21's I2): a class test is a terminality
   test, and terminality is exactly what this generation cannot evaluate
   for a status it does not recognise. Naming the members keeps case 3 free
   of the question — an unrecognised status simply is not one of the three,
   so it falls through the pass to the table's unknown-status row, which is
   the same answer case 4 gives for the same reason (round 19's B1: revision 19 asserted this
   refusal in CP6B and in row 2's parenthesis while no stated mechanism
   performed it, and the record reconciled to `FAILED` through the
   `COMPLETED`-rule-fails row — a durable write carrying
   `TransitionNotObservedError`, a confident and wrong diagnosis, over the
   evidence of the malformation).
4. **Derived-field disagreement** — `status` disagrees with
   `selected_action.declined`: `DECLINED` with `declined: false`, or any
   **recognised** status with `declined: true`. `status` is *derived* from
   `selected_action.declined` at record-write time, so a disagreement means
   the record was written by something that did not derive it. This is a
   pass case rather than a table row because the record round 14's I2 named
   is `DECLINED`, which is **terminal**: a row would have been routed to
   "report it" before ever being consulted, and the malformed record would
   have been reported as a legitimate declined outcome — the exact harm
   (round 15's B1).

**Every refusal carries the terminal carve-out round 8's I2 established**:
**non-terminal** → `StaleJobRecordError`, naming the record and the reason,
**aborting the call**, because it describes possibly-live work;
**terminal** → surfaced in the result **marked malformed** (case 4) or
**unreadable** (case 1 or 2), never raised, because a terminal record is
history and one bad file from an old generation must not stop the
reconciliation of live work beside it.

**Case 3 always takes the non-terminal branch, by construction rather than
by accident** (round 20's O1). All three of its rules key on `PLANNED`,
`LAUNCHED` or `COMPLETED` — the non-terminal set, named member by member
since revision 22 rather than described as a class — so its
terminal branch can never fire and the carve-out above does not list it —
revision 20 listed it on both sides, which is a rule that cannot fail in
one of its two directions. The carve-out is still stated once for all four
cases because it is the same rule; what differs is which cases can reach
each branch, and that is now stated rather than implied. A terminal record
carrying a malformed outcome is not lost: it has no `worker_outcome` clause
to violate, because terminal records are reported and never reconciled.

**Terminality is read from the record's `status`, and the pass says what it
does when that status is not one this generation knows** (round 19's I2).
The question is not hypothetical for case 1 in particular: a newer
generation adding a status is the paradigm case, this generation's own
enumeration has changed twice within Generation 1 alone, and an unknown
`schema_version` is precisely the field that says how to read the rest, so
the record may carry no `status` at all.

- **Cases 1 and 2 treat an unrecognised or absent status as
  non-terminal**: `StaleJobRecordError`, aborting. This is the fail-closed
  direction and it is chosen deliberately over the carve-out, because the
  carve-out's premise does not hold here. Round 8's I2 protects *this
  generation's own history* — a terminal record it wrote and can no longer
  read — from stopping live work beside it. A record from a **newer**
  generation is not this generation's history; it is possibly-live work
  belonging to a generation that supersedes this one, and after a CP8
  handoff the correct state for a Generation 1 process in that tree is
  stopped, not reconciling. Guessing *terminal* there would downgrade a
  live newer-generation record to a note, which is the one outcome the
  refusal exists to prevent.
- **Cases 3 and 4 cannot reach the question, and case 3 is written that
  way on purpose.** Case 3 keys on the three **named** statuses `PLANNED`,
  `LAUNCHED` and `COMPLETED`, each recognised by definition. Revision 20
  keyed it on `COMPLETED` alone and revision 21 on *"any non-terminal
  status"* — a class test, and therefore a terminality test, which is the
  one question this paragraph exists to answer and which that phrasing
  quietly reopened for a record like `status: "PARTIALLY_DONE"` carrying
  `worker_outcome: "PARTIAL"`. Revision 22 states the rule over the members
  instead, so the question cannot arise here at all (round 21's I2). Case 4 ranges over the
  enumeration's own members: an unrecognised status has no terminality this
  generation can determine — *a status this generation does not know cannot
  be classified as terminal before it is read*, round 7's I2 exactly — so
  it falls through the pass unjudged to the table's **unknown-status row**,
  which raises `StaleJobRecordError` naming the status (round 16's I4). The
  pass narrows nothing that row covers.

**The ordering is stated, not left to be inferred, and it is stated because
the inference went the other way.** Revisions 1–18 carried these as *rows*
in the table below, positioned after the **five** status-keyed rows —
four through revision 15, and five since revision 16 added the
`COMPLETED`-with-failing-rule row for round 14's I3; revision 19 wrote the
superseded figure while enumerating all five in the next breath, which
inverts the argument, since without row 5 the table is **not** total and
the promoted rows could have fired (round 20's O2). Those
rows are **total** over the non-terminal set — `PLANNED` matches
*"anything"*, `LAUNCHED`'s three rows partition its complement, and
`COMPLETED`'s two rows are complementary by construction — and the only
ordering rule this document states for the table is *"evaluated before the
rows below it"*. So as rows they could never fire: a `controller_generation:
2` record at `COMPLETED` whose post-state satisfied step 8's rule would have
been written `FINISHED, transition_verified: true` by a generation-1
process, the precise thing case 1 of the validation pass now forbids,
and one at `PLANNED` would have been marked `INTERRUPTED` *"and allow a
fresh `step`"* — a generation-1 worker launched against a target generation
2 was driving. A mixed-generation jobs directory is not hypothetical here:
CP8 hands one `.controller/` tree from generation A to generation B, and
`resume` loads every record in it. This is round 15's B1 one level over —
a fail-closed rule placed where a total, earlier rule pre-empts it — and it
takes the same fix, promotion into the validation pass with the terminal
carve-out preserved — cases 1 and 2 of it.

Then the dispatch. Terminal records are **reported, never reconciled**:
surfaced in the result and left exactly as they are. Non-terminal records
are reconciled against authoritative state — Workflow state and Git, never
the Controller's own optimism.

**A record whose `status` this generation cannot read is dispatched as
non-terminal**, so the closed table below is what judges it and its last
row is what it matches (round 28's I1). Terminality is read from `status`,
and a record that survives the validation pass with an absent or
unrecognised one — a first flush that deferred the field, or a foreign
record from the mixed-generation `.controller/` tree a CP8 handoff leaves
behind — has none this generation can evaluate. Dispatching it as terminal
would surface it as history and never judge it; dispatching it as
non-terminal sends it to the table, where nothing but the unknown-status
row matches and that row raises. Revisions 27 and 28 stated the **outcome**
for such a record in step 4 and never the **routing** that produces it,
which left the sentence a build is assembled from only inferable:

| Recorded status | Observed reality | Reconciliation |
|---|---|---|
| `PLANNED` | anything | nothing can have happened — the record was flushed before the launch was prepared: mark `INTERRUPTED` and allow a fresh `step`. Round 1 found this row missing, and revision 23 gave the status the writer this row had always assumed (round 22's I1): CP6 **step 4** flushes `PLANNED` and only then upgrades the same record to `LAUNCHED`, so a crash between the two flushes leaves a non-terminal record no row matched, and the `resume` loop would have fallen through on a status it did not recognise |
| `LAUNCHED`/`COMPLETED` | **CP6B step 8's rule holds**, all three clauses: the record's `worker_outcome` is `SUCCESS` or `INTERRUPTED`, or **absent on a `PLANNED`/`LAUNCHED` record**, which are written before the worker returns (stated positively since revision 21 — round 20's I1 — because the negative form admitted every value that was not `FAILURE` or `AMBIGUOUS`; a `COMPLETED` record always carries an outcome and a `PLANNED`/`LAUNCHED` record never does, and any record contradicting the step that owns its status — an outcome present at all on `PLANNED`/`LAUNCHED`, or absent or unrecognised on `COMPLETED` — is malformed and refused by case 3 of the validation pass above, never reaching this table) **and** post-phase ∈ `expected_transition.to_any_of` **and**, whenever the row **carries an evidence predicate at all**, that predicate holds against the pre-state — evaluated **unconditionally** when the row's own `WriterCall.branch` is `None`, and otherwise (the row's writer runs on one named branch only) evaluated exactly when the observed post-phase equals the row's own `from_phase` (restored to byte-verbatim agreement with step 8's **third clause** at revision 66, round 65's `O1`, and the aside re-scoped from "step 8's sentence" to "step 8's third clause" at round 66's `O1` — the third clause is what was actually verified by extraction, and step 8's own standing claim is corrected to match: revision 65 moved this restatement with the repair but dropped the qualified field name and the parenthetical gloss, two divergences in the one revision that moved it, against this cell's own *"restates it verbatim rather than paraphrasing it"*; the row-level value the qualified name denotes is property 3's total, fail-closed derivation over `writer_calls`, revision 66, round 65's `I1`. The third clause's trigger is keyed on the row's declared `branch` since revision 65, round 64's `B1` — it was the predicate's bare presence, unconditionally, through revision 64, which verified row 7 correctly but evaluated row 3's `BLOCK`-specific predicate on `APPROVE`/`REVISE` too, where it is false, failing the Controller's two ordinary `/review-plan` outcomes; and it was *"where the observed post-phase equals the record's pre-phase"* through revision 63, a condition row 7's `NO_PHASE` pre-phase can never satisfy, so row 7's predicate was declared and never evaluated on this path either; this restatement moves with step 8's rule, which is what *"restates it verbatim rather than paraphrasing it"* is for) | the action **already succeeded**: mark `FINISHED`, `transition_verified: true`, `reconciled_at` set. **Never relaunch.** |
| `LAUNCHED` | phase unchanged, the predicate does **not** hold, and target HEAD unchanged | nothing durable happened: mark `INTERRUPTED` and allow a fresh `step` to retry |
| `LAUNCHED` | phase unchanged and the predicate does not hold, but target HEAD moved; or phase moved somewhere outside `to_any_of` | `UnreconcilableJobError` — fail closed, report both observations, require a human |
| `COMPLETED` | CP6B step 8's rule does **not** hold — **including** the case where the durable transition is plainly there and the rule fails on its *first* clause alone, because the worker reported `FAILURE` or returned an `AMBIGUOUS` result | the worker ran and returned, and the transition was not produced or not verified before the process died: reconcile to `FAILED` with `TransitionNotObservedError` evidence, exactly as CP6B step 8 would have — which is now true for every clause rather than for the two durable-state ones (round 17's I1). For the `FAILURE`/`AMBIGUOUS` case the evidence names the worker outcome **and** the observed transition separately, so the report says "the phase moved and the worker did not claim it" rather than either half alone; `resume` still never relaunches it, which is what *"`AMBIGUOUS` requires reconciliation rather than retry"* means at this end. Revisions 1–14 keyed the three failing branches on `LAUNCHED` alone, so a record interrupted between CP6 step 6 and CP6B step 9 matched no row (round 14's I3) |
| `DECLINED` | any | terminal: **reported, never reconciled, never relaunched.** No worker ran, so there is nothing to reconcile; the record exists so an outer supervisor can see which phase this generation declined and what it named as next |
| `INCOMPLETE` | any | terminal: **reported, never reconciled, never relaunched.** The rule is not "the phase it leaves behind is one no command can run from" — that is a property of its single current instance — but *a status whose meaning is "the action produced no durable change and said why" is never made truer by repeating the action*, which generalises to a second instance |
| any | the recorded status is not one this generation knows at all | `StaleJobRecordError`, naming the status — the table is closed, and a status it does not recognise is never silently skipped |

**The `LAUNCHED`/`COMPLETED` row is `REQ-T13`**, "no replay of an
already-completed action", and it is the reason step 4 of CP6 persists the
expected transition *before* launching: reconciliation needs to know what
success would have looked like, and it cannot ask the worker after the
fact. (Revisions 1–5 called this "the first row"; the first row is the
`PLANNED` row round 1 added, which permits a fresh attempt.)

**Why the predicate clause is load-bearing here and not merely tidy**
(round 5's B1). **Two of the table's rows — rows 3 and 5 — have `to_any_of`
∋ their own `from` phase** (six of six at revision 10's narrowing, seven
from revision 63: row 7 never joins this set, since `NO_PHASE` -- row 7's
own `from_phase` -- can never be a member of any `to_any_of`, which only
ever contains real Workflow phase strings; row 7 is predicate-bearing for
the independent reason its own paragraph above states, not this one), a
count revision 10's narrowing left as "six of six" by editing the
denominator without re-deriving the numerator (rounds 13's B1a and 14's
B1a — the first pass fixed this sentence and left the three below it).

Without the clause, an unchanged phase satisfies this row for **those two
rows**, and this row is evaluated before the two below it, so both of those
become unreachable **for rows 3 and 5**. That is a minority of the table
and it is still the whole of the risk, because rows 3 and 5 are exactly the
rows where a legitimate outcome leaves the phase where it was — which is
the only situation in which "already succeeded" and "nothing happened" are
the same observation.

**The worked case is row 5.** A `"1"`-governed `/apply-plan-review` worker
is killed after `publish_plan_revision` and before step 5's regeneration.
`publish_plan_revision` maps `"1"` back to `AWAITING_EXTERNAL_PLAN_REVIEW`
(`scripts/workflow_state.py:7791-7792`), so the phase is unchanged and *in*
`to_any_of`; a predicate-blind row 2 reconciles it to *"already succeeded —
`FINISHED`, never relaunch"* for a round that published no bundle. Note
that a weaker "did the worker write anything at all" test would also have
passed, because `publish_plan_revision` bumps both `plan_revision` and
`state_revision` before dying — which is why row 5's predicate is
`bundle_generated_digest`, the generator's own completed output, and why it
must actually be consulted rather than merely declared.

Revisions 10–14 carried a `/milestone-implement`-at-`IMPLEMENTING` worked
case here. That action has had no `ExpectedOutcome` row since the narrowing
and `decide()` can never select it — CP4's sentinel assertion now proves
that at all eight report-only phases — so the case has been restated over
a row that exists, rather than renamed in place (round 14's B1c).

The clause also makes the two declared CP7 tests instantiable together.
Without it, "a `LAUNCHED` record whose target already shows the expected
post-phase reconciles to `FINISHED`" and "a `LAUNCHED` record with nothing
changed reconciles to `INTERRUPTED`" describe the *same* fixture on a
pre-phase-inclusive row and demand opposite outcomes; whichever ordering an
implementer picked would be wrong for half the table — predicate-blind row
2 first reports crashes as successes, row 3 first relaunches legitimate
no-transition outcomes such as a `/review-plan` `BLOCK` or a
`same_content` post-fix round, which is the replay `REQ-T13` forbids.

The `UnreconcilableJobError` row is deliberately a refusal rather than a
heuristic. A moved HEAD with an unmoved phase and an unsatisfied predicate
means a worker committed something the Controller cannot account for;
guessing whether to retry could duplicate a commit or skip real work.
Failing closed and naming both observations is the correct Generation 1
behaviour, and the milestone brief's "stale Controller execution metadata
is reconciled or explicitly rejected" explicitly permits rejection.

**Tests** (`REQ-T12`/`T13`). Three of these are revision 16's, each the
**failing instantiation** the corresponding rule lacked — round 7's rule,
which this document states **five** times and which revision 15's three
additions each skipped (round 15's I1). **Nine** more have been added since,
one each in revisions 17, 18, 20, 21 and 29 and two each in revisions 22
and 64 — **twelve bullets in all**, re-derived by counting them in
revision 64 rather than by editing the tail of this sentence again (round 22's O1: *"two more"* was
true when revision 18 wrote it, and four revisions each added a bullet and
named themselves at the tail without re-deriving the figure at the head).
Each is identified below by the revision that wrote it rather than by its
position in the list: inserting a bullet mid-list is what swapped the two
ordinals revision 18 wrote here, and this document warns against ordinal
cross-references twice elsewhere (round 18's O1). The walk below runs to the newest addition rather than stopping at an
arbitrary revision (round 29's O1: it ran 17 → 22 while the same
sentence's own count named revision 29). Revision 17's pins the
one branch of revision 16's precondition that had no stated outcome (round
16's I4); revision 18's pins the one case that distinguishes the two
readings of row 2 (round 17's I1); revision 19 adds the readability and
absent-outcome cases below; revision 20 adds the undeterminable-terminality
case the validation pass's own answer needs (round 19's I2); revision 21
adds the `LAUNCHED`-side case that the positively-stated clause 1 and the
broadened case 3 exist to close (round 20's I1); revision 22 adds the two
that separate a *value*-keyed case 3 from a *presence*-keyed one (round
21's I1); and revision 29 adds the **reader**-side missing-`status` case
that the dispatch rule pins — round 26's missing-tests item, which
revision 28 answered in CP6 with a writer-side instantiation instead
(round 28's I1):

- **the `status`/`declined` disagreement**, asked in rounds 13, 14 and 15:
  a **non-terminal** record with `declined: true` raises
  `StaleJobRecordError` and aborts the call; a **terminal** `DECLINED`
  record with `declined: false` is surfaced marked malformed, naming both
  values, and does **not** raise — the two halves asserted separately,
  since a single case cannot distinguish **case 4 of the validation pass**
  from a table row;
- **the `COMPLETED`-with-failing-rule row**, the only row in the closed
  table no declared test exercised: a record left at `COMPLETED` whose
  post-state does not satisfy CP6B step 8's rule reconciles to `FAILED`
  with `TransitionNotObservedError`, not to `FINISHED` and not by falling
  through;
- **every non-terminal status has a reachable row *and* a real writer**:
  enumerate `{PLANNED, LAUNCHED, COMPLETED}` against the table's keys and
  assert each is matched by at least one row on both branches of step 8's
  rule — which is what would have caught round 14's I3 mechanically — and,
  since revision 23, assert each also appears in the `status` sequence a
