could not hold out.

**Revision 45 adds the complexity half's polarity fixture, which is the one
case none of that half's existing cases can reach** (local round 44's
`OPUS-R44-B1`). The cases this section already declares for the half are
revision 15's deliberately-wrong-complexity case, which must fail; revision
18's fixture whose only off-registry occurrence is the superseded half of a
marked pair, which must not; and revision 19's fixture naming two checkpoints
with one figure marked and the unmarked one stale, which must fail. **None of
the three fixes a polarity**, and that is why none of them discriminates the
decision the half's declaration now states: each names the construct without
saying which half of the pair is written in this half's own occurrence form,
so a build that recognises only the convention's illustrated *current-first*
shape satisfies all three while being red at two of the three marked pairs
the live document actually carries. The new case is a fixture whose marked
pair is written **superseded-first**: the occurrence in this half's own form
is the old figure, it disagrees with that fixture's registry, and the current
figure standing beside it is a bare bold decimal. It must **not** fail. A
build reading bare bold decimals as figures is green against it; a
current-first build is red, which is the defect the fixture exists to catch.
It does not substitute for revision 19's case and that case does not
substitute for it: that one is discriminated by the co-occurrence rule and
stays red with the polarity recogniser deleted outright, while this one is
green under every co-occurrence build and red only under a current-first
reader.

**Revisions 40 and 41 add two pins the review record says this apparatus
still needs, and both are about figures these halves *publish* rather than
about the predicates they check** (local round 39's missing-tests list).
Round 40 accepted both needs and rejected both instruments: each pin was
declared in a form the build it was written to force would not be measured
by, one of them against an authority the suite cannot read at all. Revision
41 keeps the requirements and rebuilds the declarations. Neither is a new
half and neither is a new test file; both are cases inside the suite this
section already declares, and both are anchored on committed repository
content only.

- **The command-line half's fixtures pin its published components, not only
  its survivor count, and they read every site that publishes them.** This
  document states five figures — the
  strict total, the loose total, the loose total's three components, clause
  (ii)'s removal and the survivor count — and until revision 40 only the
  last of them was pinned, and until revision 42 only one of the three
  sites that publish them was read. A component figure standing beside a measured
  total as a hand-count is precisely the defect of `OPUS-R37-I1` and
  `OPUS-R39-I1`, one revision apart, the second inside the correction
  written for the first, and each time the unpinned half is the one that
  drifted. Every figure the paragraph publishes is an **output of the same
  extraction** that produces the totals, read from the published text, with
  the two arithmetic identities the figures owe each other asserted as
  well: the three components sum to clause (ii)'s removal, and the strict
  total plus that removal is the loose total.

  **The subject and the notation are declared**, as every other half
  declares its recogniser and as revision 40 did not (local round 40's
  `OPUS-R40-I1`). **The subject is every site that publishes one of these
  figures, which is three regions and not one** (local round 41's
  `OPUS-R41-I1`): revision 41 declared the pin over the paragraph alone
  while the same figures stood at two further sites, so a component figure
  beside a measured total remained the unpinned hand-count `OPUS-R37-I1`
  and `OPUS-R39-I1` were raised about — the structural twin of
  `OPUS-R39-I2`, a figure stated at more than one site with only one of
  them covered. The three regions, each named by the literal that opens it:

  - **R1**, the four-halves table's own command-line row — the table row
    whose first cell opens with the literal
    `every **command line this document types**`.
  - **R2**, the paragraph opening with the literal
    `**The prefix is matched with its trailing space, and the choice does
    not change the answer**`.
  - **R3**, the verification list's command-line item — the list item
    opening with the literal `The **command-line half**`.

  **All three steps this pin performs — finding a region, delimiting it and
  extracting its figures — run over one declared text model, and it is
  declared here rather than left to whichever of the three happens to
  mention normalisation** (revision 44, local round 43's `OPUS-R43-I1`).
  Revision 43 declared the model the *figure* extraction runs over, under
  clause (d), and left region discovery and delimiting without one; the two
  are not interchangeable here, because **R2's own opening literal occurs on
  no single line of this document** — it wraps mid-sentence — so a build
  that searches for the opening literals the way the delimiting rule was
  phrased, over lines, locates R1 and R3, never locates R2, and takes clause
  (a) red and clause (c) unrunnable against a document with nothing wrong in
  it. That is the failure shape this document names, one instrument over
  from where `OPUS-R42-B1` found it.

  The model is stated as three definitions, and every step below runs over
  them. A **blank line** is one that is empty once its whitespace is
  removed. A **block** is a maximal run of consecutive lines none of which
  is blank. A block's **normalised text** is its lines with each line's
  leading and trailing whitespace removed, joined by single spaces, with
  every remaining run of whitespace collapsed to one space; the offset at
  which each line's text begins within it is known by construction, which is
  what lets a line-start test survive normalisation. Blocks are the unit
  because the two boundaries the delimiting rule names — a blank line, and
  the start of a line — are destroyed by normalising the document as a whole
  and preserved by normalising within a block.

  **Finding a region.** Each region's opening literal, normalised the same
  way, is searched for in each block's normalised text, and it must sit at
  the **start of the object the region names**: R1's at the start of a table
  row's first cell (a line whose text begins `|`), R2's at the start of a
  block, R3's at the start of a list item's content, immediately after its
  marker. That positional requirement is what excludes the three quotations
  of these same literals in the bullets just above, each of which sits
  inside a code span in the middle of a list item — the literals occur twice
  each in this document under normalisation, and exactly one occurrence of
  each opens an object.

  **One delimiting rule covers all three**, stated because revision 41
  called R2 both *"one blank-line-delimited block"* and *"the paragraph"*
  and those are not the same object here, and restated in revision 44 in
  terms that survive normalisation: a region begins at its opening literal
  and runs to the **end of its block**, except that it stops earlier at the
  first line-start position, after the line the literal opens on, whose line
  begins — once its leading whitespace is removed — with a **list-item
  marker** (`- `, `* `, or a decimal followed by `. ` **whose decimal reads
  exactly `1`**); and except that a region whose opening line is a table row
  runs to the end of that row's own line and no further. The block boundary
  is the blank-line half of the old phrasing and the line-start test is its
  list-item half, so the rule is restated rather than changed and answers
  the same three spans it did at revision 43.

  **The decimal marker's value is qualified to `1`** (revision 48, local
  round 47's `OPUS-R47-B1`), and the qualification is CommonMark's own rule
  for an ordered list, not a new one this document invents: a decimal other
  than `1` cannot open an ordered list that interrupts a paragraph, so a
  line beginning with such a decimal is prose continuing the block, never a
  region boundary, while a genuine ordered-list item opening `1. ` still
  stops the region exactly as before. This is stated as a rule rather than
  left as a rewrap because a rewrap alone survives only until the next
  revision's own figure edit reflows the same sentence: revision 44's
  published text wrapped *"unmoved through revision 46"* so that `46. `
  opened a line, which under the unqualified marker test stopped R2 six
  figures in — before its own survivor count — and took clause (a) red and
  clause (b) unrunnable against a document with nothing wrong in it
  (`OPUS-R47-B1`). Revision 47 republished the same wrap unmoved, since
  nothing had told the marker test the two shapes apart; only the value-`1`
  qualification, not a fourth rewrap, stops `48`, `49` and every later
  revision counter from reproducing it. Re-run over all three regions after
  this qualification and after this revision's own rewrap of that sentence,
  below: R1 is a single table-row line, immune to the line-start test by
  construction; R3's block carries no line beginning with a decimal and
  `. ` at all, so nothing in it changes; and R2 now carries no such line
  either, so it runs uninterrupted to the end of its block — the following
  `- **The fixture pair is declared in the argv notation**` bullet, whose
  own `- ` marker is unaffected by this qualification and still ends the
  region there, exactly as revision 44 stated. Both readings — with or
  without the qualification — now answer the same three spans, since the
  wrap this qualification exists to survive is also removed below; the
  qualification is what keeps that agreement from depending on the next
  figure edit's own line breaks.

  Within each region, and over the same normalised text, the figures are
  the **bold spans whose whole text is a decimal number**, taken in
  document order. R2 and R3 each carry **seven**: the strict total, the
  loose total, the loose total's three components in the order work-item
  ids, tool-name spans, route spans, clause (ii)'s removal, and the survivor
  count. R1 carries **one**, the survivor count. Four clauses: **(a)** R2's
  and R3's sequences are each exactly seven long and are **identical**;
  **(b)** R1's single figure equals the seventh element of both; **(c)** the
  two identities hold on that sequence — elements three, four and five sum
  to element six, and element one plus element six equals element two; and
  **(d)** the sequence equals what the command-line half's own extraction
  answers over the published text, which is the clause that makes the other
  three a pin rather than an internal-consistency check.

  **A figure published in any other form is not read, and that is used as a
  scope marker rather than tolerated.** No bold span in R1 or R2 is numeric
  apart from the ones above — which is why revision 41 moved the components
  out of parentheses and the survivor count out of an English word, since a
  positional rule over one notation is an extraction and a rule over three
  is a description. R3 states two further quantities that are **not** among
  these figures — the span clause (iii) removes, and R2's own count of its
  numeric bold spans — and both stay **English number-words** there, which
  is what keeps R3's decimal sequence equal to R2's under clause (a). That
  is the same notation-as-scope device the fixture pair below and the
  partition pin's quotation of its own literal use, and it is declared here
  so a later editor does not "unify" those two words into decimals and turn
  clause (a) red against a correct document.

  **The failing instantiation is the one revision 41 restates, because
  revision 40's did not discriminate the build it was declared for**
  (`OPUS-R40-I1`). Revision 40 declared a fixture with one component off by
  one; that breaks the first identity, so it is already red against a build
  that asserts the two identities and the survivor count and extracts
  nothing from the published text — and that build is **green** against
  revision 39's own paragraph, the exact text this pin exists to reject,
  because revision 39's set was internally consistent: strict 8, loose 21,
  components 2 / 6 / 5, removal 13 and survivors 7, with 2 + 6 + 5 = 13 and
  8 + 13 = 21. The declared failing instantiation is therefore a fixture
  whose published figures are **internally consistent** — strict 8, loose
  24, removal 16, components 2 / 6 / 8 and survivors 7, so 2 + 6 + 8 = 16
  and 8 + 16 = 24 both hold — and whose own body the extraction reads as
  2 / 7 / 7: it must **fail**. That fixture is green under the
  identity-only build and red only under one that extracts each component,
  which is the discrimination the pin claims and the reason the identities
  are necessary but never sufficient.

  **The second failing instantiation belongs to the widened subject**
  (`OPUS-R41-I1`), and no single-region build can see it: a fixture in
  which R2 and R3 are each **internally consistent** — both identities hold
  in each, and each region's own seventh figure is its survivor count — but
  which publish **different** sequences, R2's loose total reading 24 and
  R3's reading 21, must **fail** through clause (a). A build reading R2
  alone is green against it, and so is a build reading R3 alone; only one
  that reads both and compares them is red. That is `OPUS-R39-I2`'s shape —
  a figure stated at more than one site with only one covered —
  instantiated against this pin rather than described.

  **Two false-positive instantiations.** The first is a fixture whose
  components agree
  with the extraction over **its own body** while every figure in it
  differs from the live document's: it must **not** fail. That is what
  keeps the case reading the fixture rather than a set of constants copied
  out of this paragraph — the other way a figure pin becomes a figure that
  cannot fail. The second pins the notation-as-scope device rather than
  leaving it in prose: a fixture whose R3 additionally states clause
  (iii)'s removal and R2's own span count as **English number-words**, in
  the positions the live document states them, must **not** fail — a
  decimal recogniser does not see an English word, so R3's sequence stays
  seven long and equal to R2's, and a build that read *every* bold span
  rather than every bold **decimal** span would be red against a correct
  document and is caught here.

- **The Blocking-finding partition is pinned inside the repository, as one
  sentence stated three times.** At revision 39 this document stated the
  partition of a seven-finding window at two sites and the two disagreed —
  one of them summing to six under a stated total of seven — and none of
  the four halves could see it, because each compares this document against
  the registry or the ADR and none compares it against itself.

  **Revision 40 pinned it against `TEST_RESULTS.md` §0c, and that authority
  is not available to the suite** (local round 40's `OPUS-R40-B1`).
  `.ai-review/` is entirely gitignored, so a clean checkout and every CI
  runner have no such file at all; `resolve_bundle_dir` answers the same
  `current/` directory for the plan and the implementation stages, so by
  the time CP9 — the checkpoint that writes this case — is reached, the
  file at that path is an implementation-stage record with no §0c in it;
  and a case whose authority is absent is either red against a correct
  build or unable to fail, which are this document's own two named failure
  shapes. That role — the round's own independent bundle-time measurement,
  recomputed by each reviewer — is not pinned to a letter today and needs
  no letter (revision 47, local round 46's `OPUS-R46-O1`: a §-lettered
  citation is a positional pointer that every later renumbering moves, the
  same class this document already renamed its line-number references out
  of): `TEST_RESULTS.md`'s own current bundle-time section, whichever
  letter it carries this round, keeps that advisory role, and the **pin**
  itself needs none of it, being re-anchored on committed content only.

  **The notation is declared and the three sites are rewritten into it**,
  because a partition parsed from three differently-worded sentences is an
  occurrence set classified by description. Over whitespace-normalised
  text, an occurrence is a sentence — at the start of the text or
  immediately after a full stop and a space — opening with the literal
  phrase `Of the nine Blocking findings of rounds 34-38,` and running to
  the first `.` after it; within that span each category is a **bold
  English number-word** followed, in parentheses, by the code-span finding
  ids it counts, in the fixed order apparatus, Controller test fixture,
  Controller. The quotation of the phrase in this bullet is inside a code
  span and is not sentence-initial, so it is not an occurrence — the same
  device the fixture pair two hundred lines above uses, a notation that
  keeps a declaration out of its own extraction. **Five** clauses, every one
  decidable from this document alone: **(i)** at least three occurrences
  exist; **(ii)** all occurrences are identical after normalisation;
  **(iii)** at each occurrence every number-word equals the number of ids
  enumerated beside it; **(iv)** the total the opening phrase states
  equals the sum of the three categories; and **(v)** the ids the sentence
  enumerates are exactly the Blocking-finding ids the disposition sections
  declare for the rounds the sentence names, and the stated total is their
  count.

  **Clause (v) exists because the other four compare the sentence against
  itself, and revision 41 shipped a false sentence with all four green**
  (local round 41's `OPUS-R41-B1`). Clause (iv) is the one that looks
  external and is not: the total it reads is the number-word inside the
  recogniser's own declared literal, so it is a constant by construction and
  the clause reduces to *the categories sum to the number in the literal*.
  No clause among (i)-(iv) ever asks whether the ids enumerated **are** the
  Blocking findings of the named window, which is how a window rename that
  changed the population from seven to nine passed a pin built one revision
  earlier to stop exactly this class. That is this document's own recurring
  failure — a required test satisfied by the wrong fixture — reappearing
  inside the instrument added to close it.

  **Clause (v)'s authority is outside the pinned sentence and still inside a
  clean checkout**, which is the constraint `OPUS-R40-B1` imposed and which
  this clause keeps. **Each of the three recognisers it invokes states the
  text model it runs over, because an illustrative quotation is not a text
  model** (revision 44, local round 43's `OPUS-R43-B1`). Revision 42 stated
  two of the three by description plus one example, and the example's form
  occurs **nowhere inside the window the clause reads**, so the only build
  the declaration supported found no prose count in any of the five sections
  and reported five failures or five skips — a required suite red against a
  correct document, or a case that cannot fail, which are this document's
  own two named failure shapes. The three steps are therefore declared as
  forms, in the order a build performs them.

  **Finding the section, over lines.** For each round `n` between the two
  endpoints the sentence names inclusive, the authority is the section whose
  heading line **opens with** `## Plan review round <n> — disposition`;
  whatever that line carries after the prefix — the stage parenthetical
  rounds 1 through 38 append, and nothing else in this document — belongs to
  the heading and is not part of the match. The section runs from that line
  to the next line beginning `## `, exclusive. **The prefix reading is
  load-bearing rather than a convenience**: matching the whole heading for
  equality is satisfied by **none** of rounds 34 through 38, every one of
  which appends a stage parenthetical, and by **every** round from 39 on,
  which append none — so an equality build reports the rule working right up
  until it is pointed at the rounds the clause exists for. Headings are line
  objects and none of them wraps, which is why this step is line-oriented;
  the row step below is line-oriented for the same reason and the prose step
  is not.

  **Finding the rows, over lines.** Within the section, a **Blocking-finding
  row** is a table row — a line whose text begins `|` — whose first cell
  opens with a bold code span matching `` `<PREFIX>-R<n>-B<k>` `` — the
  prefix is any of this document's reviewer prefixes, `OPUS` and `EXT-PLAN`
  — immediately followed by `(Blocking)`. A Markdown table row is a single
  line by construction, so this step needs no normalisation. The required id
  set is the union of those rows' ids over all rounds in the window; clause
  (v) asserts set equality against the ids the sentence enumerates, and
  equality between the stated total and that set's size.

  **Finding the prose count, over whitespace-normalised text**, because
  prose wraps and a count that wraps is still one count — the same reason
  the round-count half normalises, and the reason this step cannot inherit
  the two above. The sections carry a **second, independent statement of the
  same figure**, and the recogniser for it is: over the section's text with
  whitespace normalised to single spaces, the **first bold span whose text
  begins `<integer> Blocking` or `no Blocking`**, reading the integer as a
  decimal and `no` as zero. Clause (v) asserts, per round, that this count
  equals the number of rows found; a disagreement is a genuine defect in the
  authority rather than in the sentence, which is why it is reported as its
  own failure and not folded into the set comparison. **Round 38's section
  states two counts and this rule picks the right one with no special
  case**: local round 38's `APPROVE` with nothing Blocking is unbolded
  prose, so it is not a candidate at all, and the first bold span the
  recogniser matches is the external reviewer's — which is the count the
  clause wants, since it is the external stage that puts round 38 in the
  window. That section's own first bold span is `**the manual external
  stage**`, which begins with neither form and is skipped; that is the whole
  reason the recogniser is *the first matching span* rather than *the first
  bold span*.

  **The recogniser's coverage is declared rather than assumed, because the
  window is read from the sentence and has moved once already**
  (`OPUS-R41-B1`). Run over every disposition section in this document, it
  answers on **rounds 12 and 15 onward**, and it covers all three bolded
  notations this document has used for the figure: `**1 Blocking**, 3
  Important and 1 Optional` (rounds 12, 15, 18 and 19); `**no Blocking
  findings**` (rounds 16, 17 and 20 through 30); and `**<n> Blocking, <m>
  Important and <k> Optional**` (rounds 31 onward, round 38's external
  sentence and round 31's external half included). Rounds 1 through 11, 13
  and 14 state their counts in **unbolded** prose, so the recogniser matches
  nothing in them. **That is a declared coverage gap, and the behaviour at
  it is declared with it**: a section in which the recogniser finds no match
  is a **failure** of clause (v), reported as such and naming the round —
  never a skip, never a pass. A window reaching back into those rounds
  therefore goes red until the recogniser is extended, which is the correct
  outcome; a skip-on-no-match build would be a case that cannot fail, which
  is the shape this whole clause was added to stop. **A distinct, transient
  gap is recorded here rather than left implicit** (revision 55,
  `OPUS-R54-I2`'s third paragraph): between revisions 54 and 55, this
  document had no `## Plan review round 53 — disposition` section at all —
  not a section stating its count unbolded, which this paragraph's
  declared-gap clause already covers, but no section for the recogniser to
  scan there in the first place, so the coverage sentence above was, for
  that one revision, not a true description of the document. That is
  different from every other gap this paragraph names: a missing section
  is neither a match nor a failure, since clause (v)'s own window (rounds
  34–38) never reached round 53, so no instrument was red. Revision 55
  backfills the section with a bolded count in the current notation, which
  restores the sentence above to being true again rather than requiring it
  to be restated.

  **Run over the live document at revision 44 from these three declarations
  rather than by reading the sections**: five sections found by the prefix
  rule for rounds 34 through 38; their prose counts extract **by rule** to
  3, 2, 2, 1 and 1; their `(Blocking)` rows are `OPUS-R34-B1`, `-B2`, `-B3`,
  `OPUS-R35-B1`, `-B2`, `OPUS-R36-B1`, `-B2`, `OPUS-R37-B1` and
  `EXT-PLAN-R38-B1`; the two agree round for round, and 3 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 =
  9 equals the size of the id set, which is set-equal to what the sentence
  enumerates.

  **The recogniser's literal and the stated total move together, and the
  consequence is declared here rather than discovered by an implementer.**
  The opening phrase carries the total *inside itself*, as a number-word,
  and carries the window's endpoints the same way. Two things follow, and
  both are properties of the pin rather than notes about it. First, what
  the recogniser matches is the phrase **form**
  `Of the <number-word> Blocking findings of rounds <a>-<b>,` — the
  number-word and the two endpoints read **from the document**, never
  hardcoded — which is what lets a fixture copy declare its own population
  and be judged on it; clause (ii) already forces every occurrence to agree,
  so the form has exactly one instance in any document that passes, and
  *the literal* means that instance. Second, and this is the reason clause
  (v) exists: because the total is read from the same phrase clause (iv)
  then checks it against, clause (iv) is **not** an external check — it
  reduces to *the categories sum to the number the sentence states about
  itself*. A build that hardcodes the number-word instead of reading it is
  a different defect and is caught the moment the population is corrected:
  it finds **zero** occurrences and goes red through clause (i), which is
  the correct outcome, not a false positive — the pin's declared subject
  and its implementation are one edit, never two.

  **The window is named by its endpoints rather than as *the last seven***,
  which is the other half of `OPUS-R40-B1`: a moving window goes stale the
  moment a round lands, so a pin over it can only ever be green against a
  document rewritten every round, and the figure it pins is not
  reproducible from the document a reviewer actually holds. Rounds after 38
  are recorded where the convergence argument needs them — challenge
  question 9 and the disposition sections — and never inside the pinned
  sentence.

  **Four failing instantiations, chosen so that no two are caught by the
  same clause and none is passed by a build implementing only the others.**
  A fixture whose occurrences are
  identical and whose every number-word matches its own id list, but whose
  opening phrase states a total exceeding their sum, must **fail** — clause
  (iv), and it is revision 39's exact defect, three plus one plus two under
  a stated seven. A fixture whose occurrences are each internally
  consistent — every word matching its own list and every total matching
  its own sum — but which assign one finding id to different categories,
  must **fail** — clause (ii), which clause (iv) cannot see, and it is the
  half of revision 39's defect that round 39 did not name. **The third is
  revision 41's own published text, and it is the one every earlier clause
  passes**: a fixture whose three occurrences are identical, whose every
  number-word equals its own enumerated id list, and whose stated total
  equals their sum — three plus one plus three under a stated seven, all of
  (i) through (iv) green — but whose disposition sections for the rounds the
  sentence names carry two further `(Blocking)` rows, `OPUS-R34-B1` and
  `OPUS-R34-B2`, that the sentence does not enumerate: it must **fail**,
  through clause (v) alone. It is the discrimination the whole clause exists
  for, and it is chosen as the fixture precisely because a build omitting
  clause (v) certifies it green — which is what happened.

  **The fourth belongs to clause (v)'s second authority, and none of the
  three above exercises it** (revision 44, local round 43's `OPUS-R43-B1`):
  a fixture whose sentence, occurrences and `(Blocking)` rows are all
  correct — so clauses (i) through (iv) and clause (v)'s own set equality
  are green — but in which one round's section states a **prose** Blocking
  count that disagrees with that round's row count, must **fail**, through
  the prose sub-assertion alone. It is needed because the third failing
  instantiation is discriminated by the *row* recogniser and stays red with
  the prose reader deleted outright, so before this fixture existed a build
  that read no prose count at all passed every declared case — which is how
  a sub-assertion declared by example survived a round that certified it
  green by reading the sentences rather than by running the rule.

  **Three false-positive instantiations, one per authority the pin now
  reads and one for the prose recogniser's declared notation set.** The
  first is a fixture whose three occurrences are
  identical after normalisation but wrapped at three different columns, one
  of them breaking a line in the middle of the parenthesised id list: it
  must **not** fail — the same wrapped-occurrence hazard that made the
  round-count half read two of its three sites until revision 37. The
  second belongs to clause (v): a fixture naming a **different** window,
  whose disposition sections declare a different Blocking id set, and whose
  sentence enumerates exactly that set under a matching total, must **not**
  fail. That is what keeps clause (v) reading the fixture's own disposition
  sections rather than a list of nine ids copied out of this document — the
  same way the component pin's false-positive keeps its extraction reading
  the fixture's body, and the same failure mode in both cases: a figure pin
  that has become a figure. **The third belongs to the prose recogniser**
  (`OPUS-R43-B1`): a fixture in which the sections state their counts in a
  **different one of the declared notations** — `**no Blocking findings**`
  against a round with no `(Blocking)` row, and `**1 Blocking**, 3 Important
  and 1 Optional` against a round with one — must **not** fail. A build that
  implements the recogniser as the single notation the live window happens
  to use is red against it, which is the defect this fixture exists to
  catch: the coverage the declaration claims across three notations is
  asserted by a case rather than by the sentence claiming it.

Each half of this property, and each of the two pins above, now has a
failing instantiation and a false-positive instantiation, which is what
turns "scoped honestly" from a claim into a check.

CP9's verification gate gains this suite alongside the others, **and one
stated, open obligation against it**: `REQ-42` (revision 64, round 63's
third missing test) requires the complexity half's own **occurrence** form
to be widened to admit a bare bold decimal presented as current — the
shape the marking convention itself writes every live current half in —
together with that widened form's coverage, no-match and
negative-instantiation obligations, and the fixture whose only stale
figure is such a half. It is open rather than resolved because widening a
required property's declared subject is plan design, with its own risk of
the cannot-fail shape, and revision 64's scope is the `NoWorkItemYet`
repair plus the 2.5.x baseline. The three sites in that shape are correct
as published at revision 64, verified by running the extraction; what is
missing is the instrument that keeps them so, and this checkpoint's gate
cannot pass while it is missing — the same instrument `REQ-31` already
uses for property 5's unresolved row-5 branch.

**CLI surface** (capability 10's "inspect/status; run/step; resume;
explain/waiting", with names chosen freely as the brief permits):

| Command | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `workflow-controller inspect <repo>` | managed-repo verification + Workflow state summary; read-only |
| `workflow-controller explain <repo>` | the next-action decision with full evidence, and, at a gate, exactly what a human must do |
| `workflow-controller step <repo>` | execute exactly one automatic action, validate the transition, stop |
| `workflow-controller run <repo> [--max-steps N]` | repeat `step` until a gate, a **declined** phase, a **no-action phase** (`LEGACY_READY`, `MILESTONE_COMPLETE`), a failure, an **incomplete step**, or a pending handoff; `--max-steps` defaults to 20 and is itself a stop reason, exiting 16 |
| `workflow-controller resume <repo>` | reconcile non-terminal job records, then report |
| `workflow-controller status` | Controller-owned view: pinned identity, job records, pending handoff |

Global options, declared on the **top-level** parser and therefore accepted
only *before* the subcommand: `--runtime-dir`, `--work-item`,
`--workflow-manager`, `--claude-binary`, `--permission-mode`, `--timeout`,
`--allow-dirty-source`, `--json`. **One environment variable belongs to
this surface and is declared here rather than only where the runtime root
is defined** (revision 36, local round 35's `OPUS-R35-O2`):
`WORKFLOW_CONTROLLER_HOME` sets the runtime root when `--runtime-dir` is
absent, and the precedence is `--runtime-dir` > `WORKFLOW_CONTROLLER_HOME`
> default — the ladder above under "Controller-owned runtime state", where
the reason the flag must win is recorded. It is the only environment
variable that is part of the CLI's operator-facing contract;
`PYTHONPATH` and `WORKFLOW_CONTROLLER_EXEC_HANDOFF` are internal to the
re-exec and are not operator inputs. That position is load-bearing for one of
them — CP1's re-exec builds its child argv around it, and the reason is
recorded there (revision 34, local round 33's `OPUS-R33-O2`). **`--allow-dirty-source` no longer means "run the mutable
worktree and record `HEAD` for it"** (revision 32): it means "materialise
the snapshot from the working tree instead of from a commit", so the run
still executes from an immutable tree and is identified by
`controller_source_tree_digest` with a `null` commit. Without it a dirty
source refuses. `--json` emits the same information as machine-readable
output on stdout, which is what makes the Controller usable as the outer
orchestrator for later generations.

**An install that is not the Controller's own checkout serves only the three
read-only commands** (revision 35, local round 34's `OPUS-R34-B3`). `step`,
`run` and `resume` each materialise a snapshot from `origin_source_root`,
which for an unpinned process is where the Controller's own module sits — so
a `pip install .` into `site-packages` refuses all three with
`SourceSnapshotError`, since that directory is not a Git repository. CP1's
`origin_source_root` bullet states the rule and the measurement; this table
and `README.md`'s installation section both say it in the place they give the
install command, because until revision 35 both read as though any install
were usable for the whole surface.

`run` is a bounded loop, not a daemon: it terminates, it does not poll, it
holds no socket and it schedules nothing. That boundary is what keeps
capability 10's "do not build a daemon" honest.

An `INCOMPLETE` step is a stop condition, not progress: no durable Workflow
change was produced, so continuing would re-decide the same row and relaunch
the same refusal. `run` exits **35** and names the job record so the human
can read the worker's own explanation.

**Disposable managed-repository integration evidence** (`REQ-T18`,
capability 5). `tests/test_integration_disposable_repo.py`. **`REQ-T18` is
the end-to-end integration proof; `REQ-40` (CP3/CP4/CP6/CP6B, revision 63,
B2) is the underlying architecture it proves** — the `NoWorkItemYet`
outcome, `decide_no_work_item`'s bare-`/milestone-plan` action, and row 7's
key-set-difference predicate are unit-tested directly at their own
checkpoints regardless of whether this opt-in live test ever runs; `REQ-T18`
alone was never meant to be that architecture's sole normative definition,
only its real-worker confirmation:

1. Creates a throwaway repository under `tempfile.mkdtemp()` — never
   RepFlow, and never this repository.
2. **Installs a Workflow release that is a member of
   `VALIDATED_WORKFLOW_RELEASES`, named explicitly, never the Manager's
   default** (revision 69, round 68's `B1`; supersedes revision 64's
   "whatever the `2.5` line's newest installed release is", which the
   revision-68 admission rule made unsafe). The rule is stated once, here,
   and the two mechanisms below are both bound by it:

   **The rule.** The fixture reads `VALIDATED_WORKFLOW_RELEASES` — the same
   constant CP2 admits on, imported from the Controller rather than
   re-typed — and installs a member of it: `REFERENCE_WORKFLOW_RELEASE` when
   it is itself a member of that set, otherwise any named member, with step
   3b below as the admissibility check either way, so the rule needs no
   assumption about the relationship between the two constants. As at
   revision 69 the set has exactly one member and `REFERENCE_WORKFLOW_RELEASE`
   names it, so the two mechanisms currently choose the same release,
   `2.5.1`. The fixture **never** derives the
   release from what the Manager happens to hold as newest and never from
   what *this* repository happens to be installed at, because neither is a
   statement about validation: the Manager's newest is a distribution fact
   and this repository's own installed release is an operations fact, and
   round 68's `B1` is precisely the observation that revision 64 treated
   one of them as though it were an admission fact.

   **Preferred mechanism**: `workflow-manager --release-version <release>
   bootstrap <tmp>`, so the fixture uses the real installation path while
   naming the release it wants. `--release-version` is a **global** option
   and is written **before** the subcommand, which is measured rather than
   assumed (Environment facts, revision 69: the `bootstrap` subparser
   accepts only `--profile` and `--force`, and the release selector sits on
   the top-level parser) — the same positional hazard this checkpoint
   already records for the Controller's own `--permission-mode` and
   `--allow-dirty-source` in step 4.

   **Fallback** if the Manager's `distribution/` is not reachable from the
   test environment: copy this repository's own `.claude/commands/`,
   `scripts/`, `docs/ai-workflow/` (state and config reset to the bootstrap
   template) and `.workflow-manager/installation.json` — **and only if the
   copied `installation.json` declares a `workflow_version` in
   `VALIDATED_WORKFLOW_RELEASES`.** If it does not, the fallback does not
   silently produce an unvalidated fixture and does not quietly rewrite the
   manifest to claim a release it did not copy: it fails with the named
   assertion of step 3b below. The fallback remains a fixture detail, not a
   reimplementation of install semantics — CP2 still asks the real Manager
   to verify the result, and if the Manager refuses the fixture, the test
   fails rather than proceeding.

   **Why a pinned, validated release rather than the installed one, and
   what that costs.** Through revision 63 both of this step's mechanisms
   produced whatever release the Manager held as newest, or a copy of
   *this* repository's installed tree; that meant a 2.5.1 target which
   CP2's 2.3.1-only admission set refused with
   `UnsupportedWorkflowVersionError` **before any worker launched**, so
   `REQ-T18` could not reach row 7 for a second reason entirely
   independent of the `NoWorkItemYet` defect revision 63 was written for.
   Revision 64 removed that refusal by widening admission to the `2.5`
   line, and argued on that basis that naming "the installed release"
   rather than a literal kept the next Manager update from restaling this
   step. **Revision 68 removed the premise that argument rested on**:
   admission is now exact membership of `VALIDATED_WORKFLOW_RELEASES`, so
   the moment the Manager ships a `2.5.2`, "the newest release the Manager
   holds" is a release CP2 refuses — reinstating round 63's `B6` failure
   mode at exactly this fixture, which is what round 68's `B1` found. So
   the direction revision 64 declined is now the correct one in the only
   form that was ever wrong about it: the objection to pinning was never to
   pinning as such, it was to pinning to **2.3.1**, a superseded release
   the Controller is not pointed at in practice. Pinning to a *validated*
   release is the opposite case — it names the release the Controller's own
   inventories were measured against and the only kind of release CP2 will
   admit.

   The cost is stated rather than absorbed, and it is the same accepted
   cost the "Supported Workflow baseline" section records for
   `VALIDATED_WORKFLOW_RELEASES` generally: when the Manager updates and
   this repository moves to an unvalidated `2.5.x`, `REQ-T18` keeps
   exercising the *validated* release and therefore stops exercising *this
   repository's* installed one. That divergence is a signal, not a silent
   degradation, and step 3b is what makes it audible.
3. Seeds a trivial milestone in the target's `docs/ACTIVE_MILESTONE.md` and
   commits, so `/milestone-plan` has something real to plan. **The target's
   `WORKFLOW_STATE.json` gains no `work_items` entry at this step** (revision
   63, B2, `REQ-40`) — this is deliberate, not an omission: it is exactly
   the zero-non-terminal-work-item precondition `NoWorkItemYet`/`decide_no_work_item`
   exist to handle, and the fixture's own point is to exercise that path
   for real rather than pre-seed around it.

   **Step 3b — the fixture asserts its own admissibility before it launches
   anything** (`REQ-T18C`, revision 69, round 68's missing test). After step
   2's install and before step 4's run, the fixture reads the *target's*
   `.workflow-manager/installation.json` from disk — the file the Manager
   actually wrote, never the value the fixture asked for — and asserts that
   its `workflow_version` is a member of `VALIDATED_WORKFLOW_RELEASES` and
   its `profile` a member of `SUPPORTED_PROFILES`, both read from the
   Controller's own constants rather than re-typed as literals, so a
   revision that grows either set cannot leave this assertion behind.
   The failure message names three things: the observed `workflow_version`,
   the current membership of `VALIDATED_WORKFLOW_RELEASES`, and the
   "Supported Workflow baseline" growth procedure — re-derive the three
   inventories and re-run the seven baseline-verification suites against
   the newly-installed release, then add it to the set by name in a plan
   revision that states what was measured.

   **What this assertion is for, and what it is not.** It is not a second
   copy of CP2's admission gate and is not asserting Controller behaviour:
   CP2's own unit cases, including `REQ-T18B`, already own that. It is a
   **fixture precondition**, and its whole value is *where it fires*. Both
   failure modes it catches are otherwise silent or misleading. If the
   preferred mechanism's `--release-version` is dropped, mistyped, or
   stops being honoured by a future Manager, the fixture installs the
   Manager's newest release, and — once that is an unvalidated `2.5.x` —
   the run dies four steps later inside step 4 at an opaque CP2
   `UnsupportedWorkflowVersionError`, which reads as a Controller defect in
   the one test whose whole purpose is real evidence. If the fallback
   mechanism copies an `installation.json` that this repository's own
   Manager update has moved to an unvalidated release, the same thing
   happens for a different reason. In both cases step 3b converts the
   failure into a named, self-explaining one that says *the fixture is
   unvalidated* and points at the procedure that fixes it — which is also
   the intended revalidation trigger. It is therefore the one instrument
   that keeps `REQ-T18`'s divergence from this repository's installed
   release (step 2's stated cost) audible rather than silent.
4. Runs `workflow-controller --permission-mode bypassPermissions step <tmp>`
   -- **with no `--work-item` argument** (revision 63, B2): this is what
   selects the `NoWorkItemYet`/row-7 path rather than an
   `AmbiguousWorkItemError` refusal (zero non-terminal candidates, none
   named explicitly) or a nonexistent-id refusal (an explicit `--work-item`
   would itself refuse per frozen `milestone-plan.md`'s own contract, never
   reaching row 7 at all — the two paths are disjoint by construction, not
   merely by this fixture's choice not to exercise the other one) --
   with the **real** `claude` binary and **its working directory set
   explicitly to this repository's root** rather than inherited (revision
   33, local round 32's `OPUS-R32-B1`) — the invocation an operator actually
   makes, and the one revision 32's exec looped in, so the integration
   evidence exercises the repaired path instead of avoiding it.
   `--allow-dirty-source` is added — **also before the subcommand, since it
   too is a global** — when `git status --porcelain -- controller
   pyproject.toml` is non-empty, which it normally is during CP9 since this
   test is written in the same checkpoint that runs it. **Both options move
   ahead of `step` in revision 35** (local round 34's `OPUS-R34-B2`):
   measured against a parser of exactly the shape declared above,
   `["step", "/tmp/x", "--permission-mode", "bypassPermissions"]` and the
   same line with `--allow-dirty-source` appended both answer `error:
   unrecognized arguments` and exit **2**, so this test — whose green result
   is the acceptance criterion *"disposable integration evidence is green"*
   (`REQ-T18`) — could not reach the property it exists to measure against a
   build that followed CP9's own CLI declaration. The
   assertion is on `controller_source_tree_digest`, which is present under
   both outcomes and identifies the exact bytes the run executed;
   `controller_source_commit` is the commit or `null` according to the
   scope rule, and asserting on the digest rather than on the commit is what
   keeps this evidence stable across both — which is the point of revision
   32's model rather than a concession to it.
5. Asserts a genuine, durable Workflow state change, identified the same
   way row 7's own predicate is (revision 63, B2): the target's
   `WORKFLOW_STATE.json`'s `work_items.keys()` after the run, minus the
   fixture's own recorded pre-run `work_items.keys()` (empty, per step 3
   above), is **exactly one key** -- the id frozen `/milestone-plan` step 1
   derived from `docs/ACTIVE_MILESTONE.md`, never a name this fixture
   chose or predicted. That single new entry is at phase
   `AWAITING_LOCAL_PLAN_REVIEW`, its registry/mapping/artifacts files exist
   at the paths its own `WORKFLOW_STATE.json` entry declares, and the
   Controller's job record records `transition_verified: true` with the
   worker's real `session_id`.
6. Deletes the temp tree.

`/milestone-plan` is chosen as the genuine operation because it is the
cheapest Workflow command that produces a *durable, observable* lifecycle
transition from a clean start. It needs no prior approval and no human
input, and its post-state is unambiguous.

This test is **opt-in**, skipped unless `CONTROLLER_LIVE_WORKER=1` is set,
because it requires a live `claude` binary, network access and real spend —
none of which the default suite may depend on. **It is nevertheless run for
real, once, during CP9**, and its output (worker `session_id`, pre-phase,
post-phase, target commit, wall-clock and cost) is recorded verbatim in the
implementation bundle's `TEST_RESULTS.md` and in the functional-review
checklist. "Disposable integration evidence is green" is an acceptance
criterion, so the evidence is produced and recorded, not merely made
producible.

**Documentation**, including the scope Generation 1 carries: it executes
automatic actions at the five plan-stage phases the mapping marks
automatic — `PLANNING`, `AWAITING_LOCAL_PLAN_REVIEW`,
`AWAITING_MANUAL_EXTERNAL_PLAN_REVIEW`, `AWAITING_EXTERNAL_PLAN_REVIEW`
and `REVISING_PLAN`, carrying six triples between them — plus the
`NoWorkItemYet` bootstrap, which has no phase at all — and
**reports** at every later phase, eight of them under the revision-64
baseline (see "Scope reassessment (revision 10)" and the two-shape table
in CP4). `README.md` states
the boundary and the ADR records why it is where it is — the four
asymmetries between the plan-stage and implementation-stage commands, and
the nine review rounds that established them. Inspection, decision, gate
reports, resume and handoff work on any managed target at any phase.

`docs/adr/0001-controller-generation-1-architecture.md`
records the decisions most likely to be revisited by Generation 2: exit
code as the Manager's authoritative verdict; the four-outcome worker
classification including `AMBIGUOUS`; persist-before-launch as the basis of
resume; generation-number comparison against the source repository's
committed `HEAD` as the handoff trigger, with both halves reading that same
`HEAD`; and — added in revision 2 — **the normative exit-code table
itself**.

Round 1's O2 is the reason the table lives there. `README.md` is excluded
at *both* stages (repository housekeeping a concurrent work item may
write), so anything only in `README.md` is never bound by
`technical_approval`. The exit-code contract is the Controller's interface
to an outer supervisor and is exactly the kind of thing that must not drift
unreviewed, and `docs/adr/` **is** protected at the implementation stage.
So the ADR carries the normative table and `README.md` points at it.

`README.md` still gains installation, the CLI surface, the runtime-state
layout, and the safety model (never writes Workflow state, never crosses a
human gate, never hot-reloads) — usable documentation, with the one
normative table by reference.

**A note on where these two files sit in the projections**, so the reviewer
is not surprised: `docs/adr/` is *excluded* at the plan stage and
*protected* at the implementation stage for a `product` item, so the ADR is
bound by `technical_approval` — correct. `README.md` and
`.github/workflows/controller-tests.yml` are *excluded at both stages* by
the inherited declaration (repository housekeeping and shared CI territory
respectively), so neither is approval-bound. The CI workflow is a small,
named addition that runs the Controller suite on push/PR alongside the
existing frozen conformance workflow, which it does not touch. If the
reviewer considers CI out of scope, it can be dropped without affecting any
other checkpoint.

**Full verification** (this repository's real command set, since
`milestone-implement.md` step 3 names RepFlow-Android's Gradle commands,
which do not exist here):

```bash
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -t . -v            # the Controller suite
cd scripts && python3 workflow_fingerprint_test.py       # the seven frozen
cd scripts && python3 workflow_state_test.py             # conformance suites
cd scripts && python3 workflow_test_harness_test.py      # CI runs, re-run to
cd scripts && python3 workflow_integration_test.py       # prove no regression
cd scripts && python3 workflow_acceptance_matrix_test.py
cd scripts && python3 workflow_state_completion_obligations_test.py
cd scripts && python3 workflow_fingerprint_generalization_test.py
CONTROLLER_LIVE_WORKER=1 python3 -m unittest tests.test_integration_disposable_repo -v
```

The gate is: the Controller suite fully green — including
`tests/test_plan_document_consistency.py` — the seven conformance suites
at **no worse than the revision-64 baseline table above**, which is all
seven green, **and run on the interpreter that table names**, since *no
worse* is a comparison and one made across two interpreters is not one;
and the live integration test green with its evidence recorded.

**Revision 64 replaces the `base_commit` table with the revision-64 one as
this gate's comparand, and the difference is not cosmetic** (round 63's
`B6`). The `base_commit` table was measured against Workflow 2.3.1 and
permitted exactly one pre-existing `workflow_integration_test.py` error;
under the installed 2.5.1 that test skips and the suite is green, so
carrying the old table forward would have licensed a *real* regression to
hide behind a permitted exception that no longer has a cause. It also
named a figure — `workflow_state_test.py` at 616 tests — that the
installed suite does not have, which is how revision 63 reported that
suite green while it was red. **The gate is a comparison against a table
re-measured on the release the suite will actually run under**, and the
table is re-measured rather than inherited whenever the release it was
measured on changes.

**Re-derived at revision 69** (round 68's required acceptance criterion 5).
Revision 64 wrote that last clause as *"a future Manager update inside the
`2.5` line re-measures it again"*, which read the re-measurement as
something a Manager update triggers on its own — true only while line
membership was admission. Under `VALIDATED_WORKFLOW_RELEASES` a Manager
update triggers nothing by itself: it moves this repository onto a release
the Controller refuses, and the re-measurement happens as part of the
**deliberate revalidation** that grows the set — the same act the
"Supported Workflow baseline" growth procedure names, of which re-running
these seven suites against the candidate release is one half and
re-deriving the three inventories the other. The comparand table is
therefore re-measured per *validated* release, not per Manager update, and
`REQ-T18C` (step 3b, above) is what refuses to let this checkpoint's live
evidence run against a release that has not been through that act.
