## Artifacts declaration — what was changed and why

`docs/ACTIVE_MILESTONE.md` flags this as load-bearing and requires it to be
settled during `SELF_REVIEWING_PLAN`, before this bundle was generated and
before any approval exists. It was.

`generate_artifacts_declarations(..., work_item_type="product")` emits a
RepFlow-Android-shaped template (`app/`, `gradle/`, `config/`,
`docs/adr/`, the Gradle root files). **None of this milestone's own
deliverable paths are classified by it at either stage**, and an
unclassified changed path raises `UnclassifiedPathError` and fails closed —
at the plan stage that projection is recomputed all the way through
implementation, so the failure would land *after* the plan-approval hard
gate (salvage audit `B4`/`I8`). The following edits were therefore applied
to `docs/ai-workflow/registry/workflow-controller-generation-1-artifacts.json`
before generation:

| Stage | Set | Entry | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| plan | `excluded_prefixes` | `controller/` | Controller package source: implementation content built after plan approval; the plan document is the design under review, not the code |
| plan | `excluded_prefixes` | `tests/` | the Controller's test suite: implementation content written after plan approval |
| plan | `excluded_paths` | `pyproject.toml` | packaging/entry point: implementation content built after plan approval |
| plan | `excluded_prefixes` | `.controller/` | Controller-owned runtime/job state, gitignored and never tracked |
| plan | `excluded_prefixes` | `.workflow-manager/` | the Manager's own installation manifest, written by the Manager, never by this item |
| implementation | `protected_prefixes` | `controller/` | this milestone's deliverable — exactly what `technical_approval` must bind |
| implementation | `protected_prefixes` | `tests/` | this milestone's deliverable; the suite is reviewed acceptance evidence |
| implementation | `protected_paths` | `pyproject.toml` | this milestone's deliverable |
| implementation | `excluded_prefixes` | `.controller/` | runtime state, never a reviewed deliverable |
| implementation | `excluded_prefixes` | `.workflow-manager/` | Manager-owned; a Manager update must never stale `technical_approval` |

Each entry carries a one-line justification in the file itself. Both edits
were made *before* any approval exists, which is the cheap case
(`REVIEW_PROTOCOL.md`, "Repairing an artifact declaration after an
approval", case 1). No exclusion was widened to avoid a re-review.

### Justification corrections (revision 2, round 1 findings I2 and O1)

Round 1 read the justifications as this item's reasoning — which is what
the sentence above invites — and found five that were unmodified
`workflow-v2-1-core` boilerplate describing, in four cases, the **opposite**
of this milestone's constraints. All five were verified verbatim in the
file and all five are rewritten:

| Set | Entry | What the inherited text claimed | Why it was wrong |
|---|---|---|---|
| plan `excluded_prefixes` | `.claude/commands/` | "workflow command files this milestone creates … or modifies (the eight existing v1 commands)" | this milestone must **never** modify `.claude/commands/`; the brief and this plan's own non-change 1 both say so |
| plan `excluded_prefixes` | `scripts/` | "this milestone's own tooling scripts, present … and future (WF1a's state validator)" | `scripts/` is frozen v2.3.1 content this milestone must never touch, and the Controller never even imports it |
| plan `excluded_paths` | `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | cites "the protected `docs/TECHNICAL_DECISIONS.md`" and "unrelated Android build/lint/test steps" | neither file exists in this repository, and `docs/TECHNICAL_DECISIONS.md` is *excluded*, not protected, four entries above in the same file |
| plan `excluded_paths` | `CLAUDE.md` | "WF4a-ii's gate-count depointer" | a `workflow-v2-1-core` checkpoint, not this milestone's |
| plan `excluded_prefixes` | `docs/adr/` | the generic "product/repository content outside this process work item's declared scope" | contradicts this plan's own non-change 2, which says `docs/adr/` is inherited and **wanted** because CP9 writes an ADR there (O1) |

These are **justification-value** edits only — no set key was added,
removed or renamed. Per `REVIEW_PROTOCOL.md`'s "Repairing an artifact
declaration after an approval" table, a value-only change does not move
either stage's `review_content_id`, and this was verified empirically
before and after the edit: the plan-stage digest was identical across it.
Round 1 independently reproduced the same result. So the record is now
accurate without any classification having changed, which is the outcome
to want — a misdescribed classification is exactly how salvage audit
`B4`/`I8` says these go wrong later.

**Three deliberate non-changes**, stated so the reviewer can see they were
considered rather than missed:

1. **`.claude/commands/` and `scripts/` stay excluded at both stages.** They
   are workflow-manager-managed frozen Workflow v2.3.1 files this milestone
   must never modify, and a Manager update to them must never stale this
   item's approvals. `docs/ACTIVE_MILESTONE.md` requires exactly this.
2. **The inherited Android-shaped implementation-stage entries (`app/`,
   `gradle/`, `config/`, `build.gradle.kts`, `gradlew`, `gradlew.bat`,
   `gradle.properties`, `settings.gradle.kts`, `docs/DOMAIN_GLOSSARY.md`,
   `docs/UX_FLOWS.md`) are left as generated.** None of these paths exists
   in this repository and none will be created by this milestone.
   Protected-but-absent costs nothing at the implementation stage, where
   only *changed* ∩ *protected* is measured (`AbsentProtectedPathError` is
   a plan-stage-only rule), and the plan stage never reads the
   implementation-stage half at all. Removing them would be a change to the
   reviewed classification sets for no behavioural benefit. `docs/adr/` is
   inherited and *wanted*: CP9 writes an ADR there.
3. **`.claude/` outside `commands/` is left unclassified.** The only file
   there is `settings.local.json`, which `.gitignore` now covers, so it can
   never enter a diff. A future tracked `.claude/settings.json` would fail
   closed, which is the correct default; pre-emptively excluding a
   directory this milestone will not touch would be an unjustified
   widening.

## Technical decisions

`/milestone-plan` step 5 requires this plan to be checked against every
"Open decision" row in `docs/TECHNICAL_DECISIONS.md` that it touches.
**That file does not exist in this repository** (`git ls-files` confirms),
so there are no open decision rows and nothing is being silently finalised
there.

This plan does, however, make architectural choices that a reviewer should
treat as decisions rather than details. They are recorded in
`docs/adr/0001-controller-generation-1-architecture.md` during CP9 rather
than in a `TECHNICAL_DECISIONS.md` this repository does not use, and the
four most consequential are:

1. **Workflow Manager verdicts are taken from exit codes, not parsed
   prose.** Alternative rejected: parsing `status`/`verify` output. That
   would re-derive drift semantics from strings, which the brief forbids,
   and would break on any Manager output change.
2. **The Controller never writes Workflow state, enforced by a containment
   guard rather than by convention.** Alternative rejected: allowing the
   Controller to "repair" obviously-broken state. The brief forbids it and
   the failure mode (a Controller silently fixing a state file a human
   needs to see) is severe.
3. **Persist-before-launch.** Alternative rejected: recording the job after
   the worker returns, which is simpler but makes an interrupted run
   indistinguishable from a run that never started.
4. **Handoff triggers on generation number, not commit inequality.**
   Alternative rejected: treating any new commit as a handoff, which would
   stop the Controller on every ordinary development commit and make it
   unusable as its own supervisor.

## Risks, and how this plan handles them

| Risk | Handling |
|---|---|
| The real `claude` worker is slow, expensive or flaky, making the suite unusable | every worker test uses `tests/fake_claude.py`; the real binary is exercised once, in an opt-in test, and its evidence recorded |
| `workflow-manager` output format changes | only exit codes are interpreted; text is stored, never parsed |
| `AWAITING_EXTERNAL_IMPLEMENTATION_REVIEW` hosts several duties | after revision 10 the Controller only *reports* there, so a misclassification costs a human one wasted step rather than a wrong durable write — which is the whole reason the narrowing was taken |
| The narrowed scope is quietly re-widened by a later checkpoint | two set-wide assertions, both able to fail: CP4's tests `automatic=False` at all five report-only phases and `automatic=True` at the six automatic triples, two-directionally; CP6's launches a sentinel-creating worker binary and asserts no sentinel exists at any of the five. Re-widening is a deliberate test change, never a silent one. (Revisions 10–12 stated this as *"return no action"*, which is false for the two declined phases — they name their action deliberately — and as *"`decide()` launches no worker"*, which is vacuous) |
| An unclassified deliverable path fails a projection mid-implementation | the artifacts declaration was corrected before this bundle was generated; `.gitignore` gains `.controller/` in CP1 before any Controller run |
| CP6 was the largest checkpoint and could overrun a session | resolved in revision 2: the execute-and-record / post-state-validation seam is pre-declared as CP6 (complexity **5** today; 4 as declared then) and CP6B (complexity **3** today; 2 from revision 10's narrowing until revision 62, and 3 when first declared) rather than left to a mid-implementation plan revision. Their dependencies (CP2–CP5) each land fully tested first, so both are composition rather than invention |
| The pre-existing `workflow_integration_test.py` error masks a real regression | the baseline table above names the exact test; CP9's gate is "no new failures relative to it", and any second failure is a regression |
| `--pause-file` test surface leaks into production use | it is undocumented in `README.md`, checked only at the orchestration boundary, and flagged here for the reviewer to challenge |
| The Controller could be pointed at this repository and edit its own source while running | CP1 executes every non-read-only command from an immutable, content-verified snapshot under `<runtime root>/source/<tree_digest>/`, so an edit to the origin worktree cannot reach the running process by any import or resource read — a property of the import root the re-exec constructs with `-P`, **not** of `PYTHONPATH`, which the process's working directory outranks for `python -m` and which was all revision 32 set (revision 33, local round 32's `OPUS-R32-B1`); a dirty source refuses outright unless `--allow-dirty-source` snapshots the working tree under a content digest with no commit; CP8's handoff stops the run when the approved generation moves |

## Explicitly out of scope

Generation 2; broad Controller lifecycle automation; review-convergence
automation; RepFlow orchestration; remote fleet management; daemons; cloud
workers; GUIs; web services. No checkpoint above expands this boundary, and
`REQ-14` maps the boundary to CP1 and CP9 so it is a reviewed requirement
rather than a note.

Two adjacent things this plan also does **not** do, called out because they
are natural next steps someone might expect here: it does not add a second
`work_items` entry or otherwise drive this repository's own Workflow with
the Controller (Generation 1 supervises *other* repositories and a
disposable fixture), and it does not attempt to fix the frozen Workflow
release's `workflow_integration_test.py` portability defect.

**A document-structure commitment for the next generation** (revision 32,
external round 31's `EXT-PLAN-R31-O2`, recorded here rather than only in a
disposition row so that the generation it binds will actually read it):
**Generation 2's plan document keeps its normative design and checkpoint
contract separate from its review-disposition history** — the dispositions
go in a non-normative appendix or a sibling artifact, not inline in the
document a fresh reviewer reads as the design. This plan is not
restructured to that shape, on the finding's own instruction not to reopen
a revision solely to shorten it; the commitment binds the next document,
where it costs nothing. The reason is measurable in this one: of sixty-six
rounds, the twelve local rounds from 20 through 31 found no Blocking design
defect and their findings were overwhelmingly about this document's
commentary on itself, which is review effort spent on a surface that has no
effect on what gets built. Rounds 32 through 36 are the counter-examples that
keep the commitment honest rather than absolute: reading the same document,
each found a Blocking defect in the immediately preceding revision's own new
material — round 32 in revision 32's mechanism, round 33 in revision 33's
evidence layer for it, round 34 in the one thing neither had run, which is
the mechanism's own first execution, round 35 in the two places revision 35
wrote new material without running it against the document and the machine
it describes, and round 36 in revision 36's **bookkeeping** about material
whose design it measured and found intact — which is exactly the finding a
reader reaches sooner when the design is not interleaved with thirty rounds
of commentary about itself. Round 36 is also the first of the five whose
findings touch no mechanism at all, and that distinction is the one this
document's own convergence argument now turns on. **Round 37 is not a sixth
counter-example, and it is the strongest evidence for this commitment in the
record** (revision 38, local round 37's `OPUS-R37-B1`): its Blocking finding
is not in the preceding revision's new material at all but in **revision
34**'s, which three consecutive verification records certified green by
describing the occurrence set rather than extracting it — and it touches no
mechanism either. A self-audit that goes unrun for three revisions inside the
very document it audits is the failure mode this commitment predicts, and it
is why revision 38 makes that audit smaller rather than more elaborate.
**Revision 61 does not revisit this commitment or move any content** — it
adopts the historical disposition provenance policy stated just before
"Plan review round 1 — disposition", below, which is narrower than physical
separation and answers a different question: not where the disposition
history lives, but which sentences in it are still live proof obligations.
That policy is the same self-audit-going-unrun failure mode round 37 found,
recurring six more times (rounds 56 through 60) in the growing apparatus
that re-verified this document's own commentary; its fix is to stop treating
a past round's commentary as a live claim, not to relocate it.

**Concurrent Controller runs against one runtime root** (revision 33, local
round 32's `OPUS-R32-O2`). Generation 1 assumes one Controller process per
runtime root at a time. It takes no lock and does not serialise; two
overlapping runs that materialise the same `tree_digest` from different
provenance would otherwise cross their identity metadata through the shared
`SOURCE_PIN.json`. The consequence is bounded — `tree_digest` identifies the
executed bytes exactly either way — and the crossing is turned into a
refusal rather than a silent mis-attribution by the handoff cross-check in
`materialise()` step 3. Making concurrency actually safe is Generation 2's.

## Self-review record

`SELF_REVIEWING_PLAN` was performed against this plan and the following
changes were folded in rather than left for the reviewer to find:

1. **The verification command set was wrong.** The first draft inherited
   `milestone-implement.md` step 3's Gradle commands. This repository has no
   Gradle. CP9 now names the real Python command set, and the plan records
   why the command file's own text does not apply.
2. **A pre-existing red suite would have looked like a regression.** The
   baseline table and the `workflow_integration_test.py` analysis were added
   after actually running all seven suites at `base_commit`, and CP9's gate
   was reworded from "everything green" to "no worse than baseline".
3. **`.controller/` had no `.gitignore` entry in the first draft's CP1**,
   which would have made the first Controller run poison the bundle diff.
   It is now an explicit, ordered CP1 requirement *and* a both-stage
   exclusion.
4. **`.workflow-manager/` was unclassified at both stages.** A Manager
   update would have failed the projection closed. Now excluded at both
   stages with a justification.
5. **`AWAITING_EXTERNAL_IMPLEMENTATION_REVIEW` was originally a single row**
   in CP4's mapping. Re-reading `MILESTONE_WORKFLOW.md`'s "Vocabulary
   states" showed it is also where the technical-approval gate sits; the
   disambiguation and its tests were added.
6. **`AWAITING_FUNCTIONAL_REVIEW` was originally marked purely manual**,
   which would have wedged a supervised run: `/prepare-functional-review`
   has to run first, and it is automatable. Now conditional, with both
   sub-cases tested.
7. **The user-only denylist was originally only in CP4.** A hand-written
   task string could still have reached the worker, so CP5 gained the second
   enforcement layer and CP4 gained a *total* assertion over every phase
   rather than a spot check.
8. **`AMBIGUOUS` was originally folded into `FAILURE`** in the worker
   outcome classification. Separating it is what lets **CP5 classify and
   CP6 report** what actually happened — a failure is the worker saying it
   could not do the job, an ambiguous result is the Controller admitting it
   cannot tell — which are different human responses to the same exit code.
   **It buys CP7 nothing, and since revision 18 that is deliberate**: both
   outcomes fail step 8's first clause, both reconcile to `FAILED`, both
   are terminal and neither is ever relaunched, differing only in the
   evidence string. The retry/no-retry distinction CP7 makes is between the
   `INTERRUPTED` *status*, which permits a fresh `step`, and `FAILED`,
   which does not — not between two worker outcomes (round 18's I3;
   revisions 2–18 claimed the CP7 distinction, and revision 18's own fix is
   what made the claim false).
9. **The handoff test was originally in-process.** That cannot demonstrate
   "the running process did not reload", because the test and the subject
   would share a module cache. It is now a real subprocess test, which is
   what forced `--pause-file` into existence — and that is flagged as a
   reviewer challenge point rather than buried.
10. **Requirement coverage was originally 15 capability requirements.** The
    eighteen named testing requirements were not individually traceable, so
    `REQ-T1`–`REQ-T18` were added, one per brief list entry, and bidirectional
    coverage is now machine-validated.

## Historical disposition provenance policy (adopted at revision 61)

This policy is scoped by **kind of paragraph**, not by where that
paragraph physically sits in the document — a range description under-
and over-reaches the set below, `OPUS-R61-B2`. Three kinds of paragraph
are a **frozen historical record**, not currently normative design and
not a set of continuously re-verified claims, wherever in this document
they appear: every per-round disposition table (below, and any future
one); each "What revision *N* changed" entry in "Specific areas the
reviewer should challenge"; and that section's own challenge-question
answers where they recount a past round's finding. Each sentence in them
was true, and reproducible, as of the round and revision that wrote it,
and that is what it continues to assert going forward.

**Explicitly excluded, despite sitting physically inside the span these
three kinds mostly occupy: the round-46 "Missing tests this walk's own
self-application surfaces" block, below** (`OPUS-R61-B2`). That block is
live, forward-looking checkpoint-specification text, not a disposition
table, a "What revision *N* changed" entry, or a challenge answer — the
live design region cites it normatively by cross-reference at several
sites (items (5), (16), (17) and (18) among them), and those citations
are unaffected by this policy and remain normative. Only the items this
policy's fourth point names as retired (items (14), (15) and (20)
through (26), each now marked at its own definition site in that block)
are no longer live; every other item in the block is unaffected.

**This is a bounded, operator-directed structural response to round 60's
review** (`OPUS-R60-B1`, `-I1`, `-I2`), not a new review finding and not a
weakening of anything any of the three findings caught. Round 60's
Blocking finding was real: the `OPUS-R58-I1` disposition row (round 58's
table, below) asserted a present-tense fact about "this bundle" that had
stopped being true the moment a later revision touched the file it
measured. Rounds 56 through 60 record five further findings of the
*same* shape — `OPUS-R56-B1`, `OPUS-R57-B1`, `OPUS-R58-B1`, `OPUS-R59-B1`
and this one, plus the two enumeration/scope findings `OPUS-R59-I1`,
`OPUS-R59-I2`, `OPUS-R60-I1` and `OPUS-R60-I2` — each one either a stale
reproduction or a miscounted enumeration inside this document's *own
account of its review history*, never inside the Controller's design.
That is a closed class with one root cause: text about a past round was
written and checked as if it were a live, continuously-reproducible claim
about the current bundle, and every later revision that touched the
surrounding document put that reproducibility at risk again. Answering
each instance with another missing-tests item — the apparatus reached
items (14) through (26), two standing rules and a "restated sites"
enumeration by round 60 — treated the symptom at the rate new instances of
the same cause kept appearing, which is why round 60's own review named
the apparatus "self-generating" and suggested, as an operator decision
rather than a review finding, exactly the resolution adopted here.

**The fix is the distinction itself, made explicit and enforced going
forward, rather than another repair layer:**

1. **A disposition row, a "What revision *N* changed" entry, or a
   challenge answer that names a past round is provenance.** It
   documents what a specific reviewer found and what was done about it,
   as of that round. It is not re-run, not re-counted, and not required
   to keep reproducing against a document that has grown around it
   since — that is what "historical" means. `OPUS-R59-I2`'s and
   `OPUS-R60-I1`'s "restated sites" enumerations, and `OPUS-R60-I2`'s
   standing-rule-scope audit, are exactly this kind of claim (a count of
   how many *other* historical sites use a given phrase) and are retired
   as live proof obligations under this rule — see "Plan review round 60
   — disposition", below.
2. **A sentence is a live, current-bundle claim, subject to grep/count
   reproduction each round, only if it is written in the present tense
   about "this bundle" or "the current bundle" and does not name the
   round or revision it was measured at.** Everything else in a
   paragraph of one of the three covered kinds is written in the past
   tense or names its own round/revision explicitly, and is provenance
   under point 1. Outside those three kinds of paragraph — including the
   round-46 "Missing tests" block, excluded above — the Controller's own
   architecture and checkpoint text, the registry/mapping, and this
   policy's own governing text remain fully live and are unaffected by
   this change.
3. **A historical row is corrected, not left standing, exactly when it is
   miscategorised** — when it makes a present-tense claim about "this
   bundle" without naming which bundle, as the `OPUS-R58-I1` row did.
   That is `OPUS-R60-B1`, repaired at its site, below, by restating the
   row in the explicit historical-provenance form this policy states
   generally, rather than by widening its published figure to match one
   more regeneration — the corrective round 60's own required repair
   explicitly warned against, since a widened figure is a function of how
   many times a self-referential section quotes itself and would be
   stale again at revision 62.
4. **The counting apparatus that existed only to keep historical rows
   honest — standing rules 1 and 2 in `TEST_RESULTS.md`, and
   missing-tests items (14), (15) and (20) through (26) in this
   document's own round-46 "Missing tests this walk's own
   self-application surfaces" block, below — is retired as of this
   revision, not replaced one-for-one.** `TEST_RESULTS.md`'s proof
   obligations from revision 61 onward are the load-bearing ones already
   stated at its own §1 and §2 — the frozen conformance suites and
   `workflow-manager verify` — plus registry/mapping regeneration and the
   registry-table re-embed, plus reproduction of whatever the *current*
   round's own new, present-tense prose claims. §0 is no longer a
   growing, self-referential sweep over rounds 1–60's disposition text;
   a round with a structural finding like this one states its own
   resolution directly, and a round with an ordinary content finding
   states and reproduces that finding's own repair, the same way every
   checkpoint's own findings always have been. A parallel, open-ended
   enumeration of "every command with a published figure anywhere in the
   plan" (round 60's own missing-tests item 1) is exactly the kind of
   obligation that scales with document size and history length rather
   than with what changed, which is what this policy exists to stop
   generating; it is not added.

**What this does not change.** No Controller architecture, checkpoint,
requirement, invariant, or test specification is touched by this policy —
see "Plan review round 60 — disposition", below, for the one content
correction it makes (`OPUS-R60-B1`) and that section's own list of what
stays unaudited. The registry and mapping are unaffected: no checkpoint,
requirement or complexity changes at this revision. `workflow-manager
verify` still confirms frozen Workflow v2.3.1 untouched. This is a change
to how this document's *account of its own review history* is written and
checked from here forward, not to what it is a history of, and it is
narrower than, and does not revisit, the Generation-2 document-structure
commitment stated earlier in "Explicitly out of scope" — that commitment
is about where the disposition history lives; this policy is about which
sentences in it, wherever it lives, are still live proof obligations.

command being partial-progress. It looked for a fifth asymmetry cutting the

verdict: *"the reassessment is sound and I would not want it reversed"*.

phases changed category in one edit and the structures that consume a
category were not revisited. *A scope reduction is a change to the same
class of declared data as a scope addition, and this plan's own discipline
applies to it symmetrically.* That is the rule revision 11 takes from this
round, and it is the third in the family — round 5's "name every reader",
round 6's "name every writer and where it is captured", and now: **it
applies to removals as much as additions.**

## Plan review round 31 — disposition (both stages)

Round 31 is the first round in which **both** stages of the two-stage
protocol ran. `LOCAL_MODEL_PLAN_REVIEW` reviewed bundle `abf8c1fa…` at plan
revision 31 and returned **`APPROVE`** with no Blocking, no Important and 3
Optional findings — the first `APPROVE` in thirty-one rounds.
`MANUAL_EXTERNAL_PLAN_REVIEW` then reviewed the same bundle at the same
`review_content_id` and returned `REVISE` with **1 Blocking, 1 Important
and 2 Optional** — four findings, and the first Blocking finding since
round 19.

The running count of rounds with nothing Blocking stays at **thirteen**:
round 31's local stage found none, but its external stage found one, so
this round does not join them. That is also the concrete answer to round
30's challenge question 6, which asked whether further rounds were buying
anything. The local stage's last Blocking finding was round 19's, twelve
rounds earlier; the external reviewer, reading the same bytes, found an
evidence gap and a live invariant weakness, neither of which is
disposition commentary. **The two stages disagreeing is the protocol
working rather than a defect in either.**

| Finding | Disposition (each verified against the file before this row was written) |
|---|---|
| **`EXT-PLAN-R31-B1`** (Blocking) — the external review bundle omits the frozen sources the plan derives its command, gate and transition claims from | **Accepted, and answered with a stated derivation rule rather than a hand-picked list**, because a set chosen by judgement is exactly what the finding distrusts. `CONTEXT_FILES.txt` now carries three mechanically re-derivable clauses: **(i)** *every* path `.workflow-manager/installation.json` lists as `managed` under `.claude/commands/` or `scripts/` — the complete frozen v2.3.1 command and tooling surface, **fifteen** command files and **thirteen** `scripts/` files, byte-for-byte as installed, which is a superset of every authority the finding names, including the two command files this document never names by slash-command; **(ii)** every other tracked repository path this document cites by name that is neither this item's own protected content nor already carried by the diff, which is `README.md` alone — `MILESTONE_WORKFLOW.md`, `PLAN_REVIEW_WORKFLOW.md` and `REVIEW_PROTOCOL.md` have been listed since revision 1; and **(iii)** `docs/ai-workflow/WORKFLOW_V2_1_OPERATOR_REFERENCE.md`, which this document cites nowhere and which is included anyway because it is the frozen operator description of the phase/command surface the finding's own re-review focus asks to be re-derived independently. Clause (i) is checkable against a file the bundle already contained, so the reviewer can verify completeness without trusting this row. **No frozen file was modified to make any of this easier**: the bundle copies are of the installed bytes, and `workflow-manager verify` is re-run against the regenerated bundle's HEAD as part of this round's evidence |
| **`EXT-PLAN-R31-I1`** (Important) — `--allow-dirty-source` and mutable-source execution contradict the immutable generation identity REQ-9 claims | **Accepted on all three limbs, and the model is changed rather than the wording.** The finding is right that `pin()` recorded a commit while the interpreter imported from the mutable worktree, that a `--allow-dirty-source` run recorded a clean `HEAD` that did not identify the executed bytes, and that CP8's test proved only that an *already-loaded* behaviour did not change. The route taken is the finding's **first**, strengthened by the second rather than chosen against it: **every non-read-only command executes from an immutable, content-verified snapshot** under `<runtime root>/source/<tree_digest>/`, materialised from a clean `HEAD` or — under `--allow-dirty-source`, whose meaning changes rather than disappearing — from the working tree with a `null` commit and a content-addressed identity, which is the finding's own second-listed remedy for the dirty case. Eager loading and a no-late-resource-read scan are kept as an *independent* second argument, not as the primary one. Locations changed: CP1's identity block in full (the dataclass, the closed `source_kind` enumeration, the positive guard and the two mechanisms that carry it — `cli.main`'s materialise-and-re-exec and `require_pinned_execution()`'s entry assertion — `materialise()`, `pin()`'s snapshot branch, the generation-source rule, the re-exec and its structural termination argument, eager loading, the no-late-read scan, and seven new tests); the refusal taxonomy (`SourceSnapshotError`); the runtime-state tree (`source/<tree_digest>/`); the runtime-root default and containment paragraphs; the job-record schema (`controller_source_dirty` **removed**, `controller_source_tree_digest` added, `controller_source_commit` now nullable); CP6's `execute_step` signature, its `PLANNED`-flush identity-block bullet and its record-content test sentence; CP8's approved-generation rule, its no-hot-reload paragraph (three ways → **four**), its historical `--allow-dirty-source` sentence (marked, not rewritten) and its subprocess test (a new step 7 with three assertions); CP9's global-option list and integration-test step 4; the risk table's own row; and the checkpoint table's follow-up sentence, since CP1 rises 3 → 4 in the registry |
| **`EXT-PLAN-R31-O1`** (Optional) — require the installation profile Generation 1 actually supports | **Accepted, and the contract the finding could not see was measured rather than assumed.** Workflow Manager 2.3.1 defines exactly two install profiles, `runtime` and `full`, and both install its whole `distribution` category — which contains every `.claude/commands/*.md` and every `scripts/` file. Only `full` adds the `conformance` category, and nothing in it is read by the Controller. So the answer is not the finding's first branch (refuse everything but `full`) nor its second (assert `full` is the only profile): **both** profiles are supported, and CP2 gates on the `(workflow_version, profile)` **pair** as one closed set, `SUPPORTED_INSTALLATIONS`, checked before any command file or Workflow state is read. A profile the Manager adds later is refused until it has been measured. Locations changed: CP2 step 5, CP2's second design bullet, CP2's test list (three new cases, one of them pinning the ordering by making CP3's own failure the tell), the Environment-facts table (one new measured row), the refusal taxonomy (`UnsupportedInstallProfileError`) and the registry, where CP2's name is widened from "unsupported-version" to "unsupported-installation" refusals — the only checkpoint rename in thirty-two revisions when revision 32 wrote this row, and still the only one; the live sentence names no number, since this one grows every round — recorded in the checkpoint table's follow-up sentence |

The commitment is recorded where a later generation will read it rather than only here: see "Explicitly out of scope". Revision 32's own edits are confined to mechanism and to the two stale-commentary items round 31's local stage had already identified, so this round adds one disposition section and changes no other historical one |

## Plan review round 32 — disposition (`LOCAL_MODEL_PLAN_REVIEW`)

Round 32 reviewed bundle `01890b51…` at plan revision 32 and returned
`REVISE` with **1 Blocking, 0 Important and 2 Optional** findings — three in
total, and the local stage's first Blocking finding since round 19. The
running count of rounds with nothing Blocking stays at **thirteen**: round
32 does not join them, for the same reason round 31 did not.

**All three are accepted, and all three are mechanism.** The round confirmed
round 31's two external findings as genuinely resolved by re-deriving them
from the frozen sources rather than from this document — the `managed`-set
derivation rule for `CONTEXT_FILES.txt` holds exactly at 15 + 13 = 28 with
all 59 managed files hash-matching, and the two-profile contract was
re-measured from `workflow_manager/release.py` — and then found that
revision 32's *own* new mechanism did not do what its argument claimed.
That is the pattern worth recording: **the defect was not in what revision
32 removed, it was in the replacement, and it was found by measurement
rather than by reading.** Revision 32 wrote "at most one exec can occur, and
the bound is a property of which branch runs rather than of an environment
variable a caller could forge" while depending on an environment variable
(`PYTHONPATH`) that loses a precedence contest it never checked. The
generalisation this document should carry forward: **when a design proves a
property from an environment variable, measure what actually wins the
precedence; and when a test reconstructs its subject's environment instead
of reading it, it cannot see a defect in that environment.**

| Finding | Disposition (each verified against the file before this row was written) |
|---|---|
| **`OPUS-R32-B1`** (Blocking) — the specified re-exec loads the origin worktree, not the snapshot, whenever the invoking directory contains `controller/`; the "at most one exec" bound is false and the failure is an unbounded exec loop | **Accepted in full, and reproduced before it was applied rather than taken from the finding.** `PYTHONPATH=<snap> python3 -m controller` from a directory containing `controller/` resolves to that directory's package, with `sys.path[0]` equal to the invoking directory — so revision 32's child re-entered `pin()`'s `"unpinned"` branch and re-execed without bound, which is neither of the two outcomes the design named. Applied as the finding's own first remedy, which it rightly calls the strongest: the exec passes **`-P`**, and `PYTHONPATH` is **assigned** rather than appended to an inherited value, so the child's `sys.path` is the snapshot plus the standard library and nothing ambient. The termination argument is rebuilt on the two facts that actually deliver it — the constructed import root **(a)** and the branch `SOURCE_PIN.json` selects **(b)** — with revision 32's superseded claim quoted and dated in place rather than deleted. A **refusal-only** fail-safe is added beyond what the finding asked: `WORKFLOW_CONTROLLER_EXEC_HANDOFF` carries an `exec_depth`, and reaching the `"unpinned"` branch with `exec_depth >= 1` is `SourceSnapshotError` — it can only ever refuse, never admit, so it does not reintroduce the trusted marker revision 32 was right to avoid, and it means a future recurrence is a named error instead of a loop. All four of the finding's required acceptance criteria are applied: CP1 test 1 now names its working directory and runs **from the source checkout** (the looping case); new test 8 adds the exec-count case with a *decoy* `controller/` package in the working directory, chosen over a bare counter because it converts "the wrong root was imported" from a timeout into an attributable failure and so cannot be repaired green by pointing the fixture somewhere harmless; CP8 step 2 and CP9 step 4 set their working directories explicitly, with the reason each was previously wrong stated; and CP8 step 7's probe now runs under the child's **recorded** `sys.path` — a new `interpreter_sys_path`/`interpreter_safe_path`/`interpreter_executable` block in `.controller/identity.json`, written by the child from its own interpreter — instead of over a reconstructed `[source_root]`. Challenge questions 2 and 5 are rewritten to ask what is now open rather than what round 32 has closed |
| **`OPUS-R32-O1`** (Optional) — "dirty" is never given a scope, and the two readings differ materially | **Accepted, and resolved toward the pathspec reading rather than the whole-worktree one the finding read out of CP9.** `materialise()` step 1 now names the command: the tree is dirty **iff `git -C <origin> status --porcelain -- controller pyproject.toml` produces any output**, untracked non-ignored files under those paths included. Pathspec scoping is the stronger choice on the model's own terms — the snapshot holds exactly those two paths, so an edit to `docs/`, `tests/` or this plan leaves the extracted bytes byte-identical to `HEAD`, and `source_kind: "commit"` with that commit is then *accurate*; whole-worktree scoping would make `controller_source_commit` null for essentially every development-time launch while the bytes were identified by a commit exactly, which discards the provenance the field exists for. New test 9 pins the rule from both sides — dirt outside the pathspec runs without the flag and records the commit; dirt inside it refuses without the flag — so the scope is asserted rather than left to the implementer. CP9 step 4 is restated to match: the flag is added on the pathspec-scoped condition, and the assertion moves to `controller_source_tree_digest`, which is present under both outcomes |
| **`OPUS-R32-O2`** (Optional) — snapshot reuse rewrites `SOURCE_PIN.json`, so concurrent runs sharing a digest can cross identity metadata | **Accepted, and both halves of the finding's own choice are taken rather than one.** The scope is stated where a reader will find it — "Explicitly out of scope" now says Generation 1 assumes one Controller process per runtime root, takes no lock and does not serialise — *and* the crossing is made loud instead of silent: the child verifies the `source_kind`/`source_commit` it reads from the reused `SOURCE_PIN.json` against the pair its own parent recorded in `WORKFLOW_CONTROLLER_EXEC_HANDOFF`, and refuses with `SourceSnapshotError` on disagreement. That is the finding's second remedy, carried by the variable revision 33 was already adding for the exec-depth fail-safe, so it costs no new surface; and like that check it can only refuse, never admit. The finding's own bound is recorded with it: `tree_digest` identifies the executed bytes exactly under either outcome, which is the property `EXT-PLAN-R31-I1` actually demanded, so what the check buys is that a job record can never quietly attribute one run's bytes to another run's commit |

## Plan review round 33 — disposition (`LOCAL_MODEL_PLAN_REVIEW`)

Round 33 reviewed bundle `1c8bc51a…` at plan revision 33 and returned
`REVISE` with **1 Blocking, 2 Important and 3 Optional** findings — six in
total, the largest round since 16 and the second consecutive local round
with a Blocking finding. The running count of rounds with nothing Blocking
stays at **thirteen**.

**All six are accepted; none is rejected, deferred or narrowed.** The round
confirmed revision 33's central repair by rebuilding round 32's simulation
against it rather than by reading it — exec count exactly 1, `safe_path`
true in the child, `sys.path[0]` the snapshot, an inherited hostile
`PYTHONPATH` neutralised by assignment — and confirmed the two Optional
dispositions from round 32 as applied mechanism. What it then found was
**one layer out from the repair**: of the nine tests revision 33 wrote to
pin the immutable-execution model, one asserted a property that is false in
this plan's own default configuration, three read an instrument the document
never defined, and one named an error the specified path cannot raise. Each
was established by running it.

That is the pattern worth recording, and it is round 32's lesson displaced
by exactly one layer: **revision 32 argued a mechanism it had not measured,
and revision 33 measured the mechanism but not the evidence written to
demonstrate it.** A test is code, and specifying one is specifying a
mechanism; the same standard the document applies to `sys.path` claims —
*run it, do not read it* — applies to the assertion that observes them.
The generalisation to carry forward: **an assertion must be checked against
a correct build, not only against the defect it was written for; a test that
names an instrument obliges the document to define that instrument; and a
branch word like "otherwise" is a specification of every state it covers, not
only of the one its author had in mind.**

| Finding | Disposition (each verified against the file before this row was written) |
|---|---|
| **`OPUS-R33-B1`** (Blocking) — the pinned child's recorded `sys.path` is asserted never to lie inside the origin checkout, but the runtime root defaults to `<origin>/.controller`, so `sys.path[0]` always does; CP1 test 1 is unsatisfiable against a correct implementation | **Accepted in full, and the contradiction was reproduced at the plan's own default layout before it was applied.** With no `--runtime-dir`, the snapshot is `<origin>/.controller/source/<tree_digest>/` and it is `sys.path[0]`, so revision 33's sentence asserted of one and the same entry both that it equals `source_root` and that it is not inside the origin tree. Applied as the finding's own required fix and in its narrower-and-stronger form: the property is restated as **no entry is the origin checkout root, and no entry lies inside the checkout other than the snapshot the Controller itself constructed under `<runtime_root>/source/`** — which forbids the one entry that would reintroduce the mutable package and admits exactly one exception, a directory named by the digest of the bytes in it. The correction is made in the **identity bullet**, which is the sentence CP1 tests 1 and 8 and CP8 step 7 all derive from, and carried into both CP1 tests. Test 1 takes the finding's first branch rather than its second: it runs at the **default** runtime root, named explicitly, because that is the layout an operator actually gets — the cheapest repair of the old assertion was to pass `--runtime-dir` outside the checkout, which would have greened the test by moving it off the only case worth covering, this document's own recurring class. CP8 step 7 keeps its unqualified *"inside the clone"* form and now states **why** it is satisfiable there — step 2 passes `--runtime-dir <tmp>` outside the clone — so the two cases between them cover the default and the relocated layout, and neither reads as a contradiction of the other |
| **`OPUS-R33-I1`** (Important) — "the exec counter" is the instrument three tests assert on, and the plan defines it nowhere; without it, "at most one exec" is not measured by anything | **Accepted, and resolved by the finding's own cheapest form.** `.controller/identity.json` gains **`exec_depth`** — the integer the process read from `WORKFLOW_CONTROLLER_EXEC_HANDOFF` at entry, or `0` when absent — recorded alongside the three interpreter fields and written **before** the child deletes the variable, which the fail-safe bullet now says. It needs no new plumbing: the value is already in the handoff variable and the record already exists so that a claim about `sys.path` is checkable from outside the process. The reason a *count* is required rather than the three fields already there is stated with it — a build that execs three times and still ends pinned is byte-identical in `source_root`, `interpreter_safe_path` and `interpreter_sys_path` to one that execs once, so only a depth separates them, and the at-most-one bound is the whole termination argument. Tests 1 and 8 now read that field by name. **Test 2 is answered differently and deliberately**, because the finding asked how *"no exec occurred"* is observed when no child is ever created: it runs **in process**, and the assertion is that `cli.main` raised `DirtyControllerSourceError` and returned control at all — `os.execv` never returns, so a call that comes back is itself the proof, and it is a stronger instrument than a record a replaced process could not have written |
| **`OPUS-R33-I2`** (Important) — `materialise()` step 4 `os.replace`s onto an existing snapshot directory whenever step 3's verification fails; that raises `OSError: [Errno 39] Directory not empty`, not a named refusal — and it is exactly the state CP1 test 5 constructs | **Accepted, and resolved toward refusal rather than rebuild.** Step 4 is split into the two states its *"otherwise"* silently covered: the directory does not exist — publish by `os.replace`, unchanged — or it exists and fails step 3's verification, which now discards the temporary tree and refuses with `SourceSnapshotError` naming the directory and the binding that failed, leaving the directory **untouched**. Refusal is chosen over silently rebuilding because a snapshot that does not match its own name is evidence of tampering or of an interrupted publish, and rebuilding destroys that evidence while the recovery — delete the named directory — stays an explicit human act. This was the one refusal path in the design that did not end in a `ControllerError`, in a taxonomy whose whole premise is that every refusal is named and mapped to an exit code. Step 3 gains an explicit definition of **verifies** — the recomputed digest equals both the directory's own name and its `SOURCE_PIN.json`'s recorded `tree_digest` — because step 4 now branches on its outcome. CP1 test 5 is restated to name the error the specified path actually raises, the entry point (`materialise()`, not `pin()`) and the exit code (20), with a third case added for `pin()`'s own side of the binding, where the entry point genuinely is `pin()` |
| **`OPUS-R33-O1`** (Optional) — test 8's invocation route is unspecified, and the obvious one imports the decoy in the *parent*; the claim that the case is "an unbounded exec loop" under revision 32 is also inaccurate for a decoy | **Accepted, both halves, and the route was measured across all three candidates.** The route is now named — the installed `workflow-controller` console script — in **both** tests 1 and 8, with the reason: for a script Python prepends the *script's* directory rather than the working directory, so the parent loads the installed Controller and the child stays the process under test, whereas `python -m controller` from the decoy directory imports the decoy in the parent (`RuntimeError: DECOY IMPORTED`, exit 1, out of `runpy`) and `python -P -m` hands the parent the flag under test. CP8 step 2 and CP9 keep `python -P -m` with an explicit `PYTHONPATH`, which is correct there and for a different reason: those steps must select a specific *clone* as the origin, which a console script cannot express. The second half is a correction rather than an addition: revision 33's *"under revision 32's specification this case is an unbounded exec loop"* contradicted its own next sentence, since a decoy that raises on import kills the child on the **first** exec — the looping case is test 1's, and the pair's division of labour is now stated instead of overlapping |
| **`OPUS-R33-O2`** (Optional) — the re-exec appends `--runtime-dir` after the subcommand, while CP9 declares it a global option; argparse answers `unrecognized arguments` and exits 2 | **Accepted, and it is upgraded in consequence rather than in classification.** The finding calls it Optional because the failure is loud at the first `step`; what makes it worth applying exactly as written is that exit **2** is *"CLI usage error (argparse default)"* in this document's own contract, so the Controller's own construction would have been reported as the operator's typo — and read that way by an outer supervisor, which is the audience the exit codes exist for. The resolved `--runtime-dir` now precedes `argv[1:]` in the child argv, and any caller-supplied `--runtime-dir` is dropped from what follows, in both the `--runtime-dir X` and `--runtime-dir=X` spellings: the resolved absolute value supersedes it, and leaving both in argv would make the child's runtime root depend on argparse's last-wins ordering rather than on what the parent resolved. CP9's CLI surface now states that global options are declared on the top-level parser and accepted only before the subcommand, which is the fact the exec argv is built around |
| **`OPUS-R33-O3`** (Optional) — `tree_digest` is specified as a hash over concatenated paths and bytes with no delimiter and no mode, where this repository's own bundle identifier does both | **Accepted, and pointed at the answer already in this repository rather than at an invented encoding.** Step 2 now hashes the canonical JSON serialisation of a **mapping** keyed by POSIX repository-relative path, each entry carrying `mode` and the file's content `sha256` **separately** — exactly `workflow_fingerprint.compute_bundle_id`'s shape, which this plan already cites elsewhere and which solves both halves for the same reasons. The ambiguity was real if uninteresting (`ab`/`c` and `a`/`bc` hash alike; two trees differing only in an executable bit share a directory), and the reason to spend a clause on it is that this is the field the entire immutable-execution model is identified by. `SOURCE_PIN.json`'s exclusion from the mapping is restated where the mapping is defined, since step 3's reuse-verification recomputes over the same rule |

## Plan review round 34 — disposition (`LOCAL_MODEL_PLAN_REVIEW`)

Round 34 reviewed bundle `ae635f43…` at plan revision 34 and returned
`REVISE` with **3 Blocking, 1 Important and 2 Optional** findings — six in
total, matching round 33, and the third consecutive local round with a
Blocking finding. The running count of rounds with nothing Blocking stays at
**thirteen**.

**All six are accepted; none is rejected, deferred or narrowed.** The round
confirmed all six of round 33's repairs as applied mechanism, each verified
against the file rather than read off the disposition table, and re-derived
every mechanical claim revision 34 makes. What it then found is the layer
neither of the two preceding rounds had reached: **revision 33 measured the
mechanism, revision 34 repaired the evidence written to demonstrate it, and
nobody had run the mechanism's own first execution.** Built literally from
this document's own text — step 2's mapping, step 3's verification
definition, step 4's two states, `pin()`'s two-way binding, the `-P` re-exec
— the design refuses on its first pinned run, because importing `controller`
out of the snapshot writes `controller/__pycache__/*.pyc` **into** the
snapshot before `pin()` recomputes. The second run then meets revision 34's
own new step-4 refusal branch, working exactly as specified, and refuses
permanently. The central claim — *an immutable, content-verified snapshot* —
was false of the directory as specified, because the act of executing it
modified it.

The generalisation to carry forward, and it is one turn further than round
33's: **a specification of a mechanism is not run until something has run it
twice.** Round 33's lesson was *run the assertion, do not read it*; round 34's
is that a first run and a second run are different experiments, and the state
a correct first run leaves behind is part of the specification whether or not
the document mentions it. Two of this round's other findings are the same
class one layer out again — a repair applied at one of the three places it
belongs (`OPUS-R33-O2` reached the re-exec argv and CP9's declaration but
neither command line this document types), and a coordinate named without
naming the thing that decides its behaviour (*the installed console script*,
across three installation modes of which two make the test red against a
correct build).

| Finding | Disposition (each verified against the file, and each measured on Python 3.14.7, before this row was written) |
|---|---|
| **`OPUS-R34-B1`** (Blocking) — importing the snapshot writes `__pycache__` into it, so `pin()`'s digest recomputation refuses on the first pinned run, and revision 34's new step-4 branch then poisons the snapshot permanently on the second | **Accepted in full, and resolved toward the stronger of the two answers the finding offers, with the choice stated rather than left to the implementer.** Measured first: `PYTHONPATH=<snap> python3 -P -m controller` over a three-module package leaves three `.pyc` files inside `<snap>/controller/__pycache__/`, and the same command with **`-B`** leaves the directory byte-identical. The exec argv gains **`-B`** alongside `-P`, in `argv` and for the same stated reason — it must apply to this exec alone and not to anything the child later launches — so *executing a snapshot cannot change it* and step 2's digest stays literally **total** over the directory with `SOURCE_PIN.json` as its only exclusion. The finding's second answer, excluding `__pycache__/` and `*.py[co]` from the digest, is named and **declined** with its reason: a `.pyc` whose header matches is loaded in preference to the source, so everything that exclusion admits is executable content outside the verified set, and the property this document claims is that the digest covers everything in the snapshot that can execute. Two further clauses close what the choice implies: a snapshot run **directly** by a human takes the same flag (`PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1`), and omitting it poisons that directory by design — the recovery is step 4's own explicit human act; and the **origin** side is stated rather than left to be rediscovered, since the unpinned parent does write bytecode into the checkout, where `git archive`, the not-ignored-copy branch and the `git status --porcelain -- controller pyproject.toml` dirty scope all exclude it because `.gitignore` carries `__pycache__/` and `*.py[cod]` — without which every fixture checkout would read as dirty. **CP1 test 4 is rewritten to be the instrument**, exactly as the finding requires: two real pinned runs rather than two calls to `materialise()`, asserting reuse, the two-way digest binding after each, and that `controller/__pycache__/` does not exist inside the snapshot |
| **`OPUS-R34-B2`** (Blocking) — `OPUS-R33-O2` was applied to the re-exec argv only; CP8 step 2 and CP9 step 4 still pass global options after the subcommand, so both required evidence runs exit 2 | **Accepted, and the finding's own grading argument is adopted rather than the classification round 33 gave the same defect.** Measured against a parser of exactly the shape CP9 declares: `["run","/target","--runtime-dir",…,"--pause-file",…]`, `["step","/tmp/x","--permission-mode",…]` and the same with `--allow-dirty-source` appended all answer `error: unrecognized arguments` and exit **2**; the pre-subcommand forms parse. What makes this Blocking rather than a second Optional is that these are not product code that fails loudly and gets fixed — they are the *specified form* of the plan's two required evidence runs, CP8's end-to-end handoff test (`REQ-T15`/`T16`/`T17`) and CP9's live disposable-repo integration test (`REQ-T18`), the latter an explicit acceptance criterion. Both command lines are corrected in place, each with its measurement recorded beside it, and `--pause-file` is left where it is with the reason (it is `run`'s own option, not a global). The first of the finding's two remedies is taken; the second — declaring the globals on the subparsers too — is declined because it reopens the reasoning the re-exec argv is now built on. **The mechanical check the finding asks for is added as a fourth in-scope half of the document-consistency property**: every command line this document types for the Controller's CLI must parse under `controller.cli`'s own parser object, with the failing/false-positive fixture pair this document requires of every half |
| **`OPUS-R34-B3`** (Blocking) — tests 1 and 8 name "the installed console script" without naming the installation mode, and the plan never says how an unpinned run resolves `origin_source_root`; two of the three modes make both tests red against a correct build | **Accepted, both independent clauses, and all three modes were measured on this machine rather than reasoned about.** `pip install ./checkout` → `Path(__file__).parent.parent` is `…/site-packages`, and `git -C <site-packages> archive HEAD -- controller pyproject.toml` exits **128**; default `pip install -e` → the checkout, with **no** checkout path on the child's `sys.path`; `pip install -e --config-settings editable_mode=compat` → the checkout, **with** the checkout root itself on `sys.path` as a `.pth` entry, which is red against test 1's freshly-repaired containment assertion while the mechanism is doing exactly what this document specifies. **Clause 1**: a new bullet states that an unpinned run's `origin_source_root` **is `pin()`'s own `source_root`**, and draws the boundary that follows — a Controller installed anywhere but its own checkout serves only the three read-only commands — with CP9's CLI surface and `README.md`'s installation section now saying so where they give the install command, since both previously read as though any install were usable for `step`/`run`/`resume`. **Clause 2**: the installation mode becomes test 1's **fourth** named fixture coordinate — a default editable install — with the property it must have stated so a future packaging change is caught rather than silently weakening the test, and test 8 pointed at the same fixture. Naming the mode is chosen over restating the containment assertion to permit the compat entry, which would weaken the one property the test exists for |
| **`OPUS-R34-I1`** (Important) — when `.controller/identity.json` is written is unspecified, and four separate assertions constrain that ordering in incompatible directions | **Accepted, and resolved by stating the rule the finding shows exists, plus correcting the sentence that pointed away from it.** The record is written **exactly once per process, once the pin is resolved and the read-only/pinned guard has passed, immediately before the command body runs** — so `cli.main`'s refusals before dispatch (`DirtyControllerSourceError`, `materialise()`'s `SourceSnapshotError`, the `exec_depth >= 1` fail-safe) write **no** record, which is what makes CP1 test 2's assertion a property rather than an accident and tells test 5 to expect none either, while an unpinned read-only command does write one at `exec_depth: 0`, and CP8 step 3's wait on a **paused** child holds because the record precedes the first orchestration boundary. Revision 34's *"written … before the variable is deleted"* is **corrected**, not merely supplemented: the value is retained in memory at entry, the variable is deleted immediately so nothing launched inherits it, and the record — written later — reports the retained value. The two sentences could not both be satisfied, and the one that had to give is the earlier write |
| **`OPUS-R34-O1`** (Optional) — `PYTHONPATH` is assigned the snapshot and never cleared, so every worker the child launches inherits a `sys.path` entry pointing at the Controller's own code | **Accepted as written.** The finding's own reason for calling it Optional is the right one and is recorded with the fix: nothing collides today, since the snapshot holds only `controller/` and `pyproject.toml` while the frozen tooling imports `workflow_state` and `workflow_fingerprint`. What earns the clause is the unexplained asymmetry — this design reasons twice about not leaking the exec's environment into what the child starts, and `PYTHONPATH` is the one of the three variables that actually names the Controller's code. CP5's `launch()` now passes an explicit `env=` built from `os.environ` with `PYTHONPATH` removed, and the confirmation is added as a **case in an existing test list**, alongside the existing `cwd` and `stdin` cases, rather than as a new test; CP5's complexity is unchanged |
| **`OPUS-R34-O2`** (Optional) — `TEST_RESULTS.md` attributes the baseline run to Python 3.12 while the same file states the only interpreter in the session is 3.14.7 | **Accepted, and corrected at both ends rather than only where the finding found it.** There is no `python3.12` on this machine — `/usr/bin/python3.1*` resolves only to `python3.14`, `command -v python3.12` finds nothing, and `python3` is 3.14.7 — so the attribution was wrong and the results were right, which is why nothing downstream moves. `TEST_RESULTS.md` §5 now names the interpreter that ran. The plan's own baseline section, which made **no** attribution at all, gains one, and CP9's verification gate now requires the re-run to be on the interpreter that table names, since *no worse than the baseline* is a comparison and one made across two interpreters is not one. That CI pins 3.12 is stated as the fact it is, and the absence of a 3.12 measurement is stated rather than papered over |

The finding's reason for grading it above nothing is confirmed too, and is why it is applied rather than deferred: the paragraph it had come to follow ends *"since this rule never **excludes** that name, it only never writes it"*, and the orphan opens *"…since the file is **excluded** from its own digest"* — read in order, with *the file* unbound, the two appear to contradict. The sentence returns to the end of the opening paragraph and is re-wrapped, and its subject is **named** rather than left as *the file*, which is one word more than the finding asks for and is what stops the same drift recurring. finding rests on is exactly as it describes it, in both directions.

and the disposition says so rather than absorbing it.** Revision 38 declared
itself the last revision *whatever round 38 found*, on a count of where
recent Blocking findings had landed. Round 38's Blocking finding is in the

`OPUS-R35-B2`, and one that thirty-eight local rounds did not see. The reason
it did not is structural and is recorded under challenge question 9: this is a
*composition* defect across two frozen commands, visible only by reading their
feedback contracts against each other rather than by reading this document
against itself. That is what the manual external stage is for.

|---|---|

All four required fixes are taken. Feedback validity becomes an **explicit third question** in CP4B alongside staleness and provenance, stated as a per-path clause table rather than one generic rule; the manual column's hard set is `/record-manual-plan-review`'s own clauses **plus** the `WFR-03` ones it never reaches — presence of all three fields, and equality on `Work item:` and `Reviewed base commit:`; a hard failure is non-automatic, names the clause and both values, and launches nothing.
